title: Towards On-Board Implementation of ML-Based Helicopter Weight Estimator
summary: This paper focuses on the implementation of a novel supervised Machine Learning model for estimating helicopter weight during takeoff, utilizing extensive datasets from Airbus's global in-service fleet. The study details a learning assurance process aligned with the EASA concept paper for machine learning application, and with the on-going Eurocae ED-324. We propose a set of Machine Learning Requirements, a Machine Learning Model Description, and its implementation for a long short-term memory recurrent neural network. Finally, we verify the requirements on the implementation. Demonstrated on legacy avionics computers, the implementation is suitable for the deployment of the developed Machine Learning Model weight estimator on airborne targets for critical functions such as on-board alerting.

AI.tldr: A supervised ML LSTM model estimates helicopter takeoff weight using Airbus fleet data, with a learning assurance process aligned to EASA and Eurocae ED-324, verified on legacy avionics for onboard alerting.
AI.motivation: Improve real-time weight estimation for helicopters during takeoff and demonstrate regulatory-aligned ML development, verification, and deployment readiness for safety-critical onboard functions.
AI.method: Develop a supervised ML framework with a defined ML Requirements set and a ML Model Description, implement an LSTM recurrent neural network, train on extensive Airbus in-service data, and verify the implementation against the requirements through a learning assurance process aligned with EASA concept paper and Eurocae ED-324; demonstrate on legacy avionics computers to assess deployment feasibility for onboard alerting.
AI.result: The ML requirements are verified on the implemented model; the approach is demonstrated on legacy avionics and deemed suitable for deployment for critical onboard functions such as alerting.
AI.conclusion: The study delivers a compliant, verifiable ML-based weight estimator architecture ready for airborne deployment in safety-critical helicopters, enabling real-time weight-aware alerting and decision-support.

title: Triangular Fuzzy Rescaling Distance
summary: Decision-making in complex systems often involves dealing with imprecise or uncertain information, frequently represented using fuzzy sets, particularly Triangular Fuzzy Numbers (TFNs). A crucial aspect of many fuzzy methods is the quantification of distance between TFNs. Many distance measures assume that all values are in the same scale, requiring a preliminary normalization stage when applied to heterogeneous attributes with different scales or units. This paper proposes the Triangular Fuzzy Rescaling Distance (d_{TR}), a metric designed to address this challenge. The d_{TR} uniquely integrates Linear Rescaling (LRE) directly into the distance calculation, ensuring normalization during the comparison of fuzzy numbers. We formally prove that d_{TR} satisfies the properties of a metric, including non-negativity, identity, symmetry, and the triangle inequality. Furthermore, we demonstrate that d_{TR} is bounded, scale-invariant, and origin-invariant. These properties, combined with a weighting vector for prioritizing dimensions, make d_{TR} suitable for applications involving heterogeneous fuzzy data, such as the construction of synthetic indicators, distance-based machine learning algorithms or multicriteria-decision aiding.

AI.tldr: Proposes Triangular Fuzzy Rescaling Distance (d_TR) for TFNs that embeds linear rescaling into the distance computation, yielding a true metric that is bounded, scale- and origin-invariant, suitable for heterogeneous fuzzy data with a weighting of dimensions.
AI.motivation: Distance measures for TFNs typically assume a common scale, necessitating preprocessing to normalize heterogeneous attributes. This paper aims to remove ad hoc normalization by integrating normalization directly into the distance metric.
AI.method: Introduce d_TR that combines Linear Rescaling (LRE) with the distance between triangular fuzzy numbers. Prove that d_TR satisfies metric properties (non-negativity, identity, symmetry, triangle inequality). Establish boundedness, scale-invariance, and origin-invariance. Include a dimension-weighting vector to handle heterogeneous attributes.
AI.result: Theoretical development and proofs establish that d_TR is a valid metric for TFNs, bounded and invariant to scale and origin, with applicability to synthetic indicator construction, distance-based ML methods, and multicriteria decision analysis.
AI.conclusion: d_TR directly addresses normalization in distance computation for heterogeneous fuzzy data, enabling consistent, dimension-weighted similarity assessments across TFNs and broad applicability in fuzzy data analytics.

title: Holtercare-Bench: A Multimodal Benchmark for Evaluating Long-Term Dynamic ECG Analysis
summary: While multimodal large language models (MLLMs) excel in medical applications, most of them favor static images or short-term signals. In the critical field of dynamic electrocardiograms (ECG), models struggle with complex temporal reasoning and diagnostic report generation due to a lack of high-quality datasets and benchmarks. To address this, we introduce (i) Holtercare-23K, a large-scale multimodal dynamic ECG dataset comprising 22,980 QA pairs derived from 788 clinical Holter records and featuring a novel signal-video-text tri-modal alignment. Based on this dataset, we present (ii) Holtercare-Bench, a multimodal benchmark that evaluates models on temporal localization, clinical diagnosis, and global summarization. Zero-shot evaluations of leading MLLMs reveal a significant performance gap in processing ultra-long pathological sequences. However, fine-tuning representative models yields substantial improvements. This work illuminates the limitations of current MLLMs in electrophysiology and provides a foundational benchmark for long-term medical MLLMs. Our project is available at https://github.com/ZJU4HealthCare/Holtercare-Bench.

AI.tldr: Introduces Holtercare-23K, a large-scale dynamic ECG dataset with 22,980 QA pairs from 788 Holter records, featuring signal-video-text tri-modal alignment; proposes Holtercare-Bench, a benchmark for temporal localization, clinical diagnosis, and summarization. Zero-shot MLLMs underperform on ultra-long sequences; fine-tuning yields significant gains. Provides a foundational benchmark and dataset for long-term medical MLLMs; code at GitHub.
AI.motivation: Address the scarcity of high-quality, long-sequence multimodal data and benchmarks in dynamic ECG, enabling temporal reasoning and report generation in multimodal medical LLMs.
AI.method: Holtercare-23K: collect and annotate 788 Holter records to produce 22,980 QA pairs with tri-modal (signal, video, text) alignment. Holtercare-Bench: define tasks for temporal localization, clinical diagnosis, and global summarization. Evaluate zero-shot performance of leading MLLMs on ultra-long pathological sequences; fine-tune representative models to assess gains.
AI.result: Zero-shot MLLMs exhibit notable performance gaps on long dynamic ECG data. Fine-tuning leads to substantial improvements across benchmark tasks. The work delineates current limits of MLLMs in electrophysiology and provides a practical benchmark to guide development of long-term medical MLLMs.
AI.conclusion: Highlights the need for long-term, multimodal medical models and offers Holtercare-23K and Holtercare-Bench as foundational resources for this direction; code and data released at the referenced GitHub repository.

title: Quantum Kernel Estimation for the Discovery of Early Lung Cancer Detection
summary:
Lung cancer screening with low-dose chest computed tomography reduces mortality, but its impact is limited by uptake, adherence, and management challenges. Blood-based cell-free DNA (cfDNA) biomarkers offer a complementary approach, although early detection remains difficult because of lung cancer heterogeneity and high-dimensional, nonlinear molecular signals. We evaluated quantum-classical hybrid machine learning for lung cancer detection using DNA fragmentomics and DNA methylation. After feature selection, models were trained using 20- and 40-feature subsets. Features were encoded into quantum Hilbert space using angle and dense-angle feature maps with multiple entanglement strategies. Fidelity-based quantum kernels were computed with exact statevector simulation and integrated with precomputed-kernel SVM and kernel-PCA logistic regression and compared with an SVM model trained on the original features.
  This framework enabled systematic evaluation of how encoding and entanglement design affect classification. Across repeated held-out evaluations, quantum-kernel models achieved competitive performance on both datasets. For fragmentomics, several 20-feature configurations improved AUC relative to a classical SVM baseline, suggesting effective capture of nonlinear cfDNA fragmentation structure. For methylation, the classical SVM achieved the highest AUC, although selected quantum models remained competitive and improved specificity in some cases. Increasing features from 20 to 40 did not consistently improve performance and often increased variability. Overall, these results support quantum kernel methods as a promising approach for cfDNA-based lung cancer detection.

AI.tldr: Quantum kernel methods were applied to cfDNA-based lung cancer detection using fragmentation (fragmentomics) and methylation data. 20-feature quantum-encoded configurations often improved AUC over a classical SVM for fragmentomics, while methylation favored classical SVM; using 40 features did not consistently improve performance and sometimes increased variability. Overall, quantum kernels show promise but results are dataset- and feature-dependent.
AI.motivation: Address limited uptake/adherence in lung-cancer screening by leveraging cfDNA biomarkers and nonlinear high-dimensional signals. Quantum kernel methods may better capture complex cfDNA fragmentation and methylation patterns than classical linear models.
AI.method: Feature selection to 20/40 features. Encode features into quantum Hilbert space using angle and dense-angle maps with multiple entanglement strategies. Compute fidelity-based quantum kernels (statevector simulation) and integrate with precomputed-kernel SVM and kernel-PCA logistic regression; compare to an SVM trained on original features.
AI.result: Quantum-kernel models were competitive across repeated held-out evaluations. For fragmentomics, some 20-feature setups improved AUC over a classical SVM baseline. For methylation, classical SVM achieved the highest AUC, though certain quantum models were competitive and offered improved specificity in some cases. Increasing features from 20 to 40 did not consistently improve performance and often increased variability.
AI.conclusion: Quantum kernel methods are a promising approach for cfDNA-based lung cancer detection, with encoding and entanglement design significantly influencing performance. Further optimization and validation are needed to realize consistent gains across cfDNA modalities.

title: APPROVE: Visual End-User-in-the-Loop Robot Programming with LLMs
comment: Accepted for publication in Procedia CIRP, Proceedings of the 20th CIRP Conference on Intelligent Computation in Manufacturing Engineering (ICME 2026)
summary: Programming robots remains challenging for non-experts, as traditional methods require expert knowledge and even block-based interfaces often lack flexibility. Recent work has explored Large Language Models (LLMs) to automatically generate robot programs from natural language, but these systems remain limited by a lack of transparency, missing mechanisms to ensure alignment with user intent, and little support for reuse. We present APPROVE (AI-Powered Programming for Robots with Visual End-User Feedback), an LLM-based multi-modal end-user programming framework that integrates natural language input with a block-based interface and an explicit user confirmation step. Generated programs are visualized using a block-based interface in Blockly, allowing users to confirm, modify, or reject them before execution. Confirmed functions are stored in a library for reuse, gradually building a set of reliable program components. Our approach contributes a human-centered design for LLM-based robot programming that emphasizes user trust, intent alignment, and reusability.

AI.tldr: LLM-based robot programming framework (APPROVE) that blends natural language, Blockly-style visualization, and explicit user confirmation to improve alignment and reuse.
AI.motivation: Non-experts find robot programming hard; LLMs lack transparency, alignment, and reuse mechanisms; need user-centric, verifiable-and-reusable components.
AI.method: Integrates natural language input with a block-based interface (Blockly), uses an LLM to generate program blocks, presents them for confirmation/modification/rejection, and stores confirmed blocks in a reusable library; multi-modal feedback loop.
AI.result: Conceptual design; the abstract reports no empirical results, but outlines a prototype integration and reuse mechanism.
AI.conclusion: A human-centered design to enhance trust, intent alignment, and reusability in LLM-driven robot programming.

title: Clustering and Token Denoising for Faster and More Robust VLMs
summary: Recent Visual-Language Models (VLMs) have enhanced the capabilities of pre-trained LLMs by adding vision tokens alongside text, with approaches like LLaVA showing impressive results. However, the computational burden of processing up to 576 or 729 visual tokens makes edge deployment challenging. While various token pruning techniques require retraining, some are training-free and thus can easily adapt to architecture changes. We introduce ClustRS, a two-part, training-free algorithm for robust token pruning. Its first component is an attention-weighted, clustering algorithm that selects representative tokens from each semantic cluster. The second component, Residual Shrinkage, is a one-pass denoising step on the selected tokens. These training-free lightweight steps make LLaVA ready for real-world data, improving robustness to a wide range of image-noise types and intensities. Experimental results on the ScienceQA-IMG and MM-VET benchmarks show our method outperforms attention- and diversity-based methods by up to 20\% under extreme noise and token conditions (reducing tokens by 97\%, down to 16 tokens) on LLaVA 1.5 7b and achieves exceptional results on LLaVA-OneVision, where we match baseline performance with fewer than one-third of their tokens under mild noise conditions. Our study demonstrates a simple yet powerful alternative to both score-only and diversity-only pruning rules, paving the way for compute-efficient and noise-resilient VLM deployment.

AI.tldr: A training-free two-part token pruning method (ClustRS) for visual-language models reduces visual tokens and improves noise robustness without retraining, outperforming existing pruning methods under heavy noise and achieving token reductions of up to 97%.
AI.motivation: Visually grounded LLMs incur high computation due to many vision tokens; need a training-free, architecture-agnostic pruning method to enable edge deployment and robustness to image noise.
AI.method: ClustRS comprises two components: (1) an attention-weighted clustering that selects representative tokens from semantic clusters, and (2) a one-pass Residual Shrinkage denoising on the chosen tokens. Both steps are training-free and lightweight.
AI.result: On ScienceQA-IMG and MM-VET, ClustRS outperforms attention- and diversity-based pruning by up to 20% under extreme noise and token conditions, while reducing tokens by up to 97% (down to 16 tokens) on LLaVA 1.5 7b. On LLaVA-OneVision, it matches baseline performance with fewer than one-third of the tokens under mild noise.
AI.conclusion: ClustRS offers a simple yet effective alternative to score-only and diversity-only pruning rules, enabling compute-efficient and noise-resilient deployment of VLMs without retraining.

title: Active Inference as Context Acquisition for AI Agents
summary: Interactive AI agents must acquire the right context as efficiently as possible. When a user omits a constraint, preference, file, or task variable, an agent can proceed with a default assumption or spend tokens on a clarifying question, retrieval call, tool call, or prompt trial. We formulate this tradeoff as active inference for context acquisition. An inner inference step updates beliefs over a latent task state, and an outer decision selects the next context action, task action, or stop action to minimize expected free energy under cost. In deterministic settings, the epistemic term reduces to expected information gain, optionally normalized by token cost. We instantiate the framework in Optimal Question Asking (OQA), with exact posteriors and a dynamic programming oracle, and benchmark frontier language models on binary and multiway categorical tasks from 25 to 300 candidates. We also study clarification before generation and automated prompt optimization under token budgets. The formulation is model-agnostic and views active inference as a design principle for the context-acquisition layer of AI agents.

AI.tldr: Active inference can optimize context acquisition for interactive AI; inner latent inference and outer action selection minimize free energy with token-aware information gain; instantiated as Optimal Question Asking (OQA) with exact posteriors and DP oracle; validated on language models across multiway tasks and token-constrained scenarios; demonstrates clarification and prompt optimization under budgets; model-agnostic design principle.
AI.motivation: Efficiently acquiring user-provided context without excessive querying or costly retrievals; reduce token waste and improve decision quality in interactive agents.
AI.method: Formulate active inference for context acquisition; inner inference updates latent task state; outer policy chooses context actions, task actions, or stop actions to minimize expected free energy; in deterministic settings, epistemic term becomes information gain; instantiate OQA with exact posteriors and DP oracle; evaluate on binary and multiway categorization tasks with 25–300 candidates; study clarification before generation and automated prompt optimization under token budgets; model-agnostic.
AI.result: Demonstrates tractable active-inference-based context acquisition; benchmarks frontier LMs on 25–300 candidate tasks; finds that information-gain-driven context actions and prompt optimization yield effective performance under token budgets; supports the viability of active inference as a design principle.
AI.conclusion: Active inference provides a general, model-agnostic framework for the context-acquisition layer in AI agents and can unify questioning, retrieval, and prompting under a single principled objective.

title: Polyomino Nets Covering Three Different Boxes of Area 106 and Related Results
summary: We present new results for polyomino nets that fold into 2 and 3 different cuboids through a computer search. The main result is the finding of 40 nets that fold into all three different cuboids with a surface area of 106. The secondary results are the finding of infinite families of nets that fold into three cuboid shapes, and the calculation of the number of common nets between smaller cuboids. The algorithms used to make the searches feasible will also be explained. The algorithms include taking advantage of some hidden structures in the nets that fold into the Nx1x1 cuboids, taking advantage of how a lot of nets fold into cuboid shapes in a 'striped' way, and using a variant of Redelmeier's algorithm. The paper ends with open questions that encourage the reader to broaden our collective understanding of the subject of creating polyomino nets.

AI.tldr: Computer-assisted study of polyomino nets folding into up to three cuboids; finds 40 nets folding into all three with surface area 106, plus infinite families and counts of common nets; explains search algorithms.
AI.motivation: To advance understanding of polyomino nets that can fold into multiple cuboids, revealing structural patterns and enabling multi-target folding in tiling/packing problems.
AI.method: Computer search leveraging hidden structures in nets that fold into Nx1x1 cuboids, striped folding patterns, and a variant of Redelmeier's algorithm; includes counting of common nets across smaller cuboids and explanation of algorithmic optimizations.
AI.result: Main result: 40 nets fold into all three cuboids with surface area 106. Secondary results: infinite families of nets folding into three cuboid shapes; calculation of the number of common nets between smaller cuboids. Algorithms used are described in detail.
AI.conclusion: Open questions proposed to broaden understanding of polyomino nets and folding, with potential generalizations to other sizes and shapes, inviting further exploration of the combinatorial structure and algorithmic methods.

title: Improved Confidence Estimates for Black-Box Large Language Models
summary: Uncertainty quantification (UQ) is essential for the safe deployment of large language models (LLMs). Existing methods, from verbalized confidence to ones requiring multiple generations, are often zero-shot and produce scores quantifying uncertainty without the need for labelled data. Nonetheless, in practice one must always evaluate their performance on a dataset of interest before deployment. In this work we show that, by leveraging this dataset, we consistently outperform these existing scores. Specifically, we build simple classifiers that predict LLM response correctness by using these scores and the correctness of similar queries as features. Our method produces minimal computational overhead, making it a cheap and straightforward enhancement for UQ in LLMs for real-world applications.

AI.tldr: Dataset-adapted, low-cost uncertainty scoring for LLMs: train lightweight classifiers using existing UQ scores and similarity-based correctness to predict response accuracy, achieving better performance with minimal overhead.
AI.motivation: To make uncertainty quantification reliable in real-world deployments, zero-shot scores need validation on deployment data; leveraging the deployment dataset can improve reliability without heavy computation.
AI.method: Train simple classifiers that take as features the existing UQ scores for a response and the correctness of similar queries; uses the dataset to supervise the classifier; minimal extra computation.
AI.result: The dataset-informed classifiers consistently outperform existing zero-shot scores with negligible computational overhead, offering a cheap, practical enhancement for UQ in LLMs.
AI.conclusion: A practical approach for improving uncertainty quantification by dataset-adaptation via lightweight classifiers; useful for real-world deployment where evaluation data is available.

title: The Missing Touch: Spatially Distributed Tactile Feedback Brings Teleoperation Closer to Human Dexterity
summary: A fundamental challenge in robotic teleoperation is enabling an operator to control a remote robot as effortlessly and intuitively as their own hands. Despite the growing use of teleoperation to collect demonstration data for training autonomous robot policies, teleoperated robot performance still falls significantly short of human dexterity, even for basic tasks. Here, we present evidence that a key factor contributing to this performance gap is the absence of spatially distributed tactile feedback. Using a two-degree-of-freedom (DoF) bilateral force-feedback telemanipulator paired with a 32-DoF tactile fingertip display, we show that operator performance improves significantly when localized deformations on the remote manipulator are faithfully reproduced on the operator's fingertip. In a series of teleoperation tasks, reproducing distributed contact information not only accelerated task performance but also brought teleoperated movements closer to natural human behavior by minimizing corrective actions and task completion steps, thereby reducing the deviation between teleoperated and natural trajectories by 29$\unicode{x2013}$79%. Furthermore, we found that increasing the resolution of the tactile feedback$\unicode{x2014}$by refining how finely the measured displacements were quantized for reproduction$\unicode{x2014}$compressed the state-space distribution of teleoperated motions, which has been associated with improved training outcomes for autonomous robot policies. Together, these results suggest that spatially distributed tactile feedback is essential for closing the gap between human and teleoperated dexterity and training the next generation of autonomous robots.

AI.tldr: Spatially distributed tactile feedback via a high-DoF tactile display and a 2-DoF telemanipulator reduces teleoperation effort and brings motion closer to natural human trajectories; higher tactile resolution further tightens motion distributions, aiding autonomous policy training.
AI.motivation: To close the dexterity gap in teleoperation caused by lack of tactile feedback; enabling more intuitive control and better demonstration data for learning-based policies.
AI.method: Employed a 2-DoF bilateral force-feedback telemanipulator paired with a 32-DoF tactile fingertip display to reproduce localized remote-contact deformations on the operator's fingertip. Conducted teleoperation tasks with varying tactile feedback resolutions and measured task performance, trajectory deviation from natural motion, and state-space distribution.
AI.result: Localized distributed tactile reproduction accelerated task completion and reduced deviation between teleoperated and natural trajectories by 29–79%. Higher tactile feedback resolution compressed the state-space distribution of teleoperated motions, a profile associated with better training outcomes for autonomous robots.
AI.conclusion: Spatially distributed tactile feedback is critical for closing the dexterity gap in teleoperation and for generating high-quality demonstration data for autonomous robots.

title: SceneGTMM: A Conformal Mapping-based Scene-Aware Transferable GNN-Transformer Dual-Graph Interaction Framework for Map Matching
summary: Map matching is a key technology connecting positioning data with high precision road networks, but it faces challenges in noise robustness, cross regional transfer, and interpretability. To addr ess the limitations of existing methods in local global fusion, dynamic road network adaptation, and reliance on black box mod els, this paper proposes SceneGTMM, a transferable GNN Transformer dual graph interaction map matching framework based on a conformal mapping based scene relative strategy. 1) Conformal mapping based scene relative strategy: constructs trajectory centric local coordinate systems to reduce dependence on the training road network, supporting cross regional transfer and dynamic road network updates; 2) GNN Transformer dual graph interaction architecture: a GNN modeled road graph captures local topological constraints, while a Transformer modeled trajectory graph captures global temporal dependencies, and cross graph attention achieves noise suppression and semantic alignment; 3) CRF enhanced structured prediction: combines the global context of the Transformer with the topological transition constraints of CRF to improve path connectivity and robustness. Experiments show that SceneGTM achieves over 80% accuracy on multi source trajectories with positioning errors of 16 50 meters, representing a 5.3% improvement over HMM. In cross city transfer scenarios, it outperforms MTrajRec, GraphMM, and TMM, and enhances interpretability through attention and relative coordinate visualization. This study provides a new paradigm for high precision, transferable map matching for real time traffic perception and autonomous driving path planning.

AI.tldr: Proposes SceneGTMM, a transferable map-matching framework using conformal mapping-based scene-relative coordinates, a dual graph GNN-Transformer with cross-graph attention, and CRF-based structured prediction; achieves ~80% accuracy at 16–50 m errors and strong cross-city transfer with improved interpretability.
AI.motivation: Address noise robustness, cross-regional transfer, and interpretability in map matching; existing methods suffer from local-global fusion limitations, dynamic road-network updates, and black-box models.
AI.method: Three components: (1) Conformal mapping scene-relative strategy to build trajectory-centric local coordinates for cross-regional transfer; (2) GNN-Transformer dual graph interaction: GNN models road graph locally, Transformer models trajectory graph globally; cross-graph attention for noise suppression; (3) CRF-enhanced structured prediction to fuse global context with topological constraints.
AI.result: Empirical results show >80% accuracy on multi-source trajectories with 16–50 m positioning error; ~5.3% improvement over HMM; in cross-city transfer, outperforms MTrajRec, GraphMM, TMM; interpretable via attention and relative-coordinate visualization.
AI.conclusion: Presents a new transferable, high-precision map-matching paradigm suitable for real-time traffic perception and autonomous driving path planning.

title: Robust Metaheuristics under Uncertainty for Berth Allocation and Quay Crane Assignment: A Review
summary: The berth allocation and quay crane assignment problem (BACAP) is a representative port-terminal scheduling problem in maritime transportation and freight logistics, where vessel arrivals, berth positions, service durations, and quay?crane availability are tightly coupled. Under uncertainties such as arrival deviations, handling-time fluctuations, and resource disruptions, schedules optimized under nominal assumptions may become fragile during execution, motivating the study of robust metaheuristic optimization for BACAP in port-terminal operations. Although population-based metaheuristics have been widely used for BACAP and related port-scheduling problems, existing studies remain fragmented in their uncertainty repre?sentations, robustness criteria, search mechanisms, and empir?ical evaluation protocols. To the best of our knowledge, this paper provides the first focused review dedicated to robust population-based metaheuristics for BACAP under uncertainty. We first summarize uncertainty sources and information repre?sentations in BACAP, and then organize existing methods from a mechanism-oriented perspective, covering solution representation and decoding, robust evaluation and selection, robustness-guided search dynamics, and feasibility preservation and recovery. We further present a benchmark suite for uncertain BACAP to support controlled empirical comparison and report illustrative baseline results by combining representative metaheuristics with different robustness strategies. Finally, we identify open chal?lenges related to benchmark extension, robustness-aware search design, time-adaptive robustness, and non-stationary uncertainty.

AI.tldr: First focused review of robust population-based metaheuristics for BACAP under uncertainty; organizes methods, presents a benchmark suite, and outlines key open challenges.
AI.motivation: BACAP schedules are fragile under uncertainty; there is fragmentation in robustness representations and methods, necessitating a consolidated, mechanism-oriented synthesis and benchmarking.
AI.method: A mechanism-oriented literature review that (i) catalogs uncertainty sources and representations in BACAP, (ii) organizes existing methods by solution representation, robust evaluation/selection, robust search dynamics, and feasibility preservation/recovery, (iii) introduces a benchmark suite for uncertain BACAP, and (iv) reports baseline results by combining representative metaheuristics with various robustness strategies.
AI.result: The paper provides a consolidated review of robust population-based metaheuristics for BACAP, introduces a controlled benchmark suite for uncertain BACAP, and presents illustrative baseline results demonstrating how different robustness strategies interact with metaheuristics.
AI.conclusion: Highlights open challenges including benchmark extension, robustness-aware search design, time-adaptive robustness, and handling non-stationary uncertainty, outlining directions for future research.

title: Mechanistic Tomography: Designed Measurement for Control-Oriented Interpretability
summary:
Mechanistic interpretability seeks quantities that models do not expose directly: represented states, component effects, interactions, and responses to interventions. Patching, gradients, Hessian-vector products, and subset interventions provide different measurements under different access assumptions and may target different quantities. We formulate their shared measurement structure as mechanistic tomography: designed measurement for recovering internal mechanisms and intervention effects.
  For a chosen basis and intervention family, measurements take the form y = Ax + w, where A describes the interventions, x is the target map, and w contains nonlinear response, sampling error, and basis misspecification. This language gives a practical procedure: start with the least costly measurements, test on held-out interventions at the intended scale, calibrate simple mismatch, and expand the measurement family when structured residuals remain.
  Control provides a demanding validation setting because an estimate that guides an intervention acts as an observer. In a two-HMM model, control error rises with observer error, while target improvement can hide nuisance-state movement. Under forward-only access, sparse aggregate measurements recover a finite-effect map with fewer interventions than coordinate patching. With gradient access, finite probes improve a local attribution map. Lifted measurements and Hessian-vector products recover interactions missed by first-order maps, while Tracr shows that the required family depends on the basis. On GPT-2-small IOI, the Name Mover-Negative Name Mover interaction is the largest held-out predictive term among three tested cross-group pairs. On Qwen-2.5-7B, finite calibration makes an additive refusal-response map adequate, so held-out error does not support pairwise lifting.

AI.tldr: A unified framework (mechanistic tomography) to design and interpret measurements for recovering internal mechanisms and intervention effects in neural models; shows how different access modes map to a linear measurement y = Ax + w; demonstrates with experiments on GPT-2-small IOI and Qwen-2.5-7B; outcomes include recovery of finite-effect maps, improved attribution, and basis-dependent measurement families.
AI.motivation: To unify patching, gradients, Hessian-vector products, and subset interventions under a common measurement framework, enabling efficient, validated discovery of model mechanisms even under observer/measurement imperfections.
AI.method: Formulate mechanistic tomography with chosen basis and intervention family; measurements y = Ax + w; propose staged procedure: cheap measurements first, held-out validation, calibrate mismatch, expand measurement family; analyze effects under forward-only vs gradient access; examine lifted measurements, Hessian-vector products; use Tracr to characterize basis dependence; provide case studies: two-HMM, GPT-2-small IOI, Qwen-2.5-7B.
AI.result: Demonstrates that forward-only access recovers a finite-effect map with fewer interventions; gradient access yields better local attribution; lifted measurements expose higher-order interactions; Tracr shows measurement family depends on basis; empirical findings include Name Mover-Negative Name Mover being largest held-out predictor among three cross-group pairs in GPT-2-small IOI; for Qwen-2.5-7B, additive refusal-response map is sufficient so pairwise lifting is not supported by held-out error.
AI.conclusion: Mechanistic tomography provides a practical, basis-aware protocol for discovering internal mechanisms and intervention effects; measurement choice and calibration significantly influence what is recoverable; future work should optimize basis/intervention selection, robustness to model misspecification, and scaling to diverse architectures.

title: Learning the Right Abstraction: Neural Reduced Dynamics for Complex Robot Control
summary: High-fidelity embodied AI simulators provide realistic evaluation of complex robotic systems, but their computational cost limits their direct use for large-scale reinforcement learning campaigns. We advocate the use of less accurate but more expeditious simulations, which might draw on data-driven, e.g., neural dynamics, models. This contribution argues that the practical value of a neural dynamics model for complex robot control lies in learning the \emph{right abstraction}: a reduced state that preserves the control-relevant physics of the high-fidelity system while enabling high-throughput policy learning. We develop a neural reduced dynamics (NRD) framework that separates the state the model propagates from what can be supplied as an input or recovered analytically, trains policies entirely inside the frozen learned model, and validates them back in the high-fidelity simulator. Two case studies instantiate it across three control tasks: terrain-aware HMMWV trajectory tracking on rigid, bumpy and deformable Continuum Representation Model (CRM) terrain; and goal reaching for a stock tracked vehicle and its front-mounted articulated arm. Every policy transfers back to the high-fidelity simulator. A single policy trained inside the terrain-conditioned dynamics model, and given no terrain input of its own, attains lower median and mean tracking error than both single-terrain specialists on all three terrains, including zero-shot bumpy terrain. Quantitatively, the tracked vehicle reaches 100 of 100 goals and the arm 97 of 100, with zero contacts or joint-limit violations. The NRD models advance roughly four orders of magnitude faster in simulated time than the high-fidelity simulator scenes they replace, making iterative on-policy learning practical and supporting neural reduced dynamics as a bridge between accurate but expensive physics simulation and scalable robot learning.

AI.tldr: NRD (Neural Reduced Dynamics) learns a reduced neural model that propagates a state suitable for control, while inputs can be supplied or recovered analytically; policies are trained inside the frozen NRD and transferred back to a high-fidelity simulator, enabling large-scale RL with realism.
AI.motivation: High-fidelity simulators are accurate but computationally expensive for large-scale RL; a faster, data-driven abstraction that preserves control-relevant physics is needed to enable iterative learning.
AI.method: Introduce Neural Reduced Dynamics framework that separates propagated state from input/recoverable variables, trains policies entirely inside the frozen learned model, and validates them back in a high-fidelity simulator. Implemented via terrain-conditioned dynamics across three tasks/terrains; a single policy trained inside NRD achieves zero-shot transfer to high-fidelity scenes.
AI.result: NRD achieves ~10^4x faster simulated time than the high-fidelity scenes; a single policy trained inside NRD outperforms single-terrain specialists on rigid, bumpy, and deformable CRM terrains; tracked vehicle reaches 100/100 goals and the front-mounted arm 97/100 goals with zero contacts/joint-limit violations (on 3 tasks across terrains).
AI.conclusion: Learning the right abstraction via NRD enables high-throughput, reliable policy learning and provides a practical bridge between accurate but expensive physics simulation and scalable robot learning, allowing effective transfer back to high-fidelity simulators.

title: Does Marginal Coverage Guarantee Class-Conditional Safety for Zero-Shot VLMs Under Shift?
comment: Accepted at the ECCV 2026 Workshop on Uncertainty Quantification for Computer Vision (UNCV). 34 pages (16 main + 18 supplementary), 10 figures
summary: Split-conformal prediction provides marginal coverage under exchangeability and is increasingly used as an abstention layer for zero-shot vision-language models (VLMs). We audit this practice under deployment shift for CLIP, OpenCLIP, and SigLIP across ImageNet and non-ImageNet settings. Marginal coverage can remain relatively high while class-conditional tail coverage collapses: on ImageNet-Sketch, worst-class coverage falls to $\approx 0$ and 10-12% of classes lie below a finite-sample null floor, despite marginal coverage of about 0.86. The failure is aligned with target-domain class accuracy but is not predicted by the source-domain diagnostics we test. Source-side Mondrian calibration improves the in-distribution tail but does not transfer, while clustered conformal and Conf-OT improve marginal or average metrics without recovering the worst-class tail. Target-side class calibration substantially lifts the tail, but requires labels for every class and remains set-size-intensive. We further identify a 2-3$\times$ cross-family efficiency gap and show that native SigLIP sigmoid scores remove APS's probability-mass interpretation. The findings persist across the tested model scale, pretraining corpus, prompt, miscoverage level $α$, and shifted non-ImageNet settings. Marginal conformal coverage should therefore be treated as an average reliability statistic, not as a safety guarantee for the class tail.

AI.tldr: Marginal conformal coverage remains high under deployment shift but class-tail coverage collapses for zero-shot VLM abstention; target-side calibration helps but is costly; several source-side methods fail to fix worst-class tail; significant efficiency gap across methods; treat marginal coverage as average reliability, not tail safety.
AI.motivation: Assess whether split-conformal prediction provides reliable tail-risk guarantees for abstaining in zero-shot VLMs under distribution shift; explore how various calibration strategies affect tail coverage.
AI.method: Audit CLIP/OpenCLIP/SigLIP on ImageNet and non-ImageNet shifts (including ImageNet-Sketch). Measure marginal vs class-conditional tail coverage. Compare source-side Mondrian calibration, clustered conformal, Conf-OT, and target-side class calibration. Analyze SigLIP scores and efficiency across model scales, prompts, miscoverage levels, and shifts.
AI.result: Marginal coverage ~0.86 but worst-class coverage near 0; 10-12% of classes below finite-sample null; target-domain accuracy aligns with tail failure; source diagnostics fail to predict; some calibration methods help in-distribution tail or average metrics but not worst-class tail; target-side calibration lifts tail but requires per-class labels; 2-3x efficiency gap across methods; SigLIP scores distort probability interpretation; findings robust to scale, data, prompts, alpha, non-ImageNet shifts.
AI.conclusion: Relying on marginal conformal coverage is inappropriate for class-tail safety; tail risk persists under deployment shift; class-tail calibration offers improvement but is resource-intensive; aim for methods with per-class calibration or alternative tail-aware reliability metrics; the results highlight robustness issues across VLMs and calibration strategies.

title: How to Navigate Uncertainty About AI Consciousness
comment: 8 Pages, Proceedings of AISB 2026 Symposium on AI, Consciousness and Ethics
summary: Given deep uncertainty about the possibility of artificial consciousness, it is unclear how we should treat potentially sentient AI. On the one hand, we could assume insentience but risk doing terrible harms to entities that deserve moral standing. On the other hand, we could assume sentience and instead risk wasting resources on insentient machines. The intractability of questions around AI consciousness mean that this dilemma is hard to escape. I suggest a way out of that shifts from intractable questions of AI consciousness to tractable questions of AI valence. Specifically, we can assess whether an AI has states that would constitute valenced experiences if it were conscious. I show how this is sufficient to ground a responsible approach to the development of potentially conscious AI.

AI.tldr: Shifting from AI consciousness debates to tractable evaluation of valence states as a proxy for moral consideration and responsible development.
AI.motivation: Deep uncertainty about AI consciousness leads to moral risk and resource misallocation; a tractable criterion is needed to guide policy and design.
AI.method: Proposes assessing whether an AI can have states that would be valenced if conscious; a conceptual framework to ground responsibility in AI development.
AI.result: Argues that valence-possibility assessment is sufficient to ground a responsible approach to potentially conscious AI.
AI.conclusion: Focusing on valence provides a practical, implementable pathway to handle moral status concerns without resolving consciousness; informs governance and design criteria.

title: Uncovering the Limits of Proof Sharing for Neural Networks
comment: To appear at the 33rd Static Analysis Symposium (SAS 2026)
summary: Robustness verification of neural networks is increasingly important, due to their use in many critical domains. In certain scenarios, proof sharing has been shown to accelerate incomplete verification techniques by reusing intermediate-layer abstract states, or templates, across queries. However, questions remain as to the robustness of template-based acceleration across varying network architectures, properties, datasets, and training methods. In this work, we perform a systematic study of the effectiveness of template-based acceleration and its limits. Our study shows that template subsumption rates can vary widely across scenarios. We present a novel metric of jointly stable neurons to explain this variation, showing that in some cases template-based techniques are very unlikely to provide any speedup. Then, we present FastCert, a novel technique for automatically distributing templates across neural network layers to increase performance impact, eschewing templates entirely if they are unlikely to produce a speedup. Across a large set of covering-design based $L_0$-verification tasks, FastCert achieved an average speedup of 1.13x over an extant template-based reuse technique.

AI.tldr: Template-based robustness verification shows mixed effectiveness; a new metric (jointly stable neurons) explains variability in template subsumption; FastCert adaptively distributes templates across layers, avoiding them when unhelpful, yielding ~1.13x speedup on L0 verification tasks.
AI.motivation: To understand how robust and generally applicable template-based acceleration is for neural-network verification, given varying architectures, datasets, properties, and training methods, and to optimize speedups.
AI.method: Conducted a systematic study across scenarios; introduced jointly stable neurons as a metric to explain subsumption variability; developed FastCert to automatically distribute templates across layers and disable templates when not beneficial; evaluated on covering-design based L0 verification tasks.
AI.result: Template subsumption rates vary widely; jointly stable neurons explain the variation; FastCert achieves adaptive template distribution and average speedup of 1.13x over an existing template-based reuse technique.
AI.conclusion: Template-based acceleration has conditional effectiveness dependent on network and data properties; adaptive template distribution is beneficial, enabling speedups where feasible and avoiding wasted effort where templates are unlikely to help.

title: SCAPE: Scenario-Conditioned Simulation-Augmented Policy Evaluation
summary: Reliable performance evaluation is a central bottleneck for deploying robot-learning policies in real-world conditions. Real-world testing is faithful but costly and difficult to scale, whereas simulation-based testing scales easily but is inevitably biased by the sim-to-real gap. Existing simulation-augmented methods combine limited real-world rollouts with abundant simulation proxies, but focus on performance averaged over initial conditions and deployment settings. Such population-level averages obscure scenario-specific variation and provide limited guidance about when and where a policy can be safely deployed. We propose SCAPE, a scenario-conditioned simulation-augmented policy evaluation framework that predicts scenario-conditioned real-world policy performance using limited paired sim-and-real samples and large-scale simulation rollouts. SCAPE corrects sim-to-real bias in simulation labels before training the prediction model and calibrates prediction uncertainty through conformal prediction. We validate SCAPE on autonomous driving and quadruped velocity tracking. In sim-to-sim studies, SCAPE reduces scenario-level prediction error by 4.9%/34.7% (driving) and 14.5%/27.7% (quadruped) relative to scene-conditioned neural and aggregate statistical baselines on average. We further evaluate a velocity-tracking policy deployed on a physical Unitree Go2. SCAPE also improves testing sample efficiency, produces narrower calibrated prediction intervals, generalizes better to out-of-distribution scenarios, and enables fine-grained deployment strategies.

AI.tldr: SCAPE: a scenario-conditioned simulation-augmented policy evaluation framework that predicts scenario-specific real-world performance using limited paired sim-real data and large-scale simulation rollouts, with bias-corrected labels and conformal prediction; demonstrates improved scenario-level accuracy and deployment guidance in driving and quadruped velocity-tracking, including real-world Go2 experiments.
AI.motivation: Population-level averages from existing simulation-augmented methods obscure scenario-specific variation; real-world testing is costly and scale-limited; sim-to-real bias contaminates simulation-based labels; need scenario-aware, calibrated predictions to guide safe deployment.
AI.method: SCAPE aligns sim-to-real labels via bias correction, trains a scenario-conditioned predictor using limited paired samples plus abundant simulation data, and calibrates predictive uncertainty with conformal prediction; it operates on scenario representations to produce scenario-conditioned performance estimates and calibrated prediction intervals.
AI.result: In sim-to-sim studies, SCAPE reduces scenario-level prediction error by 4.9% and 34.7% for autonomous driving, and by 14.5% and 27.7% for quadruped velocity tracking, relative to scene-conditioned neural and aggregate statistical baselines. It enables improved testing sample efficiency, yields narrower calibrated prediction intervals, generalizes better to out-of-distribution scenarios, and supports deployment on a physical Unitree Go2 velocity-tracking policy.
AI.conclusion: SCAPE provides scenario-aware, calibrated, simulation-augmented evaluation that supports fine-grained deployment decisions, improves robustness to the sim-to-real gap, and scales with simulation data while offering reliable uncertainty estimates.

title: CAViAR: A Causal Video Dataset for Fine-Grained Accident Reasoning in Real-World Scenarios
summary: While modern autonomous driving systems excel at perception tasks such as object detection and trajectory prediction, they lack the high-level causal reasoning required to interpret traffic accidents. In particular, determining responsibility, such as identifying who is at fault and which traffic rule was violated, remains largely unexplored in current benchmarks. To this end, we introduce CAViAR (Causal Accident Video and Incident Analysis Repository), a human-annotated dashcam benchmark comprising 2,249 real-world accident videos collected from CarCrashDataset (CCD) and Nexar. Each video is annotated with structured labels spanning environmental conditions, accident type, causal explanation, apparent At-Fault Agent, affected agent, and apparent rule-violation category. We benchmark state-of-the-art vision-language models (VLMs), including Cosmos-Reason2, Qwen3-VL, and InternVL3. Once class imbalance is accounted for with majority/random baselines and balanced metrics, perceptual competence is uneven--lighting is nearly solved, whereas weather and road-condition accuracy fall at or below the majority-class baseline---and all models degrade sharply on accident type and responsibility reasoning. Overall, CAViAR exposes a practical Perception--Reasoning Gap: current VLMs may recognize salient context, but do not reliably map visible agent actions to annotated rule-relevant responsibility categories in safety-critical driving scenarios. Code, annotation schema, prompts, and evaluation scripts are available at: https://github.com/nec-labs-ma/CAViAR

AI.tldr: A new human-annotated dashcam dataset CAViAR for causal accident analysis; reveals a gap between perception and reasoning in current vision-language models, especially for accident-type and responsibility inference.
AI.motivation: To address the lack of high-level causal reasoning in autonomous driving, enabling identification of fault and rule violations, by providing a benchmark for reasoning over accident scenes.
AI.method: Develop CAViAR with 2,249 real-world accident videos from CarCrashDataset and Nexar, with structured annotations (environmental conditions, accident type, causal explanation, apparent At-Fault Agent, affected agent, apparent rule-violation category); evaluate SOTA VLMs (Cosmos-Reason2, Qwen3-VL, InternVL3) using balanced baselines and metrics.
AI.result: Lighting perception largely solved; weather and road-condition accuracy are at or below the majority baseline; models degrade significantly on accident type and responsibility reasoning; overall Perception–Reasoning Gap—models recognize context but fail to map actions to rule-relevant responsibility categories.
AI.conclusion: CAViAR serves as a practical benchmark to spur improvements in causal reasoning for safety-critical driving; code, schema, prompts, and evaluation scripts released to facilitate future work.

title: Bounded Sovereignty and the Control Tax: Pricing AI Oversight When the Deployer Does Not Own the Model
comment: 25 pages, 5 figures. Synthetic access-ablation study; not real-world payment-system evidence
summary: AI control research asks how to deploy models safely even when they may be misaligned, but many control protocols assume that the deployer can instrument the model and its surrounding pipeline. That assumption often fails for regulated organisations using frontier models through APIs or managed endpoints, where the deployer may control the business process but not the model weights, serving infrastructure, internal traces, update process, or full interaction logs. This paper introduces bounded sovereignty: partial technical and contractual access across the data, model, infrastructure, and interaction layers of the AI stack. It argues that these access conditions determine which control protocols can be executed in practice. The paper contributes a four-layer access typology, a protocol-by-layer requirements matrix, and the concept of sovereignty discount cost: the part of the control tax spent substituting for missing access through contracts, architecture, audit, vendor assurance, residual risk, or reduced system scope. It also reports a synthetic access-ablation experiment over 1.35 million synthetic case simulations and interprets the findings through an anonymised national-payments-infrastructure scenario. The experiment is not real-world payment-system evidence; it is a construct-validity exercise. The results show that complete logs improve diagnosis, a pre-execution gateway enables intervention, trace access and model-version control strengthen post-incident explanation, and scope restriction can improve safety while reducing usefulness. Control protocols proposed as general safety solutions should therefore state their access assumptions explicitly.

AI.tldr: Introduces bounded sovereignty in AI control; analyzes how partial access across data/model/infrastructure/interaction layers shapes control protocols; proposes four-layer typology, a protocol-by-layer requirements matrix, and 'sovereignty discount cost'; uses synthetic simulations to assess how access constraints affect safety and usefulness.
AI.motivation: Regulated organizations using frontier models via APIs lack full control over model/service stack; need to understand how access limitations affect the feasibility of control protocols and safety.
AI.method: Proposes a four-layer access typology; develops protocol-by-layer requirements matrix; defines sovereignty discount cost; conducts a large-scale synthetic access-ablation experiment with 1.35 million case simulations; uses anonymized national payments infrastructure scenario for interpretation.
AI.result: Finds that complete logs improve diagnosis; pre-execution gateway enables intervention; trace access and model-version control strengthen post-incident explanation; scope restriction can improve safety while reducing usefulness.
AI.conclusion: Bounded sovereignty clarifies feasible control protocols by explicitly stating access assumptions; the framework highlights critical access primitives (logs, pre-execution gating, traceability, version control) and suggests compensation mechanisms (contracts, architecture, audits) to offset limited access; safety vs. usefulness trade-offs depend on the alignment of access with control goals.

title: Longitudinal Bayesian Learning of Continuous Disease Position across the Alzheimer's Disease Continuum
summary: Alzheimer's disease (AD) progresses as a continuous biological process, whereas most existing neuroimaging-based artificial intelligence methods remain limited to discrete diagnosis or clinical score prediction from cross-sectional imaging. In this work, we propose Disease Continuum Positioning (DCP), a longitudinal Bayesian Learning framework that continuously estimates disease severity from longitudinal diffusion tensor imaging (DTI). Specifically, DCP models disease severity as a low-dimensional probabilistic latent variable by jointly integrating longitudinal observations with weak clinical supervision, from which the proposed Disease Continuum Score (DCS) is derived to quantify an individual's position along the Alzheimer's disease continuum together with its associated uncertainty. Extensive experiments on the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) cohort demonstrate that DCP consistently outperforms representative disease progression methods. More importantly, comprehensive validation analyses show that DCS accurately characterizes disease severity, exhibits strong clinical relevance, preserves longitudinal disease evolution, and predicts future disease conversion. These results suggest that DCS provides a quantitative imaging-derived representation for continuous assessment of Alzheimer's disease progression beyond conventional diagnostic labels and clinical scores.

AI.tldr: A longitudinal Bayesian framework (DCP) estimates a continuous Disease Continuum Score (DCS) from longitudinal DTI to quantify Alzheimer's disease severity and its uncertainty, outperforming discrete progression methods on ADNI.
AI.motivation: Address the need for continuous, uncertainty-aware tracking of Alzheimer's progression beyond discrete diagnoses or scores by leveraging longitudinal imaging with weak supervision.
AI.method: Jointly models longitudinal diffusion tensor imaging data with a low-dimensional probabilistic latent variable representing disease severity within a Bayesian framework; introduces DCS and its uncertainty; uses weak clinical supervision; validated on ADNI.
AI.result: DCP outperforms representative disease progression methods; DCS characterizes severity with clinical relevance, preserves longitudinal evolution, and predicts conversion; robust validation on ADNI.
AI.conclusion: DCS provides a quantitative, imaging-derived representation for continuous assessment of Alzheimer's progression, enabling beyond-label evaluation and prognosis.

title: Hybrid Feedback Sampling for Sample-Efficient Model Predictive Control
summary: Thanks to its parallelizability and flexibility, sampling-based Model Predictive Control (MPC) has become widely popular for controlling real-world robotic systems. However, for high-dimensional and open-loop unstable dynamical systems, the required number of samples to improve the control sequence will grow exponentially with the horizon, leading to poor sample efficiency and numerical instability. This paper investigates the instability of shooting methods in sampling-based MPC and shows that the optimal sampling proposal distribution can be realized by sampling with an optimized feedback policy. We refer to this algorithm as Feedback Sampling MPC (FS-MPC). FS-MPC involves a hybrid sampling design which balances local and global search based on the system stability and the available computation budget. Our theoretical analysis shows that our hybrid sampling approach achieves faster convergence than standard MPPI and better optimality than standard feedback sampling. Empirically, in diverse contact-rich control tasks like humanoid loco-manipulation and dexterous manipulation, we show that FS-MPC successfully tackles dynamically unstable tasks where standard sample-based approaches struggle, and strictly outperforms feedback policies alone. Finally, we validate our method on humanoid robot locomotion and manipulation tasks in the real world.

AI.tldr: Feedback Sampling MPC (FS-MPC) optimizes the sampling distribution via a learned/optimized feedback policy, yielding faster convergence and better performance than MPPI and pure feedback sampling in unstable, high-dimensional tasks; demonstrated on humanoid loco-manipulation and real-world locomotion/manipulation.
AI.motivation: Sampling-based MPC suffers from exponential sample demands, instability, and poor sample efficiency for high-dimensional, open-loop unstable systems as horizon grows.
AI.method: FS-MPC introduces a hybrid sampling design that blends local and global search. The optimal sampling proposal is realized by sampling with an optimized feedback policy. The approach combines theoretical analysis showing faster convergence than MPPI and better optimality than standard feedback sampling, with empirical validation across diverse contact-rich tasks and real-world experiments on humanoid robots.
AI.result: FS-MPC achieves faster convergence than standard MPPI and better optimality than pure feedback sampling. It handles dynamically unstable tasks where standard sample-based methods struggle and outperforms using feedback policies alone; validated in diverse tasks and on real humanoid robots.
AI.conclusion: FS-MPC improves sampling efficiency and robustness for high-dimensional, unstable systems, enabling reliable control in real-world humanoid locomotion and manipulation scenarios.

title: Beyond Recognition: Compact Multi-Domain Arabic Manuscript HTR with Candidate-Selection Analysis and Evidence-Preserving Review
summary: Historical Arabic manuscript transcription is not only a recognition problem. A usable scholarly system must cope with shifting hands and layouts, preserve uncertain readings, distinguish visual evidence from linguistic plausibility, and record the researcher's final decision. We present Phoenix, a 4.99-million-parameter CNN-BiLSTM-CTC recognizer, and Athar, an evidence-aware review workflow built around it. Phoenix is adapted across archival, Maghrebi, and historical manuscript domains using document-aware replay, an expanded 81-symbol codec, and forgetting guards that reject checkpoints that improve a new domain at unacceptable cost to previous domains. In a pre-specified held-out comparison against the preceding checkpoint, frozen before evaluation and scored with greedy decoding and raw references, Phoenix reduced CER from 22.12% to 17.86% on 10,594 Agapet lines and from 17.72% to 11.84% on 11,684 Omar lines, while regressing from 10.39% to 10.72% on 164 TariMa lines. Across the two large held-out sets, character-weighted CER fell from 19.98% to 14.93%, a 25.3% relative error reduction. A separate same-protocol development diagnostic found the lowest CER for Phoenix on four of four comparable domains (9.59% unweighted macro CER). An N-best diagnostic revealed a 2.15-point oracle gap between beam decoding and Oracle@25, while neural text rerankers, consensus MBR, CTC-posterior quality estimation, and local pre-CTC hidden-state quality estimation recovered less than 4% of this gap. Athar therefore preserves the visual reading, exposes bounded alternatives, uses local language models conservatively, retrieves source parallels with unique, ambiguous, or abstain states, and exports auditable TEI and PAGE-XML records. The results support evaluating manuscript HTR as auditable evidence management rather than silent text replacement.

AI.tldr: A domain-adaptive historical Arabic manuscript recognizer and evidence-aware workflow. Phoenix (CNN-BiLSTM-CTC) scales across archival, Maghrebi, and TariMa domains using document-aware replay, an expanded 81-symbol codec, and forgetting guards. Athar provides an auditable, evidence-based review around Phoenix. The approach yields substantial CER reductions across held-out domains and frames HTR as auditable evidence management rather than silent text replacement.
AI.motivation: Historical Arabic manuscript transcription is not only recognition but also handling shifting hands/layouts, preserving uncertain readings, distinguishing evidence from plausibility, and recording the researcher’s final decision. There is a need for auditable, domain-adaptive HTR that preserves uncertainty and supports evidence management.
AI.method: Phoenix: a 4.99M-parameter CNN-BiLSTM-CTC recognizer with an 81-symbol codec, plus document-aware replay and forgetting guards to mitigate catastrophic forgetting across domains. Athar: an evidence-aware review workflow built around Phoenix that preserves visual readings, exposes bounded alternatives, uses conservative local LMs, retrieves source parallels with unambiguous/ambiguous/abstain states, and exports auditable TEI and PAGE-XML records.
AI.result: In held-out tests, Phoenix reduced CER from 22.12% to 17.86% on 10,594 Agapet lines and from 17.72% to 11.84% on 11,684 Omar lines; but rose from 10.39% to 10.72% on 164 TariMa lines. Across two large held-out sets, character-weighted CER fell from 19.98% to 14.93% (25.3% relative). A same-protocol diagnostic showed the lowest CER for Phoenix on four domains (9.59% unweighted macro CER). An N-best diagnostic found a 2.15-point oracle gap between beam decoding and Oracle@25; other reranking/quality-estimation approaches recovered less than 4% of this gap.
AI.conclusion: The results support evaluating manuscript HTR as auditable evidence management, enabling bounded alternative readings and auditable provenance, with domain-adaptive training (via forgetting guards) and an evidence-aware review workflow that preserves visual evidence and allows researchers to finalize decisions.

title: Interaction valence reveals contrasting social networks in dairy cattle
summary: Social relationships shape access to resources, exposure to conflict and group stability, yet automated livestock monitoring typically treats behaviour as isolated events. Here, we present a valence-aware social-network framework that transforms video-derived interactions into herd-level representations of affiliative and agonistic organization. A pose-based computer-vision pipeline analysed 7 h 39 min of continuous video from the pre-milking area of one commercial dairy farm. After quality control, 1,183 of 1,414 candidate interactions remained, involving 36 cows and 177 dyads. In a predicted-class-balanced audit of 198 pipeline-detected clips, automated and manual labels agreed in 82.8% of cases, with an unweighted audit-sample macro-F1 of 0.872. These values describe the audited sample rather than prevalence-weighted or end-to-end deployment performance. The aggregated network was connected (density = 0.281; transitivity = 0.513; mean path length = 1.88), and predicted affiliative events formed five algorithmic communities (modularity Q = 0.429). Within the observed zone, predicted agonistic interactions comprised 72.4% of retained events and 76.0% of interaction duration. The cow with the most partners did not have the highest betweenness centrality. Separating events by predicted valence produced descriptively different affiliative and agonistic layers, with contrasting edge sets, community partitions and individual positions. Thus, pooled interaction counts can obscure the behavioural composition of an observed network. Valence-aware analysis provides a framework for testing hypotheses about competition, affiliation and welfare-relevant change, while requiring longitudinal validation before use as a welfare or health indicator.

AI.tldr: A valence-aware social-network framework for automated livestock monitoring converts video-derived interactions into herd-level affiliative and agonistic networks; validated on ~7.5 hours of dairy-farm video with good automated–manual label agreement; reveals that valence separation changes network structure and emphasizes the need for longitudinal validation before welfare deployment.
AI.motivation: Address the limitation of treating livestock behavior as isolated events by capturing social structure and valence (affiliative vs. agonistic) to better understand competition, affiliation, and welfare-relevant changes.
AI.method: Pose-based computer-vision pipeline processed 7 h 39 min of video from a pre-milking area; quality control yielded 1,183 of 1,414 candidate interactions among 36 cows and 177 dyads. An audit of 198 predicted clips showed 82.8% automated–manual label agreement and macro-F1 of 0.872. Constructed aggregated social network and analyzed its properties (density, transitivity, mean path length, modularity). Separated events by valence to produce distinct affiliative and agonistic layers and communities.
AI.result: Network was connected (density 0.281; transitivity 0.513; mean path length 1.88). Predicted affiliative events formed five algorithmic communities (modularity Q = 0.429). Agonistic interactions accounted for 72.4% of events and 76.0% of duration within retained interactions. The most-connected cow did not have the highest betweenness. Valence-based separation yielded descriptively different edge sets, communities, and individual positions, indicating pooling may obscure behavioral composition.
AI.conclusion: Valence-aware analysis provides a framework for testing hypotheses about competition, affiliation, and welfare-relevant changes, but longitudinal validation is required before using these metrics as welfare or health indicators.

title: Quantifying Event Impacts on Time Series via Multiscale Contrastive Learning
summary: Shocks that spread through the web, such as cybersecurity breach disclosures, can abruptly disrupt financial time series and cause substantial abnormal losses. While these events are disclosed as discrete records through news reports, regulatory filings, or public databases, their consequences unfold through continuous market dynamics. This creates an event-conditioned impact prediction problem: given pre-event market history and limited event metadata, the goal is to estimate short-term post-disclosure abnormal loss rather than reconstruct the full post-event trajectory. However, most time-series forecasting models focus on endogenous regularities such as trend, seasonality, and autocorrelation, and thus struggle with rare and heterogeneous external events. The challenge is further amplified by sparse high-impact events and background market noise. We introduce EventTime, a multi-resolution framework that combines long-horizon market context, short-horizon pre-event dynamics, and event metadata. It incorporates an event fusion module that couples temporal representations with event attributes to identify relevant recent market patterns. To mitigate sparse supervision, EventTime further introduces a dynamic contrastive objective that constructs event- and time-series-aware positive and negative pairs during training. We also construct SECURE, a real-world dataset aligning cybersecurity incidents with stock-market time series and structured and LLM-derived semantic features. Experiments show that EventTime consistently outperforms state-of-the-art time-series and event-aware baselines in estimating post-event financial losses. Further analyses demonstrate more event-sensitive representations, greater robustness to incomplete metadata, and more interpretable estimates of short-term market impact following cybersecurity disclosures.

AI.tldr: EventTime is a multi-resolution framework for predicting short-term post-disclosure abnormal losses from cybersecurity events, using an event fusion module and a dynamic contrastive objective, validated on the SECURE dataset with improved performance over baselines.
AI.motivation: Financial time series are disrupted by rare, heterogeneous external events (e.g., cybersecurity disclosures). Predicting immediate losses requires leveraging long-horizon market context, short-horizon pre-event dynamics, and event metadata; standard time-series models struggle with sparse supervision and non-stationarity.
AI.method: A multi-resolution architecture that fuses long-horizon market context, short-horizon pre-event dynamics, and event metadata via an event fusion module. A dynamic contrastive objective creates event- and time-series-aware positive/negative pairs to train robust representations. A real-world SECURE dataset aligns cybersecurity incidents with stock-market data and includes structured and LLM-derived semantic features.
AI.result: EventTime consistently outperforms state-of-the-art time-series and event-aware baselines in estimating post-event financial losses. Analyses show more event-sensitive representations, robustness to incomplete metadata, and more interpretable short-term impact estimates.
AI.conclusion: EventTime advances event-conditioned financial risk forecasting by integrating multi-resolution context and adaptive supervision, and is validated on a real-world dataset, showing practical applicability.

title: When Automata Meet Streams: Temporal Logic Compilation for Stream-Based Robotics Task and Motion Planning
summary: Stream-based robotics Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) integrates discrete symbolic planning with dynamically generated continuous geometric parameters, such as poses, grasps, and trajectories. However, stream-based planners typically reason only about goal reachability, whereas long-horizon tasks also demand adherence to temporal specifications, such as safety-critical ordering, invariance, and liveness constraints. No methods currently exist to enforce such temporal constraints for stream-based solvers because streams generate an expanding geometric object set via iterative stream refinement loops during planning, rendering existing temporal-logic compilation techniques incompatible. We therefore present Synchronous Action Monitoring with Token Destruction (SAM-TD), a compilation method that enforces arbitrary Linear Temporal Logic over finite traces ($\textrm{LTL}_f$) specifications in stream-based TAMP. SAM-TD translates arbitrary $\textrm{LTL}_f$ constraints into automata and embeds regressed automaton guards into action schemas, which are pre-specified before planning begins. By doing so, SAM-TD can handle objects generated by streams during planning, thus circumventing the need to enumerate a fixed object set or modify the underlying planner. During search, SAM-TD synchronously updates automaton states and uses a validity token shared across all automata to prune constraint-violating branches. We show that SAM-TD supports dynamically generated stream objects from iterative stream refinements during plan search. Experimental results provide the first ever demonstration of stream-based TAMP under $\textrm{LTL}_f$ constraints in three robotics PDDLStream environments. Furthermore, on standard discrete PDDL benchmarks, SAM-TD is competitive with state-of-the-art temporal-constraint compilation methods.

AI.tldr: SAM-TD enables LTL_f temporal constraints in stream-based TAMP by translating LTL_f into automata, embedding regressed automaton guards into action schemas, and synchronously updating automata with a shared validity token to prune constraint-violating branches, handling dynamically generated stream objects during planning.
AI.motivation: There is a need to enforce temporal specifications (safety, invariance, liveness) in stream-based TAMP, but existing methods fail due to dynamic, expanding object sets from streams; enabling LTL_f constraints without fixing object sets or modifying the planner closes a key gap.
AI.method: Translate LTL_f to automata; embed regressed automaton guards into pre-specified action schemas; use a shared validity token across automata; synchronously update automaton states during search; allow dynamically generated stream objects from iterative stream refinements; no enumeration of fixed object set or planner modification.
AI.result: First demonstration of stream-based TAMP under LTL_f constraints in three robotics PDDLStream environments; SAM-TD also performs competitively on standard discrete PDDL benchmarks compared to state-of-the-art temporal-constraint compilation methods.
AI.conclusion: SAM-TD provides a practical framework for enforcing arbitrary LTL_f constraints in stream-based TAMP, enabling long-horizon temporal guarantees without altering the underlying planner or requiring a fixed object set.

title: HiRA-CAM: Preserving Fine-Grained Spatial Relevance in Gradient-Based Visual Explanations
comment: IEEE World Congress on Computational Intelligence, Maastricht, Netherlands, June 2026
summary: Deep Learning models can include billions of parameters or more, making it difficult to explain their internal transformations and outputs. However, explainability is increasing in importance due to the use of AI in crucial applications. This paper focuses on the interpretability of convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Building on the popular gradient based method LayerCAM for extracting internal features in CNNs, we propose an improved method named HiRA-CAM, and show that it outperforms both LayerCAM and Grad-CAM on creating useful saliency maps for object classification. The main feature of HiRA-CAM is its adaptive use of activation maps from all the layers of the CNN to arrive at a more focused saliency map.

AI.tldr: HiRA-CAM adaptively fuses activation maps from all CNN layers to produce focused saliency maps, outperforming LayerCAM and Grad-CAM for object classification.
AI.motivation: Improve interpretability of convolutional neural networks by generating higher-quality saliency maps. LayerCAM and Grad-CAM rely on limited layer information; integrating multi-layer activations can yield more precise explanations.
AI.method: Propose HiRA-CAM, an extension of LayerCAM that adaptively combines activation maps from all CNN layers to produce saliency maps, resulting in more focused explanations for object classification.
