AI.result: HiRA-CAM yields more useful saliency maps and outperforms LayerCAM and Grad-CAM in object classification tasks.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive multi-layer activation map fusion enhances interpretability of CNNs; HiRA-CAM provides superior saliency maps compared to existing gradient-based methods.

title: Air Traffic Control Using Large Language Models: Prompt Engineering, Architecture, and Evaluation
summary: Air traffic control (ATC) communication is a safety-critical dialogue that remains largely human-driven even as other parts of air traffic management have been semi-automated. In this article, we experimentally evaluate whether large language models (LLMs) can generate operationally realistic ATC transmissions. An experimental general-aviation flight flying over the San Francisco "Bay Tour" route is hand-transcribed and used as ground truth (P0). Through a pilot-in-the-loop process we design five prompt structures (P1-P5) of increasing constraint and embed them in a stateful multi-turn pipeline, where the model plays ATC to a fixed pilot transcript while conditioning on the accumulating dialogue history. Across nine open- and closed-source LLMs we vary the prompt, the presence of a worked transcript from a different experimental flight as an in-context example, and whether the model conditions on its own prior replies or on injected ground-truth history. Turns are scored with lexical, structural, and semantic similarity metrics and by an LLM-as-judge (GPT-5.5) validated against human expert annotation. Supplying a worked example improves similarity, but tightening the prompt does not: the lightest prompts perform best and the most heavily scripted one collapses as its own errors accumulate through the dialogue, which injecting correct history repairs. These results outline a concrete path and its current limits toward LLM-assisted ATC.

AI.tldr: LLMs can generate operationally realistic ATC transmissions in a pilot-in-the-loop setting, but prompt design matters; worked-example prompts help, while overly scripted prompts fail as errors accumulate; injecting correct history can repair performance.
AI.motivation: Evaluate feasibility and design constraints for using large language models to assist ATC communications and identify practical limits and design guidelines.
AI.method: Pilot-in-the-loop experimentation using a transcribed Bay Tour flight as ground truth (P0). Five prompt structures (P1-P5) of increasing constraint embedded in a stateful multi-turn pipeline where the model answers as ATC to a fixed pilot transcript, conditioning on dialogue history. Nine LLMs tested across prompt variations, with and without in-context worked transcripts and with different conditioning on prior replies vs injected history. Outputs evaluated via lexical, structural, and semantic similarity metrics and by an LLM judge (GPT-5.5) validated against human expert annotations.
AI.result: Supplying a worked example improves similarity; tightening prompts does not improve and can degrade performance. Light prompts perform best; heavily scripted prompts collapse as errors accumulate unless corrected by injecting ground-truth history. The approach shows a concrete path but current limits for LLM-assisted ATC.
AI.conclusion: The study identifies a viable pathway toward LLM-assisted ATC while highlighting key constraints—prompt structure, in-context examples, and history conditioning—that determine reliability; further work is needed to address error accumulation and safety in operational deployments.

title: LLM as Detector: An In-context Learning Approach for Tabular Anomaly Detection
comment: Accepted at International Conference on Neural Information Processing (ICONIP) 2026
summary: Anomaly detection in tabular data is challenging because abnormal samples often arise as violations of cross-feature dependencies rather than simple marginal deviations. Existing detectors rely on geometric or reconstruction signals, while prior LLM-based approaches mainly fine-tune LLMs with normal samples or generate synthetic anomalies. We propose LLM-Detector, a framework that utilizes the in-context learning capacity of LLMs for structured, prompt-conditioned scoring synthesis, enabling LLMs to derive anomaly detection logic from structured normal-state knowledge. Specifically, normal training data are converted into statistical summaries, causal dependencies, and distilled prototypes that are organized into a prompt for code generation. The resulting scoring engine evaluates statistical deviation, structural inconsistency, and density-based abnormality then computes an anomaly score for each test sample. We evaluate LLM-Detector on 24 tabular datasets, comparing against 15 SOTA baselines. Results show consistent improvements across both mixed-type and continuous-only settings. Moreover, this design eliminates the need for LLM fine-tuning or neural network training, reducing computational cost and enabling practical anomaly detection in real-world tabular systems.

AI.tldr: LLM-Detector uses in-context learning with prompt-generated statistics, dependencies, and prototypes to score anomalies in tabular data without LLM fine-tuning, outperforming 15 baselines on 24 datasets.
AI.motivation: Anomalies often violate cross-feature dependencies; existing detectors rely on geometric or reconstruction signals; prior LLM-based approaches require fine-tuning or synthetic anomalies, limiting practicality.
AI.method: Convert normal data into statistical summaries, causal dependencies, and distilled prototypes; assemble these into a prompt for a code-generating LLM; a scoring engine evaluates statistical deviation, structural inconsistency, and density-based abnormality to produce per-sample anomaly scores.
AI.result: Evaluated on 24 tabular datasets against 15 SOTA baselines; consistent improvements for both mixed-type and continuous-only data; eliminates the need for LLM fine-tuning or neural network training, reducing computational cost.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates that LLMs can learn anomaly detection logic from structured normal-state knowledge via prompts, enabling cost-efficient, practical anomaly detection for real-world tabular systems.

title: Fine-Tuning VLAs with Self-Demonstrated Generative Control for Multi-Task Manipulation
summary: State-of-the-art vision-language-action (VLA) models such as $π_{0.5}$ exhibit strong semantic understanding, instruction following and task behavior. However, when deployed on new robots, even minor mismatches in hardware configuration relative to pretraining can cause severe performance drops. Finetuning the VLA on in-domain expert data from the new embodiment improves performance on the expert task but leads to a loss in its original instruction following and behavioral priors. In this paper, we propose a self-supervised method that generates online interaction rollouts from the zero-shot VLA as additional training data for finetuning. Our experiments show this finetuning scheme yields strong multi-task policies that, on the target robot, (1) inherit prior tasks distilled from the zero-shot model, (2) enable generalist instruction following, while (3) learning new skills from expert data with improved sample efficiency. We demonstrate the success of our approach across test sets probing generalization on a real ALOHA robot and a new simulation benchmark in RoboTwin. Video results are available at https://self-supervised-control.pages.dev/

AI.tldr: Self-supervised rollout augmentation for fine-tuning vision-language-action models preserves priors while adapting to a new robot embodiment, enabling generalist instruction following and efficient learning of new skills.
AI.motivation: Deploying VLA models on new hardware often causes performance drops due to embodiment mismatch. Fine-tuning on expert in-domain data improves task performance but can erode original instruction-following behavior and priors.
AI.method: Generate online interaction rollouts from the zero-shot VLA in a self-supervised manner and use these as additional training data for finetuning on the target robot, aiming to preserve priors while enabling adaptation and new skill acquisition.
AI.result: Finetuning with self-supervised rollouts yields multi-task policies on the target robot that (1) inherit prior tasks distilled from the zero-shot model, (2) support generalist instruction following, and (3) learn new skills from expert data with improved sample efficiency, demonstrated on a real ALOHA robot and a RoboTwin simulation benchmark.
AI.conclusion: A rollout-based self-supervised finetuning approach effectively mitigates embodiment mismatch, preserving pretrained priors while enabling robust adaptation and efficient acquisition of new skills.

title: VideoRun2D Demo: Markerless Body Tracking for Biomechanical Analysis of Running
comment: 5 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables. IEEE/CVF Conf. on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition Workshops (CVPRW), 2026 (1st PhysHuman Workshop: Physically Grounded Human Perception and Modeling)
summary: Human pose estimation has advanced significantly due to the development of deep learning models, increased data availability, and improved computing resources. These developments have led to highly accurate body tracking systems with direct applications in sports analysis and performance evaluation. The VideoRun2D Demo performs a biomechanical analysis during sprints using different human pose estimators. The proposed framework was evaluated using human pose trackers and expert manual annotations. The tested framework uses 314 sprints from 44 professional runners, focusing on two key joint angles in sprint biomechanics: 1) hip flexion/extension and 2) knee flexion/extension. The framework also includes a post-processing module for outlier detection. The tested results demonstrate that the average root-mean-square errors range from 11.46° to 5.83° for the best trackers. When integrated with the post-processing modules, these errors can be reduced to 9.87° and 5.30°, respectively. The VideoRun2D Demo findings suggest that human pose-tracking approaches can be valuable resources for the biomechanical analysis of running.

AI.tldr: VideoRun2D Demo demonstrates biomechanical analysis of sprinting using pose estimators; two key joint angles (hip and knee) with post-processing; RMSE improves with post-processing.
AI.motivation: Enable scalable, markerless biomechanical analysis of running performance using video-based pose estimation, reducing manual annotation burden.
AI.method: Evaluate multiple pose trackers on 314 sprints from 44 professional runners; compute hip flexion/extension and knee flexion/extension angles; compare to expert annotations; apply post-processing for outlier detection; report RMSE.
AI.result: Best trackers yield RMSE 11.46° (hip) and 5.83° (knee); with post-processing reduced to 9.87° (hip) and 5.30° (knee). Indicates viability of pose-tracking for sprint biomechanics.
AI.conclusion: Pose-tracking is a valuable resource for running biomechanics analysis, especially when combined with post-processing; useful for performance analysis, but further work necessary to broaden joint coverage and ensure robustness.

title: Outcome Monitors: Recovery Affordances for Silent Tool Failures
comment: 16 pages (9 main + 7 pages supplementary material), 3 figures
summary: When a tool call times out, the agent sees the failure and can route around it. A cached error page or negative price can instead arrive in the expected format and be consumed as fact. We introduce Outcome Monitors, which detect violations of outcome contracts mined from task-disjoint traces or derived from public schemas. On a violation, the monitor preserves the result and issues a nonbinding receipt naming the violated property and public recovery tools. In frozen, prespecified evaluations with injected failures, Outcome Monitors raise ToolMaze completion from 10.9% to 28.1% across four models in two provider families and replicate in a third. In tau-bench retail, completion improves by 14.0 and 12.0 points on two tiers. In separate ToolMaze controls, removing the recovery-tool list eliminates the measured gain and restoring it recovers the effect; diagnostic detail and timing produce no detectable differences. Gains concentrate where the fault blocks completion. On a suite transcribed from a published incident taxonomy, detection outside the mined vocabulary falls to 46%, though delivery continues and completion is unchanged. Recovery tools are the active receipt content in these controls; extending detection beyond the contract vocabulary remains open.

AI.tldr: Outcome Monitors detect violations of mined outcome contracts during tool use, preserve failed results, and provide nonbinding receipts plus recovery tools. They substantially boost completion rates in fault-injection benchmarks, but gains hinge on recovery-tool availability and vocabulary coverage; extending detection beyond mined vocab is necessary.
AI.motivation: Improve robustness of autonomous agents when tools fail or time out by surfacing recoverable information and enabling structured recovery workflows.
AI.method: Mine outcome contracts from task-disjoint traces or public schemas. Deploy monitors to detect violations; on violation, preserve the claimed result and issue a nonbinding receipt listing the violated property and available recovery tools. Evaluate in controlled injections across multiple models/provider families and in a retail benchmark, with ablations removing/reinstating the recovery-tool list and assessing detection beyond the mined vocabulary.
AI.result: Completion rates rise from 10.9% to 28.1% in a multi-model, multi-provider setup; improvements of 14.0 and 12.0 points in another benchmark tier. Removing the recovery-tool list eliminates the gain; restoring it recovers the effect. Detection outside the mined vocabulary reaches 46% but completion remains unchanged, indicating limited impact of non-detected failures. Recovery tool content is the active signal; extending detection beyond the contract vocabulary remains an open issue.
AI.conclusion: Outcome Monitors can meaningfully improve task completion under tool failures when paired with explicit recovery tools, but their effectiveness hinges on vocabulary coverage and explicit receipt content. Extending detection beyond the mined contracts is a key direction for future work.

title: When to Retrain: An Empirical Study of Retraining Policies for Streaming ML Under Concept Drift, Budget, and Latency Constraints
comment: 16 pages, 7 figures, 7 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/sa1dasari/Study-of-Drift-Triggered-Retraining-Policies-Under-Budget-and-Latency-Constraints
summary: Production machine learning systems degrade under concept drift, yet practitioners have little principled guidance on when to retrain. Retraining is costly, retraining budgets are finite, and a retrained model does not take effect instantly: training and deployment latency leave a stale model serving predictions while the data continues to move. We present a controlled empirical study of three practical model-refresh policies (periodic retraining, error-threshold triggering, and statistical drift-triggered retraining with ADWIN) against a no-retrain baseline, evaluated under a unified system model that makes retraining budgets and training-plus-deployment latency explicit. Across 3,933 experiment runs spanning three drift regimes, three budget levels, up to five latency levels, three datasets, and two learning modes, we find that the single most consequential design decision is not the retraining policy but whether the deployed model learns incrementally. With per-sample incremental updates, and for the linear online learner with immediate labels studied here, no policy differs from the no-retrain baseline by a practically significant margin in any of 54 paired comparisons, even at extreme latency. Without incremental updates, policy choice separates outcomes by 15-55 percentage points of post-drift accuracy, and simple periodic retraining significantly outperforms both reactive policies under abrupt and gradual drift, while reactive policies retain an advantage only under recurring drift. We document systematic failure modes of reactive policies and a latency-budget queueing interaction that silently halves effective retraining budgets, and release the full simulator, dataset pipelines, and per-run artifacts for reproducibility.

AI.tldr: Incremental learning capability dominates retraining policy in production ML under drift; with per-sample online updates, most retrain policies are indistinguishable from no retrain; without incremental updates, simple periodic retraining often beats reactive policies, and latency-budget constraints can halve retraining budgets.
AI.motivation: Production ML models degrade due to concept drift; practitioners face costly retraining under finite budgets and nonzero latency. There is a lack of principled guidance on when to retrain; this study aims to compare common refresh policies under an explicit system model.
AI.method: Controlled empirical study with 3,933 runs across three drift regimes, three budget levels, up to five latency levels, three datasets, and two learning modes. Compared policies: periodic retraining, error-threshold triggering, and ADWIN drift-triggered retraining, plus a no-retrain baseline. Evaluates under a unified system model with explicit retraining budgets and training-plus-deployment latency. Uses a linear online learner with immediate labels in one setting (incremental updates) and a non-incremental setting to assess policy impact. Releases simulator, pipelines, and per-run artifacts for reproducibility.
AI.result: Incremental updates are decisive: with per-sample incremental updates, no retraining policy shows practically significant improvement over the no-retrain baseline across 54 paired comparisons. Without incremental updates, policy choice causes large accuracy differences (15–55 percentage points post-drift). Periodic retraining outperforms reactive policies under abrupt/gradual drift when no incremental learning is used, while reactive policies help only under recurring drift. Reactive policies exhibit systematic failure modes and interact with latency budgets via queueing, effectively halving retraining budgets. All data, simulators, and artifacts are released for reproducibility.
AI.conclusion: The key design decision is whether the deployed model supports incremental (online) learning. If incremental updates are possible, retraining policy has negligible practical impact. If not, periodic retraining tends to outperform reactive strategies under most drift scenarios. Systems should prioritize enabling incremental updates and carefully model latency-budget interactions to avoid budget waste; otherwise, reactive policies can underperform or waste resources.

title: LF-GICP: Parameter-Free Degeneracy-Aware LiDAR Odometry via a Voxel-Normal Localizability Field
summary: Scan-to-map LiDAR odometry drifts unboundedly along the unobservable axes of geometrically degenerate environments like tunnels and corridors, and existing degeneracy handling requires environment-specific parameter tuning. This paper presents a parameter-free approach. We show that in voxelized GICP the Gauss--Newton (GN) Hessian masks translational degeneracy, because covariance regularization keeps the translation block artificially well-conditioned. We bypass this with a regularization-free voxel-normal localizability field and two of its statistics: a normalized fraction $f_0$ detecting directional anisotropy, and an absolute per-voxel mass $λ_0$ distinguishing information absence (tunnels) from dilution (dense open scenes). A temporal-median gate combines both to trigger Fisher-information correspondence weighting. Calibrated once by fixed rules on two short sequences and then frozen, LF-GICP achieves the lowest KITTI relative translation error ($0.865\%$) under an identical evaluation protocol against re-run baselines, outperforms them on GEODE tunnels and MulRan, leads the HeLiPR mean, and generalizes across four sensor types without re-tuning. We further demonstrate empirically that straight, uniform tunnels remain unobservable along their axis for LiDAR-only registration.

AI.tldr: Parameter-free degeneracy-aware LiDAR odometry (LF-GICP) uses a regularization-free voxel-normal localizability field with f0 and λ0 and a temporal median gate to weight Fisher information, achieving state-of-the-art KITTI results and generalizing across sensors, while acknowledging unobservability in straight tunnels.
AI.motivation: Scan-to-map LiDAR odometry drifts unboundedly along unobservable axes in geometrically degenerate environments (e.g., tunnels, corridors); existing degeneracy handling requires environment-specific parameter tuning. A parameter-free solution is sought.
AI.method: Introduce a voxel-normal localizability field (regularization-free) and two statistics: f0 (normalized fraction detecting directional anisotropy) and λ0 (per-voxel mass distinguishing information absence from dilution). Use a temporal-median gate to combine these to trigger Fisher-information correspondence weighting. Calibrate once with fixed rules on two short sequences and then freeze. LF-GICP generalizes across four sensor types without re-tuning.
AI.result: LF-GICP achieves the lowest KITTI relative translation error (0.865%) under identical evaluation protocol, outperforming re-run baselines, GEODE tunnels, and MulRan; leads the HeLiPR mean; generalizes across four sensor types without re-tuning.
AI.conclusion: Straight, uniform tunnels remain unobservable along their axis for LiDAR-only registration, highlighting persistent degeneracy in certain unobservable directions despite the parameter-free approach.

title: A Plug-in Interpretation of Conditioning in Score-Based Diffusion Models
summary: We propose a conditioning mechanism for diffusion models based on multi-speed joint diffusion of the target and the condition. The mechanism learns an unconditional joint score network and enforces conditioning at inference via a plug-in correction term. The plug-in term separates the conditioning contribution from the learned unconditional dynamics, offering a transparent view of how the condition steers generation of the target distribution. Building on this, we derive explicit conditional reverse-time SDEs and approximate probability-flow ODEs, enabling principled and directly comparable conditional samplers. To reduce the induced ODE--SDE discrepancy, we introduce a log-Fokker--Planck residual regularization that improves ODE sampling quality. Experiments on conditional image generation tasks demonstrate competitive performance and support the effectiveness of the plug-in conditioning view. Additional ODE--SDE comparison experiments show that the log-Fokker--Planck residual regularization improves deterministic ODE sampling.

AI.tldr: Proposes a plug-in conditioning framework for diffusion models using a multi-speed joint diffusion of target and condition with an unconditional joint score network. Introduces a plug-in correction term for conditioning, derives conditional reverse-time SDEs and approximate probability-flow ODEs, and adds a log-Fokker–Planck residual to reduce ODE–SDE mismatch. Demonstrates competitive conditional image generation and improved deterministic ODE sampling.
AI.motivation: To enable transparent, principled conditioning in diffusion models, enabling direct comparison between conditional samplers and providing interpretable conditioning contributions; to address the gap between SDE and ODE formulations and improve sampling quality.
AI.method: 1) Train an unconditional joint score network on the target and conditioning variables via a multi-speed joint diffusion process. 2) At inference, apply a plug-in correction term to enforce conditioning while separating its influence from the learned unconditional dynamics. 3) Derive explicit conditional reverse-time SDEs and approximate probability-flow ODEs. 4) Introduce a log-Fokker–Planck residual regularization to reduce ODE–SDE discrepancy and improve deterministic ODE sampling. 5) Evaluate on conditional image generation tasks and perform ODE–SDE comparisons.
AI.result: The proposed approach achieves competitive performance on conditional image generation, and the plug-in conditioning view provides interpretability of the conditioning effect. The log-Fokker–Planck residual regularization improves deterministic ODE sampling and reduces ODE–SDE mismatch.
AI.conclusion: A plug-in conditioning framework with a multi-speed joint diffusion enhances interpretability and principled conditional sampling. The explicit conditional SDEs/ODEs enable fair comparisons, and the log-FP residual stabilizes and improves ODE-based sampling.

title: Beyond Imitation: Filtering On-Policy Distillation by Reasoning Progress
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) has emerged as an effective framework for post-training language models by pairing student-generated trajectories with dense token-level supervision from a teacher. However, OPD implicitly assumes that teacher-derived rewards are an appropriate proxy for reasoning progress, and therefore treats all teacher feedback equally during policy optimization. While in practice, this assumption does not always hold. We observe that teacher-derived rewards often conflict with genuine reasoning progress, as reasoning steps with clear reasoning advancement may still receive lower distillation rewards, simply due to deviation from teacher's outputs. To address this mismatch, we propose Reasoning-Progress-Aware Reward Filtering for On-Policy Distillation (R2-OPD), which constructs two within-trajectory rankings of reasoning spans, one from teacher-derived rewards and the other from independently estimated progress reward. Distillation rewards are selectively suppressed whenever the two rankings disagree, reducing supervision that conflicts with reasoning progress while preserving effective teacher guidance. Our approach shows consistent improvement over standard OPD especially regarding reasoning performances.

AI.tldr: Proposes Reasoning-Progress-Aware Reward Filtering for On-Policy Distillation (R2-OPD) to suppress teacher-derived rewards when they conflict with independently estimated reasoning progress, improving reasoning capabilities in OPD.
AI.motivation: OPD assumes teacher rewards correlate with reasoning progress, but in practice they can diverge, causing supervision that hinders reasoning improvements.
AI.method: Compute two within-trajectory rankings of reasoning spans: one from teacher-derived rewards, one from an independently estimated progress reward. Suppress distillation rewards when the two rankings disagree, thereby aligning supervision with genuine progress while preserving useful teacher guidance.
AI.result: Consistent improvement over standard OPD, especially in reasoning performance.
AI.conclusion: Filtering rewards by reasoning-progress alignment mitigates mismatch between teacher signals and reasoning progress, yielding more effective OPD for reasoning tasks.

title: DeltaMomentum: A Key-Value based Anisotropic Momentum Update via Delta Rule
summary: Most modern optimizers form their momentum as an exponential moving average (EMA) of past gradients, forgetting every direction at one fixed rate. However, the inputs a deep network sees during training can be highly anisotropic, with a few directions queried frequently while most are seen rarely. Recent methods address this anisotropy by wrapping extra processing around this buffer, leaving the momentum update itself unchanged. We propose DeltaMomentum, which builds direction-awareness into the momentum update rule. The main observation is that the gradient of a linear layer splits into an input that acts as a key and an output-side error that acts as a value. Exploiting the key-value structure, DeltaMomentum updates the momentum buffer by the canonical delta rule, so each direction is forgotten at a rate set by how often it appears. We prove that it is a valid momentum, that it applies the input-side curvature correction without matrix inversion, and that it clears stale directions faster than EMA under both a fixed and a drifting optimum. It is a drop-in replacement for the momentum buffer of any optimizer, its coefficient transfers across widths under $μ$P, and its extra compute stays between $22.2\%$ and $25.0\%$ of a gated-MLP block's linear cost with no persistent memory. In FineWeb-Edu pretraining, AdamW with DeltaMomentum (DeltaAdamW) reaches AdamW's validation loss in up to $46.39 \pm 4.32\%$ fewer steps at 67M and $22.12 \pm 0.80\%$ at 370M over three seeds, and the gain persists at 1B on a Chinchilla-optimal budget. A Muon baseline tuned under the same protocol sits above DeltaAdamW at both language-model scales, and the gain holds for SGD, ResNet-18, and ViT-Tiny on CIFAR-10. Training-time diagnostics confirm the predicted mechanism, better gradient tracking and healthier input directions.

AI.tldr: DeltaMomentum introduces direction-aware momentum via a delta-rule that uses the gradient's input-key/value decomposition to forget directions at a rate proportional to their appearance frequency; it is a drop-in replacement for momentum with modest compute and broad applicability.
AI.motivation: Standard EMA momentum treats all gradient directions with a fixed forgetting rate, which is suboptimal for anisotropic training where some directions (features) are queried far more often than others.
AI.method: Modeling the gradient of a linear layer as a key–value split, DeltaMomentum updates the momentum buffer according to the canonical delta rule, applying input-side curvature correction without matrix inversion. It preserves a momentum-like accumulator with direction-aware forgetting rates, transferability across widths (μP), and modest extra compute (22.2%–25.0% of a gated-MLP block’s linear cost) and no persistent memory.
AI.result: DeltaMomentum–enabled optimizers (DeltaAdamW, etc.) reach the same validation loss with substantially fewer steps in FineWeb-Edu pretraining (46.39%±4.32% fewer at 67M; 22.12%±0.80% fewer at 370M across three seeds), with gains persisting at 1B on a budget-aligned Chinchilla setting. It also outperforms Muon and yields benefits when used with SGD, ResNet-18, and ViT-Tiny on CIFAR-10; training-time diagnostics corroborate improved gradient tracking and healthier input directions.
AI.conclusion: DeltaMomentum offers a practical, general-purpose improvement to momentum-based optimizers by injecting direction-aware forgetting, enabling faster convergence and healthier optimization dynamics across architectures and scales without incurring heavy memory or inversion costs.

title: Multimodal Trajectory Planning for Surface Vehicles using Turning Circle-based Control Barrier Functions
comment: This work has been submitted to an Elsevier journal for possible publication
summary: This paper presents a guide path-free multimodal trajectory planning framework for autonomous surface vehicles operating in dynamic environments. The proposed method integrates model predictive control (MPC) with a turning circle-based control barrier function (TC-CBF). Unlike conventional Euclidean distance-based CBFs (ED-CBFs), which evaluate safety solely based on proximity, the TC-CBF accounts for the nonholonomic motion and finite turning capability of a surface vehicle. Its geometric formulation identifies feasible avoidance regions according to the vehicle's turning circles and generates distinct left- and right-turning avoidance modes. These modes allow the optimization solver to explore and select topologically different trajectories without relying on globally planned guide paths, as required by many conventional multimodal planning approaches. By embedding the avoidance direction directly into the safety constraint, the proposed framework alleviates the local-minimum and deadlock problems of single-mode MPC while maintaining computational efficiency. Extensive simulations involving multiple moving vessels demonstrate that the proposed method achieves higher success rates, fewer safety violations, and smaller residual violations than single-mode baselines across all tested traffic densities.

AI.tldr: Guide-path-free multimodal trajectory planning for autonomous surface vehicles using MPC with a turning circle-based CBF (TC-CBF) to account for nonholonomic constraints and finite turning ability, enabling distinct left/right avoidance modes without a global guide path.
AI.motivation: Conventional Euclidean-distance CBFs (ED-CBFs) ignore nonholonomic turning constraints and often rely on global guide paths, leading to deadlocks or suboptimal behavior in dynamic vessel traffic. A multimodal, guide-path-free approach can improve safety, openness to multiple avoidance strategies, and computational efficiency.
AI.method: Integrate model predictive control (MPC) with a turning circle-based control barrier function (TC-CBF). TC-CBF leverages turning-circle geometry to define feasible avoidance regions that respect the vehicle's turning capabilities and nonholonomic constraints, yielding separate left- and right-turning avoidance modes. These modes are embedded into the safety constraint to enable the optimizer to explore topologically distinct trajectories without a global guide path.
AI.result: Extensive simulations with multiple moving vessels show higher success rates, fewer safety violations, and smaller residual violations for the TC-CBF-based multimodal MPC compared to single-mode baselines across various traffic densities.
AI.conclusion: TC-CBF enables safe, topologically diverse, guide-path-free multimodal planning for surface vehicles. By embedding avoidance direction into the safety constraint, it mitigates local minima and deadlocks typical of single-mode MPC while maintaining computational efficiency.

title: CVSD-Reg: Cross-Modal Visual Semantic Prior Distillation for Robust LiDAR Registration
summary: Learning-based global point cloud registration has achieved remarkable progress, yet its reliance on geometric representations makes existing methods sensitive to variations in point density, scan pattern, viewpoint, and sensor characteristics. We propose CVSD-Reg, a robust global LiDAR registration framework that distills visual semantic priors from a vision foundation model into LiDAR representations. In Stage 1, a Point Transformer V3 student learns from a frozen DINOv2 teacher through contrastive distillation and spherical-manifold alignment, which preserves the hyperspherical geometry of the teacher embedding space. Self-supervised InfoNCE consistency and soft $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ invariance further encourage viewpoint-robust descriptors. In Stage 2, the distilled representation is adapted to registration through correspondence learning, density-aware point-dropout augmentation, and end-to-end pose optimization. With a single checkpoint, CVSD-Reg generalizes to both single-sensor and zero-shot cross-sensor scenarios without sensor-specific adaptation and remains entirely camera-free at inference. On KITTI, nuScenes, and HeLiPR, CVSD-Reg achieves strict success rate (SR@0.5\,m/$1^\circ$) of 97.7$\%$, 99.0$\%$, and 99.3$\%$, respectively, including 97.3$\%$ on sparse 16-beam Velodyne scans. It outperforms state-of-the-art geometric registration methods by up to 44.0 percentage points without requiring camera inputs or post-hoc ICP refinement.

AI.tldr: A robust, camera-free, single-checkpoint global LiDAR registration method (CVSD-Reg) that distills semantic priors from a vision foundation model to LiDAR embeddings, achieving high SR@0.5m/1° across KITTI, nuScenes, and HeLiPR, including sparse Velodyne, and outperforming geometric methods without ICP.
AI.motivation: Current learning-based LiDAR registration relies on geometric representations and is sensitive to point density, scan patterns, viewpoints, and sensor characteristics. There is a need for cross-sensor robustness and camera-free inference.
AI.method: Stage 1: A Point Transformer V3 student learns from a frozen DINOv2 teacher via contrastive distillation and spherical-manifold alignment to preserve hyperspherical geometry. Self-supervised InfoNCE consistency and soft SE(3) invariance promote viewpoint-robust descriptors. Stage 2: The distilled representation is adapted for registration through correspondence learning, density-aware point-dropout augmentation, and end-to-end pose optimization. A single checkpoint enables generalization to single-sensor and zero-shot cross-sensor scenarios, with no camera inputs at inference.
AI.result: On KITTI, nuScenes, and HeLiPR, CVSD-Reg achieves SR@0.5m/1° of 97.7%, 99.0%, and 99.3% respectively, including 97.3% on sparse 16-beam Velodyne scans, outperforming state-of-the-art geometric registration methods by up to 44.0 percentage points without camera inputs or ICP refinement.
AI.conclusion: The approach demonstrates strong cross-sensor generalization and robustness by distilling semantic priors from vision models into LiDAR representations, enabling camera-free, single-checkpoint registration with competitive or superior accuracy.

title: Symposium: Trust via Auditable Records for Communities of AI Scientist Agents
summary: Symposium is a formal framework and practical implementation to record the operation of AI agents deployed by small scientific research communities. Symposium provides long-term, immutable histories of agent-driven research activity, leaving auditable trails of analyses, hypotheses, data, and scientific discourse. This shared record of published artifacts enables agents to build on prior work and preserves the evidence researchers and agents need to make purpose-dependent trust assessments. Symposium captures scientific argument, including structured claims, fine-grained evidence citations, assumptions, and explicit declarations of what material may and may not be used as evidence. Symposium differs from AI co-scientist agents or integrated AI research environments; it is a framework that separates a scientific community's durable history from the agents and other systems that operate on that history. It assumes that a community will use diverse AI systems in a rapidly evolving environment. A working implementation of the publication infrastructure, agent prompt components, and documentation are provided to enable users to rapidly set up and run their own Symposium community.

AI.tldr: Symposium proposes a formal framework and practical implementation to record AI-driven scientific activity, yielding immutable, auditable histories with structured claims, fine-grained evidence, and explicit usage rules, decoupled from agents to support trust and cumulative knowledge across diverse AI tools.
AI.motivation: There is a need for durable, auditable records of agent-assisted research that enable reproducibility, trust assessments, and cumulative knowledge building within rapidly evolving AI ecosystems.
AI.method: A formal framework plus a working implementation to capture agent-driven research activity, including structured claims, fine-grained evidence citations, assumptions, and explicit declarations of what may be used as evidence; histories are immutable and separated from the agents that operate on them; designed for use with diverse AI systems.
AI.result: A working publication infrastructure, agent prompt components, and accompanying documentation enabling communities to rapidly set up and run their own Symposium-enabled workflows.
AI.conclusion: Symposium differentiates from AI co-scientist agents and integrated AI research environments by providing a durable, community-centered archive of research activity that preserves scientific discourse and evidence, facilitating purpose-dependent trust assessments across heterogeneous tools.

title: Beyond Multimodal Alignment: Certifying Physical Language through Response Substitution and Ordered Execution
summary: World models increasingly treat compact multimodal representations as interfaces between perception and physical interaction, yet existing probes do not establish whether different sensors carry the same executable meaning or whether that meaning survives a new action composition. We introduce an operational capability hierarchy and the Disjoint-Bridge Operator-Substitution Certificate (DBOSC), which asks whether independently trained modality compilers enter a frozen response chart interchangeably on evidence outside their training panels. On Cluster Haptic, audio and acceleration representations of the same unseen surface are 4.5x closer in response space than wrong-surface pairings, with the gap holding for all 19 held-out surfaces; unsealing withheld responses confirms that every branch predicts the physics better than the population chart. We then test ordered execution in a controlled elastoplastic system with complementary modality blind spots. At the pre-registered budget, the prerequisite refuses the stack because the frozen executor cannot advance even an exact chart coordinate through a held-out program. At a converged budget, the same rank-three chart executes those programs (oracle NMSE 0.18), fusion improves on both modalities, and 14 of 16 registered checks pass; the two failures arise because a diagonal restriction of the fused information matrix performs as well as the full one. Clearing the gate is a property of the executor, not the chart: an executor emitting whole programs instead of shared per-step dynamics is 38x worse than an entity-blind predictor on the same chart. A matching non-identifiability result explains why compression and fusion alone cannot determine an unseen composition law. These results separate attribute access, response substitution, fusion closure, and ordered execution into distinct, separately testable achievements.

AI.tldr: Introduces the Disjoint-Bridge Operator-Substitution Certificate (DBOSC) and an operational capability hierarchy to test whether multimodal representations carry consistent executable meaning across sensors and actions, and to distinguish separate capabilities (attribute access, response substitution, fusion closure, ordered execution) in multimodal systems.
AI.motivation: To determine whether compact multimodal representations defined by perception–action interfaces preserve the same executable semantics across different sensors and when composing actions, and to separate distinct capabilities involved in cross-modal reasoning and execution.
AI.method: Propose DBOSC as an evaluation protocol applied to Cluster Haptic data (audio and acceleration) for unseen surfaces, measuring cross-modal proximity in response space and the fidelity of withheld responses. Test ordered execution in a controlled elastoplastic system with modality blind spots, comparing pre-registered and converged budgets, fusion effects, and per-step versus whole-program execution. Use metrics like NMSE and chart-based assessments, and analyze identifiability and information matrix constraints to diagnose failures.
AI.result: Empirical findings show that representations of the same unseen surface across audio and acceleration are 4.5x closer in response space than mismatched surfaces, with a consistent gap across 19 held-out surfaces; withheld-response unsealing confirms physics predictions outperform population charts. In elastoplastic tests, pre-registered budget blocks execution; converged budget enables rank-3 chart execution with NMSE ≈0.18, and fusion improves performance with most checks passing (14/16); failures trace to a diagonal restriction of the fused information matrix. The executor (emitting whole programs) performs far worse than a per-step predictor. Non-identifiability explains why compression and fusion alone cannot determine the unseen composition law. The work delineates attribute access, response substitution, fusion closure, and ordered execution as separable, testable achievements.
AI.conclusion: The study delineates distinct, testable capabilities essential for reliable cross-modal semantics and action composition. It shows that while fusion and cross-modal alignment can improve physics-based predictions, true orderable execution depends on executor properties and is not determined by representation fusion alone, underscoring the need for separate validation of each capability.

title: HiTac-WAM: A Hierarchical Tactile World Action Model for Contact-Rich Robot Manipulation
summary: World action models jointly predict future visual observations and actions, whereas existing tactile-aware variants typically represent future touch as an image or latent stream without modeling the physical dependencies that organize tactile states hierarchically. We present HiTac-WAM, a hierarchical tactile world action model that forecasts a sequence of future tactile states for each candidate action chunk before execution. The forecast factorizes into contact state, a 3D deformation field, and slip risk, organized as a directed hierarchy in which each downstream stage is conditioned on stop-gradient signals from preceding stages. A directed attention mask allows tactile queries to attend to the video-action context of each candidate while preventing video and action queries from attending to tactile tokens. For planning, HiTac-WAM ranks candidate action chunks using tactile forecasts and task-progress estimates. For execution, the selected tactile forecast is retained as a reference; persistent discrepancies between predicted and observed tactile states trigger corrective replanning. HiTac-WAM achieves a mean contact F1 of 0.921; under matched training budgets, the directed hierarchy reduces 3D displacement L2 error by 17.6% relative to the deformation-only predictor and improves slip AUPRC by 60.4% relative to the slip-only predictor. Across chip grasping, blackboard erasing, and USB insertion, selection guided by the hierarchical forecasts increases the average real-robot success rate from 31.1% to 61.1%, while the full system attains 72.2%.

AI.tldr: HiTac-WAM introduces a hierarchical tactile world action model that forecasts sequences of future tactile states for candidate action chunks. It factorizes forecasts into contact state, a 3D deformation field, and slip risk within a directed hierarchy (stop-gradient connections). A directed attention mask isolates tactile queries from visual-action context. Planning uses tactile forecasts and task-progress estimates; execution uses the forecast as a reference with replanning on persistent discrepancies. Demonstrates substantial improvements in tactile accuracy and real-robot success across multiple tasks.
AI.motivation: Current tactile-aware methods often represent future touch as images or latent streams and miss the physical dependencies organizing tactile states hierarchically. There is a need to jointly model tactile states across contact, deformation, and slip to improve planning and execution before action.
AI.method: Propose HiTac-WAM, a hierarchical tactile world action model that (1) forecasts a sequence of future tactile states for each candidate action chunk; (2) factorizes forecasts into three stages (contact state, 3D deformation field, slip risk) arranged in a directed hierarchy where each downstream stage is conditioned on stop-gradient signals from earlier stages; (3) employs a directed attention mask so tactile queries focus on video-action context while preventing cross-attention to tactile tokens; (4) uses forecasts for planning (ranking candidate chunks) and for execution (reference forecast with replanning triggered by discrepancies).
AI.result: Quantitative gains include mean contact F1 of 0.921; 3D displacement L2 error reduced by 17.6% relative to a deformation-only predictor under matched budgets; slip AUPRC improved by 60.4% relative to a slip-only predictor. Real-robot tasks (chip grasping, blackboard erasing, USB insertion) show average success rate rising from 31.1% to 61.1% with hierarchical forecasts, reaching 72.2% for the full system.
AI.conclusion: Hierarchical tactile forecasts that capture physical dependencies among tactile states and leverage directed attention and stop-gradient conditioning significantly improve planning and execution in tactile manipulation, across multiple tasks, compared to non-hierarchical or single-factor baselines.

title: Where Grounding Accuracy Lives on the IoU Curve: Label-Free Inference-Time Boundary Refinement
summary: Vision--language models can identify the correct referent while returning an imprecise bounding box. We study whether a frozen direct-answer model can use its own prediction to allocate one additional localized observation without accessing target annotations at inference. Label-free precision refinement (LFPR) routes predicted-small regions to a higher-resolution pass, re-grounds the expression inside a context crop, admits a candidate only under fixed geometric guards, and returns a fixed coordinate-wise midpoint. We report results across three evidence tiers. On 31,921 retrospective Ref-L4 expressions, LFPR raises mAcc$_{0.5:0.95}$ from 72.947\% to 76.013\% (Acc@0.5 88.531\%$\to$89.725\%, Acc@0.9 55.788\%$\to$61.142\%). A frozen transfer to 30,969 RefCOCO/RefCOCO+/RefCOCOg expressions improves every dataset at Acc@0.5, mAcc, and mean IoU (pooled mAcc $+0.645$, Acc@0.5 $+0.817$), while Acc@0.9 is unchanged overall: routing alone gains $+1.162$ points there, but crop, guards, and fusion give back $-1.192$, offsetting rather than showing no strict-IoU effect. A prospective, image-disjoint Flickr30K Entities evaluation improves every endpoint (mAcc $+0.973$, Acc@0.9 $+1.022$), more strongly under a single-box variant (mAcc $+2.575$, Acc@0.9 $+3.689$). The same operator applied to two released grounding specialists improves every endpoint (Acc@0.9 $+1.569$/$+6.716$ for EGM-4B/8B) at roughly twice the latency, composing with specialist training rather than replacing it. A genuine unguarded control (guard removed from the same candidates) underperforms the incumbent on every metric, showing the guard is load-bearing. Together, these results show that referent selection and boundary precision are partially separable, with different components moving opposing regions of the IoU curve -- behavior a single threshold cannot reveal.

AI.tldr: LFPR (Label-Free Precision Refinement) improves referent grounding by routing small predicted regions to a higher-resolution pass, re-grounding within a context crop using a fixed guard, and outputting a fixed midpoint, all without target annotations. It yields mixed gains across datasets, showing partial separability between referent selection and boundary precision.
AI.motivation: Investigate whether a frozen direct-answer model can self-allocate an additional localized observation to improve boundary precision without using supervision at inference time.
AI.method: Apply LFPR to a frozen model: route predicted small regions to a higher-res pass, re-ground inside a context crop, enforce fixed geometric guards, and return a fixed coordinate-wise midpoint. Evaluate across three evidence tiers on Ref-L4 (retrospective), RefCOCO/RefCOCO+/RefCOCOg (transfer), and Flickr30K Entities (prospective); compare with a baseline, an unguarded control, and grounding specialists (EGM-4B/8B).
AI.result: LFPR raises mAcc0.5:0.95 from 72.947% to 76.013% on Ref-L4. Acc@0.5 increases from 88.531% to 89.725%; Acc@0.9 from 55.788% to 61.142%. Frozen transfer to RefCOCO variants improves Acc@0.5, mAcc, and mean IoU, while Acc@0.9 is unchanged overall due to opposing contributions from routing (+1.162) and crop/guards/fusion (−1.192). Prospective Flickr30K Entities shows mAcc +0.973 and Acc@0.9 +1.022, with larger gains in single-box variant (+2.575 mAcc, +3.689 Acc@0.9). Using two grounding specialists yields improvement at roughly twice the latency (+1.569/ +6.716 for EGM-4B/8B). A guard-removed unguarded control underperforms, indicating the guard is essential.
AI.conclusion: Referent selection and boundary precision are partially separable; different LFPR components move different parts of the IoU curve, meaning a single threshold cannot capture the full effect. The approach yields consistent gains across datasets and evidence tiers, but gains in strict IoU (Acc@0.9) are context-dependent and trade-offs exist among routing, cropping, guards, and fusion.

title: From Retrieved Context to Runtime Control: Adaptive Compression for Edge-based RAG
comment: Accepted to appear in the Proceedings of the ACM AI Leadership Summit 2026. Zlatan Feric and Amir Taherin contributed equally
summary:
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves language-model responses by grounding generation in external passages, which comes with overhead: retrieved context lengthens the prompt, increasing prefill work, KV-cache footprint, memory traffic, latency, and energy. Context compression offers a natural remedy by pruning retrieved text before generation. However, state-of-the-art context-compression methods are typically used with a fixed compression budget, or with the rate selected offline and then applied at inference time. This static view ignores both workload variation and the live state of the edge device. On an edge SoC, compression is not free: the compressor itself runs on the same SoC and consumes latency and energy that can offset any generation savings.
  This paper proposes a vision for telemetry-informed adaptive compression in edge RAG, grounded in experimental evidence. We characterize the compression tradeoff on the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor using Llama and Qwen generators, Natural Questions and HotpotQA datasets, and LLMLingua-2 compression. Our measurements show that generation dominates the RAG budget for larger models, reaching roughly 90% of per-query latency and 91% of GPU energy for 7B-8B generators. Exploring the impact of the compression rate reveals an adaptive operating region: mild compression can miss energy opportunities, and overly aggressive compression can hurt inference quality. Intermediate compression can reduce GPU energy by up to 53.2%, and SoC energy by up to 48.2%, with negligible quality loss. We argue for runtime policies that dynamically manage compression, guided by workload features and edge telemetry.

title: Empirical Characterization of Learning Geometry in Hybrid Quantum Forecasting Models
summary: We characterize the learning dynamics of a compact hybrid quantum forecasting model through comparison with a structurally aligned classical baseline. Using stationary harmonic-mixture and nonstationary chirp benchmarks with controlled spectral complexity and data availability, we analyze empirical Neural Tangent Kernel dynamics through kernel-target alignment, kernel drift, spectral concentration, and training loss. The classical model exhibits stronger early target alignment, whereas the hybrid model generally develops a less concentrated kernel spectrum and smaller kernel drift. Despite these distinct optimization geometries, both architectures attain similar held-out performance across the evaluated regimes. Notably, the hybrid model uses 125 trainable parameters compared with 281 for the classical baseline and reaches its validation-selected checkpoint earlier in 15 of 18 frequency conditions. A Fourier-augmented classical baseline does not reproduce the observed training behavior, while a controlled re-uploading ablation shows that repeated encoding systematically modifies both optimization and kernel geometry. These results demonstrate that comparable generalization can emerge from substantially different learning trajectories and that individual NTK diagnostics do not provide monotonic predictors of validation convergence. Rather than claiming a general quantum advantage, the study identifies architecture-dependent learning behavior that is masked by endpoint accuracy alone.

AI.tldr: Hybrid quantum forecasting achieves similar generalization to a classical baseline despite different optimization trajectories and smaller parameter count; NTK diagnostics alone do not predict validation convergence, highlighting architecture-dependent learning dynamics.
AI.motivation: Investigate learning dynamics of a compact hybrid quantum forecasting model relative to a structurally aligned classical baseline using Neural Tangent Kernel diagnostics, under controlled spectral complexity and data availability, to assess potential quantum advantage beyond endpoint accuracy.
AI.method: Compare stationary harmonic-mixture and nonstationary chirp benchmarks with controlled spectral complexity and data availability. Analyze empirical Neural Tangent Kernel dynamics via kernel-target alignment, kernel drift, spectral concentration, and training loss. Use a Fourier-augmented classical baseline and a controlled re-uploading ablation to dissect encoding effects. Measure parameter counts and early convergence across 18 frequency conditions.
AI.result: Classical model shows stronger early target alignment; hybrid model exhibits less kernel drift and less spectral concentration. Both architectures achieve similar held-out performance. Hybrid uses 125 trainable parameters vs 281 for classical and reaches its validation-selected checkpoint earlier in 15 of 18 frequency conditions. Fourier-augmented baseline fails to reproduce observed training behavior; controlled re-uploading indicates repeated encoding systematically affects both optimization and kernel geometry.
AI.conclusion: Endpoint accuracy can obscure architecture-dependent learning dynamics; no general quantum advantage claimed. NTK diagnostics alone do not monotonically predict validation convergence; different learning trajectories can yield similar generalization. Architecture-specific learning behavior emerges as a key factor.

title: OrthoSkillVLA: Continual Skill Learning via Gradient-Informed Skill Subspace Adaptation
summary: Pretrained Vision-Language-Action models provide a strong foundation for robot learning, but sequentially adapting them to diverse skills can perturb the representations and velocity mappings used by previous skills, leading to catastrophic forgetting. Architecture-based approaches improve retention by isolating skills but lead to increased inference footprint. Recent subspace-constrained methods restrict parameter updates in an orthogonal subspace to minimize interference but impose a unified constraint on the entire model. We analyze the distinct roles of internal VLA components and identify two VLA-specific challenges. First, the VLM maintains broad semantic representations, making it vulnerable to capacity exhaustion, whereas the ActionHead refines semantics into localized velocity patterns that are highly sensitive to perturbations. Second, the final velocity decoder serves as a readout layer. Freezing it forms an output-stage expressivity bottleneck, while updating it risks overwriting previous velocity mappings. To this end, we propose OrthoSkillVLA, a parameter-efficient framework for continual skill learning in pretrained VLA models without demonstration replay. Given the representation heterogeneity, we impose separate subspace constraints on the VLM and ActionHead, preserving reusable semantic capacity while protecting localized velocity patterns. For the output layer, we introduce a lightweight feature-aware MoE decoder, where each skill is allocated a compact expert and a training-free router selects the expert according to feature-space affinity. Extensive simulated and real-world evaluations, together with ablations, demonstrate that OrthoSkillVLA better preserves prior skills while acquiring new ones.

AI.tldr: OrthoSkillVLA uses separate subspace constraints on the VLM and ActionHead and a feature-aware MoE decoder to enable continual skill learning in pretrained VLA models without replay, preserving prior skills.
AI.motivation: Mitigate catastrophic forgetting when adapting pretrained Vision-Language-Action models to new skills. VLM has broad semantic capacity prone to exhaustion; ActionHead encodes localized velocity patterns sensitive to perturbations; a unified constraint can harm performance and be inefficient.
AI.method: Impose orthogonal subspace constraints separately on the VLM and ActionHead to protect distinct representations. Use a lightweight, feature-aware Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) decoder as the output layer, with a compact expert per skill and a training-free router selecting experts by feature-space affinity; no demonstration replay.
AI.result: Extensive simulations and real-world experiments with ablations show improved preservation of previously learned skills while efficiently acquiring new ones, validating the design choices and effectiveness of the approach.
AI.conclusion: By addressing representation heterogeneity and preserving semantic capacity while protecting localized velocity mappings, OrthoSkillVLA offers a parameter-efficient continual learning framework for pretrained VLA models, avoiding replay and reducing inference overhead.

title: Stream4D: 4D-Consistency for Streaming Autoregressive Diffusion Video Models
summary: Streaming autoregressive diffusion models enable real-time, long-horizon video generation, but their training objectives optimize local frame prediction rather than the geometry and dynamics of a coherent world: long rollouts accumulate geometric drift and degrade into static or unnatural motion. Recent bidirectional approaches address this problem using rewards signals built upon 3D Gaussian-Splatting reconstruction. However, a single rigid 3d reconstruction cannot model a dynamic scene, so this critic penalizes genuine object motion as reconstruction error and is maximized by freezing the video. This shortcut is especially detrimental in the AR setting, where each chunk can propagate an already-static configuration. In this work, we propose Stream4D, which replaces the static critic with a feed-forward 4D reconstruction reward that explicitly models scene dynamics, allowing coherent motion to receive high consistency rewards. To further guide motion magnitude and quality, we add a motion prior that rewards natural scene-flow magnitude while penalizing jitter and non-rigid artifacts. Our final recipe combines these two terms with a lightweight perceptual anchor. Across various autoregressive video backbones and various generation horizons, Stream4D improves 4D reconstruction quality, preserves motion more effectively, and achieves higher human-aligned preference. Project page: https://banyuanhao.github.io/Stream4D/

AI.tldr: Stream4D introduces a 4D reconstruction reward and a motion prior to streaming autoregressive diffusion video models, replacing a static 3D critic to better capture scene dynamics and improve coherent motion across long horizons.
AI.motivation: Current streaming AR diffusion objectives optimize local frame fidelity, leading to geometric drift and static or unnatural motion. A rigid 3D critic penalizes genuine motion as reconstruction error, which discourages dynamic scenes and biases the model toward freezing. There is a need for a metric that evaluates dynamics over space-time to reward coherent motion.
AI.method: Replace static 3D Gaussian-Splatting-based critic with a feed-forward 4D reconstruction reward that models space-time consistency. Introduce a motion prior that rewards natural scene flow magnitudes while penalizing jitter and non-rigid artifacts. Combine with a lightweight perceptual anchor. The approach is validated across multiple autoregressive backbones and generation horizons.
AI.result: Stream4D improves 4D reconstruction quality, preserves motion more effectively, and achieves higher human-aligned preference across various backbones and horizons.
AI.conclusion: A dynamics-aware reward framework based on 4D reconstruction plus motion priors offers improved coherence in streaming AR video generation, enabling better long-horizon motion without sacrificing fidelity. The method is complementary to existing backbones and is compatible with lightweight perceptual guidance.

title: Enforcing LLM Safety through DMD-based Classification of Prompt-Response Embedding Dynamics
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in high-stakes applications, yet their tendency to generate toxic, harmful, or policy-violating content poses significant risks. Detecting these unsafe outputs efficiently in a black-box manner remains an open challenge. In this paper, we extend a recently proposed dynamical systems framework designed for hallucination detection to LLM safety classification. By projecting both prompts and responses into high-dimensional embedding spaces and fitting separate Koopman-based predictive models for safe and unsafe regimes, we classify new outputs using a new differential residual score that compares prediction errors of the safe and unsafe regimes. A key contribution is the incorporation of the prompt and response embedding dynamics, yielding fitted Koopman operators that capture crucial interaction patterns. We evaluate our black-box method across three safety benchmarks using three embedding models. Our results show that incorporating prompt embeddings yields consistent improvements, particularly for interaction-dependent violations when paired with causal decoders (e.g., in Llama-3), while response-only violations benefit more from dense semantic embedding representations. These findings opens the door for using dynamical systems to analyze AI systems rather than the dominant paradigm of using AI to model dynamical systems.

AI.tldr: Extends Koopman-based dynamical systems to LLM safety classification by modeling prompt and response embeddings; uses a differential residual score to distinguish safe vs unsafe outputs; prompt dynamics improve interaction-dependent violations, especially with causal decoders; validated across three benchmarks with three embeddings; suggests a dynamical-systems perspective for AI safety analysis.
AI.motivation: Address black-box LLM safety detection by capturing interaction dynamics between prompts and outputs; extend a recent dynamical-systems framework for hallucination detection to safety classification.
AI.method: Project prompts and responses into high-dimensional embeddings; fit separate Koopman predictors for safe and unsafe regimes; compute a differential residual score from prediction errors of the two regimes; incorporate both prompt and response embedding dynamics to learn interaction patterns; evaluate across three safety benchmarks using three embedding models; assess effect of decoder type (e.g., causal decoders like Llama-3).
AI.result: Incorporating prompt embeddings yields consistent improvements, particularly for interaction-dependent violations when paired with causal decoders; response-only violations benefit more from dense semantic embeddings; results are consistent across three benchmarks and embedding models.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates that a dynamical-systems (Koopman) approach is a viable framework for LLM safety classification, enabling interaction-aware analysis of AI systems and broadening the use of dynamical systems in AI evaluation.

title: In Two Minds about Lifelong Learning: Exploring Hemispheric Redundancy and Specialisation in Neural Models
summary: Persistent intelligent systems require the ability to learn continually, but current machine learning approaches face significant challenges in this area compared to biological learning systems. Machine learning algorithms typically trade off retention of previously learned information and adaptation to new or changing data patterns. When continual learning capabilities are absent, algorithms must undergo retraining using the entire data set, an approach that becomes impractical when original training data are unavailable due to storage constraints, financial or computational costs, or privacy restrictions. However, biological animals can learn continually, without experiencing catastrophic forgetting. This paper attempts to build a high-level framework for how animals learn and preserve knowledge by modelling neural components and states that are known to be related to memory consolidation. We focus on three concepts: experience replay, REM sleep, and bilaterality. We propose 4MAS (4 Module Awake/Sleep), a novel macroarchitecture demonstrating how machine learning models might benefit from asymmetric hemispheres, each with their own long- and short-term memory mechanisms, and how a period of sleep between incremental learning tasks might benefit memory consolidation. Finally, we present results showing that our architecture achieves competitive results on the Split-MNIST, Split-Fashion-MNIST and Split-CIFAR-100 datasets, with 98.3%, 84.9%, and 29.29% accuracy respectively.

AI.tldr: Proposes 4MAS, a high-level macroarchitecture using asymmetric hemispheres with long-/short-term memory and sleep-based consolidation to improve continual learning; shows competitive results on Split-MNIST variants and Split-CIFAR-100.
AI.motivation: Address catastrophic forgetting in continual learning by drawing inspiration from biological memory systems (memory consolidation, sleep, replay, and bilaterality) to enable durable, incremental learning without full retraining.
AI.method: Introduce 4MAS (4 Module Awake/Sleep) macroarchitecture with separate long- and short-term memory mechanisms per hemisphere, experience replay, REM sleep-inspired consolidation, and a sleep period between incremental tasks to reduce forgetting; evaluate on Split-MNIST, Split-Fashion-Mashion? (likely Fashion-MNIST), and Split-CIFAR-100.
AI.result: Achieves competitive accuracies: 98.3% on Split-MNIST, 84.9% on Split-Fashion-MNIST, and 29.29% on Split-CIFAR-100.
AI.conclusion: Presents a biologically-inspired framework for memory consolidation in ML; demonstrates potential gains in continual learning via sleep-based consolidation and hemispheric asymmetry, while leaving detailed architectural and training specifics for future work.

title: The Verification Gap in Networked Physical AI: A Post-Semantic Communication Framework
summary: A task-effective proposal is not yet a justified physical action. In networked Physical AI, a proposal may be understood while valid, timely, proposal-bound evidence or the authority required to finalize an action remains unavailable. We call this mismatch the verification gap and introduce a Post-Semantic Communication Framework for the systems interface between proposal formation and physical execution. The framework begins with application-declared evidence requirements, represents qualifying observations as evidence records, validates supporting and conflicting records through one path, and separates evidence sufficiency from authorized finalization and a downstream runtime gate. It further distinguishes evidence transfer, which can enlarge the record set reachable by a finalizer, from evidence coordination, which can suppress transmission around records already held at the finalization endpoint. Finite-state framework checks verify that the evaluator implements the declared distinctions consistently. Under the declared model, the controlled communication study exposes a finalizer-dependent asymmetry: sender-finalized Feedback uses evidence transfer to expand evidence reachability throughout the feasible plotted region, whereas receiver-finalized Feedback uses coordination to suppress redundant payload until loss, latency, freshness, and deadline costs shift selection to One-way. Finally, an episode-level reporting schema defines common denominators for future measured Physical-AI studies.

AI.tldr: Post-Semantic Communication Framework bridging proposal formation and physical execution in networked Physical AI, addressing the verification gap by separating evidence sufficiency from authorization, and by distinguishing evidence transfer from coordination; highlights a sender/receiver-dependent feedback asymmetry and proposes an episode-level reporting schema for standardized future studies.
AI.motivation: In networked Physical AI, a proposal can be valid and timely yet lack available evidence or authority to finalize action, creating a verification gap between proposal and execution.
AI.method: Propose a framework with stages: (1) define application-declared evidence requirements; (2) represent observations as evidence records; (3) validate supporting and conflicting records through a single path; (4) separate evidence sufficiency from finalization and a downstream runtime gate; (5) distinguish evidence transfer (expands reachable records) from evidence coordination (suppresses transmission); (6) implement finite-state checks to ensure consistent evaluator behavior; (7) conduct a controlled communication study to reveal finalizer-dependent asymmetry in feedback; (8) establish an episode-level reporting schema to standardize future studies.
AI.result: The framework articulates design principles and formal properties for evidence management and finalization gating; it reveals a sender-finalized feedback asymmetry that uses evidence transfer to increase reachability, and a receiver-finalized feedback asymmetry that uses coordination to suppress redundancy, with costs (loss, latency, freshness, deadline) guiding a shift toward one-way communication; it also provides a standardized episode-level reporting schema for subsequent Physical AI studies.
AI.conclusion: A Post-Semantic Communication Framework is proposed to formalize the interface between proposal formation and physical execution, clarifying roles of evidence and authorization, and enabling consistent evaluation through finite-state checks and an episode-based reporting schema for future experiments.

title: Block3D: Efficient Text-to-3D Generation via Block-Wise Diffusion
summary: While text-to-3D generation has advanced rapidly, achieving high geometric fidelity at low inference cost remains challenging. Existing text-to-3D methods either decode discrete shape tokens autoregressively or iteratively refine global 3D representations with diffusion or flow models. However, autoregressive decoding is sequential and cannot revise errors, whereas diffusion and flow-matching models repeatedly process the full representation, making high-quality generation increasingly expensive. In this paper, we propose Block3D, a block-wise diffusion framework that partitions the discrete shape-token sequence into contiguous blocks, generates the blocks autoregressively, and jointly denoises all tokens within the current block. To alleviate error accumulation, we introduce confidence-guided intra-block correction, which revises low-confidence tokens before each block is finalized. On a held-out set from TRELLIS-500K, Block3D reduces mean end-to-end generation time from 25.71 seconds to 4.99 seconds, achieving a $5.15\times$ speedup over the fine-tuned autoregressive baseline without sacrificing geometric fidelity.

AI.tldr: Block3D introduces a block-wise diffusion framework for text-to-3D token sequences, enabling autoregressive block generation with intra-block denoising and confidence-guided correction to speed up generation while preserving fidelity (5.15x faster on TRELLIS-500K).
AI.motivation: To achieve high geometric fidelity at low inference cost in text-to-3D, overcome limitations: autoregressive decoding is sequential and cannot revise errors; diffusion/flow-based methods are expensive as they repeatedly process the full 3D representation.
AI.method: Partition discrete shape-token sequences into contiguous blocks; generate blocks autoregressively; within each block jointly denoise all tokens; apply confidence-guided intra-block correction by revising low-confidence tokens before finalizing the block.
AI.result: On TRELLIS-500K held-out set, mean end-to-end generation time reduced from 25.71s to 4.99s; 5.15x speedup over a fine-tuned autoregressive baseline; geometric fidelity preserved.
AI.conclusion: Block3D provides a faster, fidelity-preserving approach for text-to-3D generation by combining block-wise diffusion with intra-block corrections, offering a practical trade-off between autoregressive and diffusion-based methods.

title: Scientific Data Skills: Enabling Agent-Ready Scientific Data Services at Scale
summary: Scientific data are increasingly used by AI agents, yet existing dataset representations provide limited support for autonomous discovery, interpretation, and invocation. This limitation stems from the fragmentation of scientific data across heterogeneous repositories and from dataset representations designed primarily for human use. To address this limitation, we introduce the Scientific Data Skill (SciDSK), an agent-ready representation that packages dataset-specific knowledge and operational guidance as a reusable agent skill. A SciDSK integrates dataset descriptions, scientific context, file organization, usage procedures, quality checks, and provenance information while retaining the underlying data in its original repository. We define a structured SciDSK specification and develop a systematic construction pipeline that grounds each SciDSK in authoritative dataset records and associated supporting materials. We further establish the Scientific Data Skill Bank, a unified platform that publishes SciDSK resources across six scientific disciplines and supports package access, persistent identification, and traceability to source datasets. We evaluate SciDSK through a retrieval benchmark for dataset discovery and controlled cases for dataset interpretation. The results show that SciDSK improves agent-driven dataset discovery and provides more precise and actionable support for dataset interpretation. These findings support the value of organizing dataset-specific knowledge in an agent-ready representation.

AI.tldr: SciDSK provides an agent-ready, structured representation of dataset knowledge and operational guidance, packaged as reusable skills linked to original repositories, plus a SciDSK Bank across six disciplines to improve agent-driven discovery and interpretation.
AI.motivation: Fragmented, human-centric dataset representations across heterogeneous repositories hinder autonomous discovery, interpretation, and invocation by AI agents; a unified, agent-ready format is needed.
AI.method: Define a structured SciDSK specification; build a construction pipeline grounding each SciDSK in authoritative dataset records and supporting materials; create the Scientific Data Skill Bank publishing SciDSK resources with persistent identifiers and traceability to sources; evaluate via a retrieval benchmark for discovery and controlled interpretation cases.
AI.result: SciDSK enhances agent-driven dataset discovery and provides more precise, actionable support for dataset interpretation, demonstrating the value of organizing dataset-specific knowledge in an agent-ready format.
AI.conclusion: Agent-ready dataset representations like SciDSK can improve autonomous data discovery, interpretation, and usage; the pipeline and bank approach supports scalable coverage across multiple disciplines.

title: Continuous Adversarial MeanFlow Transfer
summary: Training fast generators on new domains with limited data remains challenging for two reasons. First, adapting a pretrained diffusion or flow model to a new domain leaves its costly multi-step sampling unaddressed, and existing acceleration methods are tied to the source parameterization--$ε$, $x$, $v$, or $u$--leaving heterogeneous pretrained models with no common acceleration target.
