Second, while adversarial refinement is proven effective for few-step quality, it is formulated only for instantaneous-velocity flows, not for the finite-interval average velocities that MeanFlow (MF) models predict. We address both problems. We propose MeanFlow-Transfer, which maps heterogeneous source outputs into a shared velocity representation, uses it to initialize an MF generator from the source weights, and optimizes an MF objective on the target domain. This unifies adaptation and acceleration in a single training loop across a broad range of pretrained models. We then introduce Continuous Adversarial MeanFlow, a post-training stage that extends continuous adversarial flow models from instantaneous velocities to MF's finite-interval average velocities. CAMF contrasts changes in a learned potential between real and predicted interval endpoints, recovering fine detail that MF regression averages away, and reduces to the instantaneous criterion in the vanishing-interval limit. Adapting four ImageNet-based source models--DiT ($ε$), SiT ($v$), JiT ($x$), iMF ($u$)--to five target domains, MF-T with CAMF matches or exceeds the fine-tuned teacher in FID and FDD at up to $125\times$ fewer Neural Function Evaluations (NFEs), while CAMF improves MF-T's few-step FID by $29\%$ on average.

AI.tldr: Introduces MeanFlow-Transfer and Continuous Adversarial MeanFlow to adapt pretrained diffusion/flow models to new domains with limited data, unifying adaptation and acceleration across different parameterizations; achieves strong efficiency and quality gains using MF-based representations.
AI.motivation: Current adaptation methods fail to address multi-step sampling acceleration across heterogeneous source parameterizations and lack MF-aware adversarial refinement; there is a need for a unified, data-efficient approach that can bridge ε, x, v, and u parameterizations and leverage finite-interval velocity representations.
AI.method: MeanFlow-Transfer maps heterogeneous outputs to a shared velocity representation, initializes an MF generator from source weights, and optimizes an MF objective on the target domain; Continuous Adversarial MeanFlow extends continuous adversarial flow models to MF's finite-interval average velocities, comparing learned potential at interval endpoints to real data.
AI.result: Applied to four ImageNet-based source models (DiT—ε, SiT—v, JiT—x, iMF—u) adapted to five target domains; MF-T with CAMF matches or exceeds the fine-tuned teacher with up to 125× fewer neural function evaluations (NFEs); CAMF improves MF-T's few-step FID by about 29% on average.
AI.conclusion: Presents a unified adaptation and acceleration framework applicable across diverse pretrained models, yielding substantial data efficiency and quality benefits for few-shot domain adaptation.

title: What Matters for Latent Actions in Robot Learning
summary: Latent Action Models (LAMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for enabling robot learning to leverage large-scale unlabeled videos through latent actions that serve as compact surrogates for physical actions. Despite rapid progress, research on LAM remains highly fragmented, with existing methods evaluating different design choices in isolation under inconsistent experimental settings, making it difficult to identify the factors that truly determine downstream robotic manipulation performance. In this work, we present the first comprehensive empirical study of latent action learning for robotic manipulation. We unify representative LAM methods within a common autoencoding framework and systematically investigate 41 LAM design choices across three dimensions, including latent action modeling paradigms, learning objectives and regularization methods, and latent action integration strategies. We further examine four proxy metrics for evaluating latent action quality and assess their ability to reliably predict downstream robotic manipulation performance. Extensive experiments on three widely used benchmarks provide strong empirical evidence that fine-tuning vision-language model (VLM) backbones with latent actions provides a stronger initialization for downstream policy learning, with further validation on real-world robot manipulation tasks.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive empirical study of latent action models (LAMs) for robotic manipulation, unifying LAMs under a common autoencoding framework and exhaustively evaluating design choices to identify factors predicting downstream performance; shows fine-tuning vision-language model (VLM) backbones with latent actions yields stronger downstream policy learning, validated on real robots.
AI.motivation: LAM research is fragmented with inconsistent evaluations, hindering identification of factors that truly impact downstream robotic manipulation performance; a large-scale, standardized study is needed to distill actionable design guidance.
AI.method: Unify representative LAM methods within a common autoencoding framework. Systematically investigate 41 design choices across three dimensions: (1) latent action modeling paradigms, (2) learning objectives and regularization methods, and (3) latent action integration strategies. Evaluate four proxy metrics for latent action quality and their ability to predict downstream performance. Conduct extensive experiments on three benchmarks and validate findings on real-world robot manipulation tasks, highlighting the benefit of fine-tuning VLM backbones with latent actions.
AI.result: 41 design choices examined; four proxy latent-action evaluation metrics analyzed for correlation with downstream performance. Main empirical result: fine-tuning vision-language model backbones with latent actions provides a stronger initialization for downstream policy learning, with additional validation on real-world tasks.
AI.conclusion: Offers evidence-based guidance on LAM design, metrics, and integration for robotic manipulation. Recommends adopting VLM-fine-tuned latent actions to improve downstream policy learning and emphasizes the need for standardized evaluation frameworks to identify robust design choices across benchmarks and real-world settings.

title: Mix&Fix-Net: A Dual-Stage Trajectory Prediction Model for AIS and Vision-Derived Vessel Data
summary: Vessel trajectory prediction is critical for maritime safety and accident prevention. While most existing trajectory prediction models rely on Automatic Identification System (AIS) data due to its precision and availability, small vessels mostly operate without AIS, resulting in a significant monitoring gap. To address this, we propose Mix&Fix-Net, a dual-stage mixer-based trajectory prediction model designed to handle vessel trajectory time-series data derived from both AIS and (non-AIS) vision data. Our architecture integrates a Primary Trajectory Predictor with a Residual Trajectory Adjuster, enabling more refined trajectory prediction. Additionally, we introduce a new video-based dataset derived from webcam streams, from which vessel trajectories are extracted to represent non-AIS data. Extensive evaluations on both AIS and non-AIS datasets across six metrics (mean squared error, mean absolute error, symmetric mean absolute percentage error, final displacement error, Frechet distance, and average Euclidean distance) demonstrate that Mix&Fix-Net consistently outperforms existing baselines across most metrics and datasets.

AI.tldr: Mix&Fix-Net is a dual-stage mixer-based model predicting vessel trajectories from AIS and non-AIS (vision-derived) data, featuring a Primary Trajectory Predictor and a Residual Trajectory Adjuster, plus a webcam-derived video dataset; it outperforms baselines on six evaluation metrics.
AI.motivation: Small vessels often lack AIS, creating a monitoring gap. Incorporating non-AIS, vision-based data aims to improve trajectory prediction and maritime safety.
AI.method: Proposes a dual-stage architecture with mixer-based temporal modeling: a Primary Trajectory Predictor generates an initial trajectory, followed by a Residual Trajectory Adjuster that refines it. Handles multi-modal inputs (AIS time-series and vision-derived features). Introduces a webcam-based video dataset for non-AIS trajectories. Evaluates on AIS and non-AIS datasets across six metrics.
AI.result: Across AIS and non-AIS datasets, Mix&Fix-Net consistently outperforms existing baselines on most metrics for six evaluated measures: mean squared error (MSE), mean absolute error (MAE), symmetric mean absolute percentage error (SMAPE), final displacement error (FDE), Frechet distance, and average Euclidean distance.
AI.conclusion: The approach effectively bridges the AIS data gap by enabling robust dual-modality trajectory prediction and provides a new video-based dataset to support non-AIS research, demonstrating strong performance gains over baselines.

title: Can Agent Memory Systems Track Evolving State?
summary: As LLM-based agents are deployed for longer and higher-stakes tasks, their memory systems continue to have crucial gaps. While existing memory benchmarks focus largely on recall-shaped tasks, we argue an effective memory system must track the evolving state of the world; as facts, constraints, and decisions are revised over a long interaction, answers must reflect the current state and not a superseded one. We define this capability as state tracking and instantiate it in StateMemBench, a benchmark of 234 multi-session scenarios spanning two conversation-length regimes. Its closed-pool grading scores whether an answer reflects the current state, the superseded state, or fails otherwise, separating state-tracking failures from other errors by construction. Our analysis shows that this task is challenging for existing memory systems, retrieval-augmented baselines, and long-context baselines. We then present StateMem, a state-first memory method that explicitly tracks supersession and relational dependencies, and show it improves current-state accuracy over the strongest same-backbone baseline by 1.8x (0.205 -> 0.363) on DeepSeek-V4-Flash and over the strongest memory system by 1.6x (0.149 -> 0.233) on Qwen-3.5-9B, while remaining competitive with the long-context baselines. Finally, we show the same state approach can be applied as a lightweight single-call wrapper over existing memory systems, lifting current-state accuracy by +32 to +67 points on StateMemBench across six memory and retrieval backends. A length- and cost-matched control attributes +15 to +32 of those points to state structure rather than added context.

AI.tldr: Introduces StateMemBench to benchmark state-tracking in long-running LLM interactions and presents StateMem, a state-first memory method; shows substantial current-state accuracy gains and a lightweight wrapper that improves performance across multiple backends.
AI.motivation: Memory in LLM-based agents exhibits gaps as facts and decisions are revised over long interactions; a robust memory system must track the evolving world state and reflect the current state in answers.
AI.method: Develop StateMemBench with 234 multi-session scenarios and closed-pool grading that distinguishes current vs superseded state. Propose StateMem, a state-first memory method that explicitly tracks supersession and relational dependencies, and demonstrate its improvements. Also show a lightweight single-call wrapper over existing memory systems to lift current-state accuracy.
AI.result: StateMem achieves 1.8x improvement in current-state accuracy over the strongest same-backbone baseline (0.205→0.363 on DeepSeek-V4-Flash) and 1.6x over the strongest memory system (0.149→0.233 on Qwen-3.5-9B); stays competitive with long-context baselines. The wrapper yields +32 to +67 points in current-state accuracy across six backends, with an additional +15 to +32 attributed to state-structure rather than added context.
AI.conclusion: Explicit state-tracking memory methods materially improve current-state accuracy in multi-session tasks; the approach generalizes to lightweight wrappers for existing memory systems, enabling more faithful long-term state tracking without large-context increases.

title: DraftFM: A FoundationModel for Day-Zero Drafting in Magic: The Gathering
comment: 28 pages, 6 figures, 13 tables. Sealed pre-registered forecast published ~36h before release; scoring note to follow. Also on SSRN (7257098). Code: https://github.com/brianward92/mtga Sealed forecast: https://github.com/brianward92/draftfm (tag draftfm-v1.0) Weights: https://huggingface.co/brianward92/draftfm Data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/brianward92/draftfm-frozen-eval
summary: Drafting a new Magic: The Gathering expansion begins before any pick from it has been observed: the complete card list is public, but the draft logs that supervised pick models train on do not yet exist. We study this day-zero regime directly. DraftFM is a discrete-choice policy that scores exactly the cards available in the current pack, conditioned on the drafted pool and the state of the draft. Every card enters as a frozen 775-dimensional function of its public card record, structured features and a fixed text embedding, with no card identities, set identities, or usage statistics anywhere in the model, so an unseen card is scored by the same machinery as a familiar one. A 1.6-million-parameter network fitted on 149 million human picks from 29 expansions predicts held-out picks in three expansions withheld in their entirety, reaching 50.8%, 60.4%, and 56.7% top-1 agreement, where uniform chance at the opening pick is about 7%. Refitted on all 32 observed expansions, the same architecture produced a card ranking for the then-unreleased set The Hobbit, sealed with its complete cryptographic provenance and published roughly 36 hours before the set became draftable on MTG Arena. The sealed ranking agrees with six independent expert reviewers roughly as much as those reviewers agree with one another. Evaluation against realized outcomes is committed to a follow-on note, whatever it shows.

AI.tldr: Day-zero MTG draft predictor (DraftFM) generalizes to unseen cards using 775-dimensional features and a 1.6M-parameter network trained on 149M human picks; achieves ~50.8–60.4% top-1 on withheld expansions (vs. ~7% chance); ranked unreleased set The Hobbit before public release with expert-level agreement; evaluation against real outcomes forthcoming.
AI.motivation: Understand draft decision dynamics and build a scoring model that operates without card identities, set identities, or usage statistics, enabling predictions on day zero before draft data exists.
AI.method: Discrete-choice policy: score exactly the cards in the current pack conditioned on the drafted pool and draft state. Each card is represented as a fixed 775-dimensional feature function of public card record, structured features, and a text embedding, with no explicit card identity. A single 1.6M-parameter network is fitted on 149 million human picks from 29 expansions and evaluated on 3 held-out expansions.
AI.result: Held-out top-1 accuracy in three expansions: 50.8%, 60.4%, 56.7%. Uniform baseline for the opening pick is ~7%. The model produced a ranking for The Hobbit (unreleased at the time) with cryptographic provenance, published ~36 hours before draftability; the rank aligned with six independent expert reviewers roughly as much as those reviewers agree with each other.
AI.conclusion: The approach demonstrates strong generalization to unseen cards and plausibly captures draft choices in a day-zero regime. The authors plan to compare predicted outcomes with realized results in a follow-on note; the method suggests viability of AI-assisted drafting without reliance on card identities or usage data.

title: Magnetically Self-Sealed MR Haptic Actuator With PWM-Based Excitation and High-Fidelity Torque Control
comment: Submitted to IEEE/ASME Transactions on Mechatronics. 16 pages, 9 figures, including supplementary material
summary: Accurate and stable torque rendering is essential for safe and perceptive human--machine interaction. Magnetorheological fluid (MRF)-based actuators offer a compact and rapidly controllable solution for haptic feedback, but their practical implementation requires reliable fluid sealing, low-hysteresis excitation, accurate torque control, and stable long-duration operation. This article presents an integrated MRF haptic system featuring a compact magnetically self-sealed rotary actuator, low-hysteresis PWM operation, high-fidelity model-based torque rendering, and stable performance during long-time operation. Magnetostatic simulation guides the arrangement of magnetic and nonmagnetic materials to focus flux in the multidisk torque and permanent-magnet sealing regions, enabling a maximum 600 N$\cdot$mm/A output. Experiments show that higher PWM frequencies reduce hysteresis and improve repeatability. At 10 kHz, the response is represented by a nonlinear model that varies with the direction and speed of torque change. The real-time controller combines feedforward, hysteresis compensation, PI feedback, and sliding-mode correction. Compared with PID, it reduces square-wave overshoot, undershoot, and steady-state RMSE by 77.4\%, 61.9\%, and 68.3\%, respectively. It tracks sinusoidal and biomechanics-model-based references, and a 1.5-h test shows only a 2.5 $^\circ$C rise near the coil with no clear tracking loss. This high-fidelity torque rendering will fundamentally transform human--robot collaboration by making interactions safer, more efficient, and more intuitive.

AI.tldr: Compact magnetorheological fluid (MRF) haptic actuator with self-sealed rotary design and high-fidelity, model-based torque rendering using 10 kHz PWM. Demonstrates low hysteresis, stable long-term operation, and improved tracking vs. PID.
AI.motivation: Provide reliable sealing, low hysteresis, accurate torque control, and long-duration operation in MRF-based haptic actuators for safe human–machine interaction.
AI.method: Use magnetostatic simulations to optimize flux focusing in multidisk torque and sealing regions; design a magnetically self-sealed rotary actuator; implement high-frequency PWM (up to 10 kHz); develop a nonlinear torque model that varies with torque-change direction and speed; implement a real-time controller combining feedforward, hysteresis compensation, PI feedback, and sliding-mode correction; validate via experiments including long-duration tests.
AI.result: Output characteristic of 600 Nmm/A; higher PWM frequencies reduce hysteresis and improve repeatability; 10 kHz yields a nonlinear, direction- and speed-dependent model; the controller reduces overshoot, undershoot, and RMSE by 77.4%, 61.9%, and 68.3% vs PID; successful tracking of sinusoidal and biomechanics-model references; 1.5-h test shows only 2.5°C coil rise with no tracking loss.
AI.conclusion: The integrated MRF haptic system delivers high-fidelity torque rendering with robust long-term performance, enabling safer, more efficient, and intuitive human–robot collaboration; the approach advances MRF-based actuation by addressing sealing, hysteresis, control accuracy, and thermal stability.

title: VGI-BENCH: Probing Visual Intelligence in Video Generation Models
summary: Recent studies suggest that video generation models can exhibit certain forms of zero-shot visual reasoning through generated frames. Yet reliable evaluation remains challenging: benchmarks should adopt inputs aligned with the visual priors of current video models, require valid evolving processes rather than only plausible final states, and calibrate task difficulty to remain challenging yet partly feasible. To this end, we introduce VGI-bench, containing 27 tasks and 810 instances, organized by a two-level taxonomy of task domains and skill tags for fine-grained evaluation of visual reasoning capabilities of video generation models. Our evaluations show that current generative systems can solve a subset of visually grounded reasoning tasks, but remain far from reliable, with even the strongest model, Seedance~2.0, achieving only 51.0% under our evaluation criteria. Our analysis further explore the output failure modes, input condition sensitivity, performance transfer boundary from synthetic fine-tuning, and internal denoising perspective revealing limited self-correction, where later steps mainly refine early hypotheses rather than correct reasoning errors. We hope VGI-bench will help stimulate the development of next-generation video generation models. We will release our code and data.

AI.tldr: A benchmarking suite VGI-bench for video-language visual reasoning comprising 27 tasks and 810 instances, organized with a two-level taxonomy to assess video generation models. Findings: current models can solve some tasks but are far from reliable; Seedance 2.0 reaches only 51% under their criteria; analyzed failure modes, input sensitivity, transfer from synthetic fine-tuning, and denoising perspective; code and data will be released.
AI.motivation: Need evaluation benchmarks aligned to visual priors of video models, requiring dynamic processes and calibrated difficulty to properly assess visual reasoning in video generation.
AI.method: Construct a two-level taxonomy of task domains and skill tags; compile 27 tasks with 810 instances; evaluate current video generation models; analyze failure modes, input sensitivity, transfer learning from synthetic fine-tuning, and denoising/correction dynamics.
AI.result: Models exhibit partial success on a subset of tasks but overall reliability is low; Seedance 2.0 achieves 51% under evaluation; observed limited self-correction where later steps mainly refine early hypotheses.
AI.conclusion: VGI-bench aims to stimulate next-generation video generation models; code and data to be released.

title: Frequency-Aware Continual Learning for Smart Contract Vulnerability Detection with Large Language Models
summary: Smart contract vulnerability detection with Large Language Models (LLMs) faces three causally linked challenges. First, new vulnerability categories demand parameter-efficient adaptation, since full retraining is prohibitive for sequentially arriving tasks. Second, training per-task adapters on a shared backbone causes catastrophic forgetting of previously learned vulnerabilities. Third, the resulting multiplicity of adapters must be consolidated into a single model, since task identity is unknown at inference time. Each challenge arises directly from the solution to its predecessor, making an integrated framework essential. We propose a three-stage pipeline in which each stage addresses one challenge and feeds into the next. The adaptation stage uses Frequency-Aware Low-Rank Adaptation (FA-LoRA), which performs adaptation in the Fourier domain with per-frequency importance gates, requiring only 0.4% trainable parameters while outperforming standard LoRA and QLoRA. The continual learning stage applies Forget-Aware Replay (FAR), which uses these frequency gates to estimate per-sample forgetting risk via loss dynamics and prioritizes vulnerable knowledge for rehearsal, achieving an average Micro-F1 of 0.8022 across sequential tasks. The deployment stage employs Anchor-Protected Progressive Merging (APPM), which exploits the asymmetric generalization produced by FAR training to identify the strongest-generalizing adapter as an anchor and consolidates all adapters into a single model via anchor-protected weighted merging with frequency-domain gate competition. APPM achieves a Micro-F1 of 0.8085, within 2.7% of the independent per-task upper bound, at a merge cost of 156 ms and no additional runtime memory. Experiments on DIVE confirm the framework effectively addresses all three challenges for evolving blockchain ecosystems.

AI.tldr: Three-stage pipeline (FA-LoRA, FAR, APPM) for LLM-based smart contract vulnerability detection to address adaptation, forgetting, and merging for a single deployable model; achieves Micro-F1 ~0.80 on DIVE with efficient parameters and low merge cost.
AI.motivation: Vulnerability categories evolve over time; full retraining is costly. To adapt efficiently, avoid forgetting, and deploy a single model when task identity is unknown, an integrated framework is needed.
AI.method: Stage 1 FA-LoRA performs Fourier-domain adaptation with per-frequency gates (0.4% trainable params). Stage 2 FAR estimates per-sample forgetting risk via loss dynamics and prioritizes rehearsal. Stage 3 APPM uses the strongest-generalizing adapter as an anchor and merges adapters with anchor-protected weighted merging and frequency-domain gate competition.
AI.result: FA-LoRA outperforms standard LoRA/QLoRA; FAR achieves average Micro-F1 0.8022 across sequential tasks; APPM achieves Micro-F1 0.8085, within 2.7% of the per-task upper bound, merge cost 156 ms with no extra runtime memory.
AI.conclusion: An integrated three-stage framework effectively addresses adaptation, continual learning, and deployment challenges for evolving blockchain ecosystems.

title: A Two-Stage Time-Aware Transformer for Short-Horizon AECOPD Risk Prediction
comment: 7 pages. Accepted for publication in IEEE Systems, Man, and Cybernetics Letters
summary: Acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (AECOPD) can worsen rapidly, making timely prediction a clinical priority. Most existing machine learning approaches rely on episodically collected clinical variables, introducing delays that limit their practical utility in home monitoring settings. Home ventilators offer a lower-latency alternative, producing a near-continuous record of respiratory status during daily use. However existing ventilator-based approaches either compress the waveform into handcrafted features or focus primarily on binary risk classification, leaving the timing of an impending event unresolved. In this paper, we present a two-stage framework that operates directly on raw pressure and flow waveforms from the most recent seven days of home ventilator use. The first-stage classification model identifies patients at high risk of a severe exacerbation. The second-stage regression model then estimates how many days remain before the event occurs. Our experimental results demonstrate that the two-stage model outperforms traditional baseline models on both risk classification and time-to-event estimation, with our selected Stage 1 classifier achieving F1 = 0.91 and our Stage 2 regression model achieving RMSE = 1.00 days and R^2 = 0.76, giving clinicians both an early warning and actionable lead time before a severe exacerbation occurs.

AI.tldr: Two-stage deep learning framework on raw ventilator waveforms predicts risk and timing of severe COPD exacerbations. Stage 1: high-risk classification (F1=0.91). Stage 2: time-to-event regression (RMSE=1 day, R^2=0.76) using last 7 days of pressure/flow data. Outperforms baselines and provides actionable lead time for clinicians.
AI.motivation: To enable timely prediction of severe AECOPD in home monitoring by leveraging near-continuous ventilator waveform data, addressing delays from episodic clinical data and limitations of binary risk alone.
AI.method: A two-stage approach using raw pressure and flow waveforms from the most recent seven days. Stage 1 is a classifier identifying high-risk patients; Stage 2 is a regression model estimating the number of days until a severe exacerbation. Evaluation metrics include F1 for classification and RMSE/R^2 for time-to-event prediction.
AI.result: Stage 1 classifier achieved F1 = 0.91. Stage 2 regression achieved RMSE = 1.00 days and R^2 = 0.76. The two-stage model outperformed traditional baselines on both tasks.
AI.conclusion: Directly modeling raw waveform data in a two-stage pipeline yields both early risk detection and actionable lead time for impending severe AECOPD, suggesting practical utility for home-monitoring deployments with ventilator data.

title: World-Model-Grounded LLM Planning for AUV and ASV Navigation Near Offshore Wind Farms
comment: This work has been accepted to the IEEE IROS 2026 AQ2UASIM workshop
summary: Large language models can turn a natural-language mission into a sequence of robot actions, but they do not have a sense of physics: they cannot judge how long a command should run, or whether it will make the robot drift into an obstacle. We proposed the use of a world model to expand the capabilities of Large Language model-based planners. Our method has three components: a physics-grounded neural world model, a three-phase gradient-based trajectory optimizer, and a Model Predictive Controller (MPC)-style closed-loop replanner with a trust-region guard. The language model decides what to do, and the world model decides how long, whether that means driving eight thrusters through 6 DOF or two differential thrusters through 3 DOF. We evaluate two marine vehicle classes operating near offshore wind infrastructure: a 6-DOF Autonomous Underwater Vehicle (AUV) and a 3-DOF differential-drive Autonomous Surface Vehicle (ASV). In five benchmark missions per platform, both vehicles reach every goal with zero predicted collisions, and both transfer to GazeboSim under ocean current, waves, and thruster dynamics, remaining collision-free and cutting GazeboSim goal-distance error versus the ungrounded baseline by 70-82% (ASV) and roughly 93% (AUV), after a residual fine-tuning pass that separately reduces surrogate rollout Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) by 60% (AUV) and 69% (ASV). For the ASV we further demonstrate a Vision language model (VLM)-assisted semantic-mapping pipeline that extracts obstacles and environmental context from satellite imagery, nautical charts, and forecast Application Programming Interface (API) instead of onboard sensors, reaching 96% navigability accuracy as a drop-in replacement for hand-specified obstacle geometry.

AI.tldr: Ground LLM-planners with a physics-grounded world model and MPC-style replanning to enable safe, accurate navigation for marine robots. Demonstrates zero-collision plans and large reductions in goal-distance error and rollout RMSE across 6-DOF AUV and 3-DOF ASV, with a VLM-based mapping enhancement for ASV.
AI.motivation: LLMs lack intrinsic physics intuition, making it hard to judge execution durations and obstacle avoidance. A physics-informed world model coupled with trajectory optimization and MPC-style replanning can ground high-level language plans into feasible, safe actions for high-DOF robotic systems.
AI.method: Three components: (1) a physics-grounded neural world model, (2) a three-phase gradient-based trajectory optimizer, and (3) an MPC-style closed-loop replanner with a trust-region guard. The LLM selects high-level goals; the world model determines how long and which actuation (e.g., 6-DOF AUV with eight thrusters vs 3-DOF ASV with two differential thrusters). Evaluation on two marine platforms (6-DOF AUV, 3-DOF ASV) across five benchmark missions per platform in GazeboSim under ocean currents and wave/thruster dynamics. For ASV, adds a Vision-Language Model assisted semantic-mapping pipeline using satellite imagery, nautical charts, and forecast API as a drop-in obstacle-geometry source.
AI.result: All missions achieved goal completion with zero predicted collisions. In GazeboSim, collision-free operation and substantially reduced goal-distance error: 70–82% improvement for ASV and ~93% for AUV compared to ungrounded baseline. Residual fine-tuning reduces surrogate rollout RMSE by 60% (AUV) and 69% (ASV). The ASV also demonstrates 96% navigability accuracy with VLM-assisted semantic mapping, replacing hand-specified onboard obstacle geometry.
AI.conclusion: Grounded LLM planning using a physics-informed world model and MPC-style replanning enables reliable, scalable navigation for complex marine environments. The added VLM-based semantic mapping further reduces reliance on onboard sensing and sustains high navigability.

title: PEA-DPO: Perception-Enhanced Alignment Direct Preference Optimization for MLLMs Alignment
summary: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) has emerged as an effective approach for aligning large language models (LLMs) with human preferences. However, its adaptation to multimodal settings remains unexplored. Through representational analysis, we identify a key limitation in multimodal preference optimization, which we term visual insensitivity: models often fail to distinguish between images and those with critical visual context removed. Our theoretical analysis further uncovers two manifestations of this problem, namely Across-Image Insensitivity and Within-Image Insensitivity. To address these challenges, we propose Perception-Enhanced Alignment DPO (PEA-DPO), a framework for multimodal LLMs alignment, which explicitly leverages visual preference signals to overcome visual insensitivity. We further provide a theoretical analysis demonstrating that PEA-DPO provably mitigates both failure modes. Empirical results demonstrate that PEA-DPO enhances sensitivity to visual context while preserving the language modeling capacity of the base model. Evaluations across three hallucination benchmarks using MLLMs of varying scales show that PEA-DPO effectively mitigates visual insensitivity, achieves stronger multimodal alignment, and substantially reduces hallucinations.

AI.tldr: PEA-DPO enhances multimodal alignment by incorporating visual preferences to overcome visual insensitivity (Across-Image and Within-Image), improving hallucination robustness without degrading LLM capacity.
AI.motivation: Identify and address visual insensitivity in multimodal preference optimization, where models fail to distinguish images from images with degraded or altered visual context, hindering alignment with human visual preferences.
AI.method: Propose Perception-Enhanced Alignment DPO (PEA-DPO), a framework that explicitly leverages visual preference signals in training for multimodal LLMs. Includes theoretical analysis showing mitigation of Across-Image and Within-Image insensitivity and empirical evaluation across hallucination benchmarks and varying model scales.
AI.result: PEA-DPO increases sensitivity to visual context, preserves language modeling capacity of the base model, achieves stronger multimodal alignment, and substantially reduces hallucinations across three benchmarks and multiple scales.
AI.conclusion: PEA-DPO effectively mitigates visual insensitivity in multimodal preference optimization, with theoretical guarantees and empirical validation demonstrating improved alignment and reduced hallucinations while preserving base LM capabilities.

title: Learning Hierarchical Skill Policies with Offline Quality-Diversity Reinforcement Learning
summary: Recent studies investigate how to leverage pre-collected datasets to improve the policy performance and sample efficiency of RL. One promising approach to achieve this goal is to employ a two-stage strategy: In the first stage, diverse skills are extracted as a low-level policy from a given dataset, and a high-level policy is trained to solve a specific task in the second stage. Typically, extraction of the low-level policy is performed based on unsupervised learning such as trajectory VAE. However, a limitation of this approach is that the quality of the low-level policy highly depends on the quality of the dataset. To address this issue, we introduce QDOS (Quality-Diversity Offline Skill learning), a unified pipeline for robust offline-to-online learning. Our approach incorporates an Advantage-Weighted Quality-Diversity pretraining objective, which weights the skill extraction and diversity objectives by the estimated advantage of each trajectory segment. This approach allows the model to extract diverse and high-value skills. By providing robust and task-relevant skill representations, QDOS significantly improves the quality of the embedded skill space used by the low-level policy. We further integrate this with a dual dataset reuse strategy, where offline data is used both for skill pretraining and for populating the online replay buffer via pseudo-labeling. Experiments demonstrate that QDOS significantly outperforms strong baselines in structured manipulation tasks and unstructured locomotion tasks, confirming its ability to accelerate exploration and improve final returns in challenging sparse-reward domains.

AI.tldr: QDOS: a robust offline-to-online RL framework that uses Advantage-Weighted Quality-Diversity pretraining to extract diverse, high-value skills from pre-collected data and a dual dataset reuse strategy to accelerate exploration and improve performance in sparse-reward tasks.
AI.motivation: Addresses dependence of low-level skill quality on dataset; aims to obtain robust, task-relevant skill representations to improve sample efficiency and final performance.
AI.method: Two-stage approach: skill extraction via Advantage-Weighted Quality-Diversity (A-AWD) objective weighting by estimated advantage; high-level policy trained on task with these skills; dual dataset reuse: offline data for pretraining and pseudo-labeling to populate online replay; evaluations on structured manipulation and unstructured locomotion.
AI.result: QDOS significantly outperforms strong baselines in both structured and unstructured tasks, demonstrating improved exploration and final returns in sparse-reward domains.
AI.conclusion: QDOS provides a unified, robust offline-to-online learning pipeline with high-quality skill spaces, enabling more efficient and effective policy learning across diverse domains.

title: Kähler landscapes for complex neural network descents and guarantees including a search and destroy of the Calabi-Yau manifold
summary: We study landscapes for complex-parameterized networks. Our approach is motivated with an information-theoretic manifold perspective of the parameter and via classical optimization guarantees although of complex geometric variety such as through Dolbeault asymptotics. The descent path admits a Kähler information metric under a cross-entropy via the Wirtinger Hessian on the log-likelihood potential. We restrict attention to a descent update rule with natural gradient descent via a differentiated loss scaled by the inverse metric, so the descent path remains in the holomorphic tangent bundle. We emphasize Calabi-Yau information manifolds which profane theoretical guarantees via an ill-curvature-conditioned landscape. Under a Calabi-Yau metric, specifically in a non-compact setting with a global potential so defined geometrically rather than invoking the topological requirements of the Calabi conjecture, a wedged nowhere-vanishing holomorphic form is the top exterior product of the Kähler form up to constants, yielding a constant determinant condition. Under a fixed determinant, a metric almost low rank up to an eigenvalue tolerance implies a blow-up effect. Moreover, it has been discovered that negative curvature subverts the loss landscape, specifically sectional curvature, so we expand on this and draw interconnections to negative-definite Ricci curvature. Our arguments primarily exist in a geometric analytic modality, although we establish roots in deep learning theory such as through asymptotics at initialization and connections through failure modes of neural network guarantees under vanishing and negative Ricci curvature.

AI.tldr: A geometric-analytic framework for complex-parameterized neural networks using Kähler/Calabi–Yau geometry; natural gradient on log-likelihood; key findings include constant determinant under Calabi–Yau metric, blow-up under fixed determinant, curvature effects on loss landscapes, and links to initialization and failure modes.
AI.motivation: To unify complex differential geometry with deep learning to study loss landscapes and training dynamics of networks with complex-valued or holomorphic parameterizations.
AI.method: Adopt an information-theoretic manifold view with Dolbeault asymptotics; use the Wirtinger Hessian of log-likelihood to define a Kähler information metric; constrain descent updates to the holomorphic tangent bundle via natural gradient descent; analyze Calabi–Yau information manifolds in a non-compact setting with a global potential; derive determinant conditions and study curvature effects on optimization landscapes.
AI.result: Calabi–Yau metric with a global potential yields a constant top exterior product of the Kähler form; under a fixed determinant, the metric is almost low-rank and can induce blow-up behavior; negative curvature (sectional and Ricci) tends to subvert the loss landscape; connections are drawn between curvature properties and neural network guarantees, including asymptotics at initialization and potential failure modes under vanishing/negative Ricci curvature.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a geometric-analytic lens for neural network landscapes, linking complex differential geometry to training dynamics and guarantees, and highlights curvature as a lever affecting descent behavior and stability in complex-parameterized networks.

title: SAGE: Ergodic Control for Autonomous and Adaptive Inspection of Subsea Infrastructure
comment: This work has been accepted to the IEEE IROS 2026 AQ2UASIM workshop
summary: Subsea Christmas Trees (XTs) are underwater structures that use valves for directing oil flow, needing constant inspection. But not every valve carries the same risk at the same time: a valve with a suspected leak needs to be revisited far more often than one with a clean history, and that risk picture changes during the mission as new leaks are found. To handle this, we present SAGE (Semantic and Adaptive Generative Ergodicity), an ergodic-control architecture that allocates vehicle time in proportion to a live, sensor-derived risk distribution rather than a scripted route. We study a two-XT scenario, with five valves in total, and compare a fixed-loop A* tour against SAGE. Both methods can be tuned to spend similar total time near a high-risk valve, but only ergodic control also checks it more often: in simulation, a dominant-risk valve was revisited every 5.8 s under ergodic control against a fixed 8.1 s for every valve under A*, regardless of risk, so a leak can go unnoticed for barely two-thirds as long. Because the tracked distribution is recomputed rather than planned once, a newly detected leak shifts vehicle behavior on the next control cycle with no explicit re-planning step and no operator in the loop, which a fixed tour cannot do without a discrete re-route. We derive the ergodic control law behind this behavior and report simulation results on the five-valve scenario.

AI.tldr: SAGE uses ergodic control to allocate AUV time to a live risk distribution rather than a fixed route, improving revisits to high-risk valves in a two-XT, five-valve submarine scenario; simulation shows faster revisits to a dominant-risk valve than a fixed A* tour.
AI.motivation: Subsea valve leaks pose uneven risk and require frequent inspection; a fixed, scripted route is inefficient as risk evolves during a mission and with new leaks detected.
AI.method: Develop an ergodic-control law (SAGE) that allocates vehicle time proportional to a live, sensor-derived risk distribution; compare against a fixed-loop A* tour in a two-XT, five-valve scenario; risk distribution is updated online as leaks are detected, enabling on-the-fly adaptation without operator intervention.
AI.result: Ergodic control revisited the dominant-risk valve every 5.8 s, versus 8.1 s for the fixed tour; total exposure time near high-risk valves is similar between methods, but ergodic control checks high-risk valves more often and reacts to newly detected leaks on the next cycle without re-planning.
AI.conclusion: Online, risk-driven ergodic control enhances adaptability and responsiveness over fixed routing in subsea valve inspection tasks, achieving more frequent high-risk checks without explicit re-planning or operator input, as demonstrated in simulation.

title: TextRefine: Improving Textual Fidelity, Spatial Placement, and Glyph Rendering for Text Editing in Product Posters
summary: Text editing in product posters entails inserting new text or replacing existing text while preserving product appearance, background content, and global composition. Despite recent progress in instruction-based image editing, general-purpose models remain unreliable in this setting: they often omit or incorrectly render the target text, place it over salient products or pre-existing content, and produce structurally distorted or visually inconsistent glyphs. We introduce \textbf{TextRefine}, a task-aligned post-training framework that combines supervised fine-tuning with operation-specific reward optimization to address these complementary failure modes. For text insertion, our text-span-level reward jointly assesses semantic fidelity and target-span coverage, penalizes spatial conflicts with products and existing text, and employs a gated structural constraint to preserve non-text regions. For text replacement, our glyph-level reward leverages the connectionist temporal classification (CTC) posterior of the target character to provide graded supervision for fine-grained defects, including missing strokes, structural deformations, and confusion among visually similar characters. We further introduce \textbf{OpenTextEdit}, a dataset comprising 100K images for text editing in product posters, with multi-text layouts, detailed text attributes, product masks, and challenging low-frequency characters. Extensive experiments on both insertion and replacement demonstrate that TextRefine consistently outperforms the evaluated image editing baselines in textual fidelity, placement reliability, and glyph quality while better preserving source-image content.

AI.tldr: TextRefine is a task-aligned post-training framework for text editing in product posters, combining supervised fine-tuning with operation-specific reward optimization for insertion and replacement; OpenTextEdit is a 100K-image dataset for robust text-edit benchmarks.
AI.motivation: General-purpose image editors struggle with text edits in posters, causing missing or misrendered text, improper placement, and distorted glyphs. The work aims to improve textual fidelity, placement reliability, and glyph quality while preserving the underlying image.
AI.method: For insertion: a text-span-level reward that jointly assesses semantic fidelity, target-span coverage, penalties for spatial conflicts with products/other text, and a gated structural constraint to preserve non-text regions. For replacement: a glyph-level reward leveraging the CTC posterior of the target character to provide graded supervision for fine-grained defects (strokes, deformations, confusions). The approach is a task-aligned post-training framework combining supervised fine-tuning with operation-specific reward optimization. OpenTextEdit: a dataset of 100K images with multi-text layouts, detailed text attributes, product masks, and challenging low-frequency characters.
AI.result: TextRefine consistently outperforms evaluated image-editing baselines in textual fidelity, placement reliability, and glyph quality, while better preserving source-image content.
AI.conclusion: The approach shows that task-aligned post-training with specialized text- and glyph-focused rewards and a large, realistic dataset can substantially improve text editing in product posters, addressing both insertion and replacement challenges.

title: Rethinking the Evaluation and Optimization of LLM-Based Social Simulation
summary: LLM-based social simulation is a promising complement to traditional methods such as surveys and behavioral experiments. A core question is how to evaluate the fidelity of LLM-simulated human behavior and optimize LLMs toward it. Prevailing practice evaluates by accuracy, checking whether the model selects the single response observed from a human, and trains the LLM to reproduce this hard label. However, human behavior is inherently subjective: the same person in the same situation may reasonably act differently, so an observed response is only one draw from an underlying response distribution, rendering accuracy-based evaluation unreliable and hard-label training misleading. To address these problems, we first introduce the subjectivity coefficient, an entropy-based quantity distinguishing objective tasks such as coding from subjective ones such as social simulation, and use it to systematically analyze how accuracy-based evaluation and hard-label training fail as subjectivity grows. Based on the subjectivity coefficient, we propose Subjectivity-Adaptive soft-Label Training (SALT): it pools observed outputs from semantically nearby inputs into soft distributional labels, with an aggregation radius adapted to the estimated subjectivity of each input; in the near-objective limit the neighborhood shrinks, so SALT naturally falls back to standard single-label training. Moreover, since existing datasets record only single observed responses and cannot support distributional evaluation, we construct SUBJSIM, a benchmark of 19,300 contexts covering 193 annotators and 100 subjective questions. Since real-world data typically provide only a single observation per input, our experiments train models from single observed outputs while evaluating them against the full response distributions, verifying feasibility in realistic settings. Results on SUBJSIM demonstrate the advantages of our method.

AI.tldr: Introduce a subjectivity-aware training and evaluation framework for LLM-based social simulations that accounts for distribution of human responses rather than single labels.
AI.motivation: Human behavior is subjective; accuracy-based evaluation and hard-label training misrepresent distributions; need a metric to quantify subjectivity and methods to train models accordingly.
AI.method: Define a subjectivity coefficient based on entropy to separate objective vs subjective tasks. Propose Subjectivity-Adaptive soft-Label Training (SALT) that aggregates nearby inputs' outputs into soft labels with an input-specific neighborhood radius. Create SUBJSIM benchmark with 19,300 contexts, 193 annotators, 100 subjective questions. Train on single observed outputs but evaluate against full response distributions.
AI.result: On SUBJSIM, SALT demonstrates advantages over hard-label training and accuracy-based evaluation, showing better alignment with distributional human responses.
AI.conclusion: Accounting for subjectivity via entropy-based measurement and soft-label aggregation improves fidelity assessment and training for LLM-based social simulations; the SUBJSIM dataset enables distributional evaluation in realistic settings.

title: Unregularized Convergence of Single-Loop, Entropy-Regularized Natural Actor-Critic
summary: While entropy regularization is widely used to stabilize and accelerate Natural Policy Gradient methods, its ability to yield faster convergence rates for the unregularized objective remains underexplored. Existing analyses often rely on double-loop architectures and invoke a linear entropy penalty. To bridge the gap between theory and practice, we analyze a single-loop, entropy-regularized Natural Actor-Critic algorithm under compatible linear function approximation. By training an uncentered critic, our critic tracking can remain stable even as the training policy approaches determinism and the Fisher information matrix degenerates. We focus on two primary regimes for the optimization landscape: a Stochastic Regime, where we fuse coupled actor-critic updates into a joint Lyapunov recurrence, and a Deterministic Regime, where we pivot to a Policy Mirror Descent framework to circumvent the collapse of Euclidean geometry. By exploiting a positive Minimal Action Gap in the unregularized Markov decision process, we introduce an Exponential Translation mechanism that maps the regularized gap to the unregularized one up to an exponentially decaying tail. By tuning the fixed temperature, our algorithm achieves accelerated unregularized convergence rates, up to approximation-error terms: $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(T_{total}^{-1})$ in the Stochastic Regime, and $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(T_{total}^{-2/3})$ for the average iterate alongside $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(T_{total}^{-1/3})$ for the last iterate in the Deterministic Regime. Here, $T_{total}$ denotes the total number of stochastic critic updates (or Monte Carlo rollouts). Furthermore, in the tabular setting, our positive-action-gap analysis yields a $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(T_{total}^{-2/3})$ average-iterate rate, surpassing the $\mathcal{O}(T_{total}^{-1/2})$ worst-case statistical barrier that applies without a positive action margin.

AI.tldr: A single-loop entropy-regularized natural actor-critic with compatible linear function approximation achieves accelerated convergence to the unregularized objective via an Exponential Translation mechanism under a positive action gap; two regimes yield distinct rates: stochastic ~O~(T_total^{-1}); deterministic average ~O~(T_total^{-2/3}) and last iterate ~O~(T_total^{-1/3}); in the tabular setting, average iterate ~O~(T_total^{-2/3}) beating the worst-case ~O~(T_total^{-1/2}) barrier without a positive action margin.
AI.motivation: Close the gap between entropy-regularization theory and unregularized objective convergence for policy optimization. Provide a stable single-loop algorithm that remains effective as the policy becomes deterministic and the Fisher information matrix degenerates, leveraging a positive action gap to translate progress in the regularized objective to the unregularized one.
AI.method: The paper analyzes a single-loop entropy-regularized Natural Actor-Critic with compatible linear function approximation, using an uncentered critic for stability. It considers two regimes: (i) Stochastic Regime with a joint Lyapunov recurrence for coupled actor-critic updates; (ii) Deterministic Regime via Policy Mirror Descent to avoid Euclidean geometry collapse. An Exponential Translation mechanism maps the regularized gap to the unregularized gap under a fixed temperature, leveraging a positive action gap.
AI.result: Accelerated unregularized convergence rates are established: in the Stochastic Regime, the objective converges at ~O(T_total^{-1}); in the Deterministic Regime, the average iterate converges at ~O(T_total^{-2/3}) and the last iterate at ~O(T_total^{-1/3}); in the tabular setting, the average iterate achieves ~O(T_total^{-2/3}). These rates hold up to approximation-error terms.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that entropy regularization, when analyzed with a single-loop NAT-AC and positive action-gap, can yield accelerated convergence to the unregularized objective. The Exponential Translation mechanism and fixed-temperature tuning are central to translating regularized progress into unregularized gains, offering practical guidance for achieving faster convergence in policy optimization.

title: Keeping the Franka Emika Panda alive: a ROS 2 stack with a reliable position interface
summary: This paper presents an open-source software stack that restores ROS 2 support for the Franka Emika Panda robot while resolving the long-standing unreliability of its external position control interface. We first analyze the root causes of unstable position control and show that the observed vibrations and protective stops arise from the timing of the external control loop and sampling jitter, rather than from limitations of the robot itself. Building on this analysis, we introduce an asynchronous hardware interface that decouples real-time communication from the ROS 2 control loop, a rate-matching mechanism for slower command sources, and a position-domain reference generation strategy that produces reliable, smooth position commands. Experimental validation shows that the proposed architecture reliably tracks velocity references by reducing motion artifacts introduced by the official implementation, and the stack is validated across motion planning, compliance control, position-controlled manipulation, and haptic teleoperation on two independent Panda platforms. By restoring a modern, reliable, and open ROS 2 ecosystem for the Panda, this work lowers the barrier to developing safe, responsive, and reproducible human-robot collaboration applications that integrate planning, perception, interaction, and shared autonomy. Code and videos are available on our website at https://sites.google.com/view/fer-ros2/.

AI.tldr: Open-source ROS 2 stack restoring support for Franka Emika Panda and addressing unreliable external position control by decoupling real-time control, rate-matching, and a position-domain reference generator; validated on two Panda arms across planning, compliance, manipulation, and haptic teleoperation; code and videos available.
AI.motivation: To fix long-standing instability in Panda's external position control interface and enable a modern, reliable, and open ROS 2 ecosystem for safe, reproducible human-robot collaboration.
AI.method: 1) Root-cause analysis showing that vibrations and protective stops stem from timing of the external control loop and sampling jitter rather than robot hardware limits. 2) Develop an asynchronous hardware interface to decouple real-time communication from the ROS 2 control loop. 3) Implement rate-matching for slower command sources. 4) Introduce a position-domain reference generation strategy producing smooth position commands. 5) Experimental validation across planning, compliance control, position-controlled manipulation, and haptic teleoperation on two Panda platforms.
AI.result: Architecture reliably tracks velocity references with reduced motion artifacts compared to the official implementation; demonstrates improved stability and smoothness; validated across motion planning, compliance, manipulation, and haptic teleoperation on two independent Panda arms.
AI.conclusion: Restores a modern, reliable, and open ROS 2 ecosystem for the Panda, lowering barriers to developing safe, responsive, and reproducible HRC applications that integrate planning, perception, interaction, and shared autonomy; code and videos available on the project website.

title: S$^2$GS: Structured Sparse Gaussian Streaming for Efficient Free-Viewpoint Video Reconstruction on Edge-IoT Devices
comment: Project Page, Code, and Supplementary Material: https://github.com/liyw420/S2GS
summary: Streaming reconstruction of Free-Viewpoint Videos (FVVs) supports immersive Internet of Things (IoT) services, such as telepresence and digital twin visualization. Existing methods suffer from high per-frame optimization time and large storage footprints, limiting deployment on resource-constrained Edge-IoT devices. To address these challenges, we propose Structured Sparse Gaussian Streaming (S$^2$GS), an FVV reconstruction framework that exploits structure-aware temporal sparsity to selectively update Gaussian residuals, enabling efficient streaming without compromising visual fidelity. In the spatial domain, a streaming octree hierarchically organizes Gaussian residuals, capturing spatial correlations that guide residual updates. In the temporal domain, a structured gating mechanism, comprising hierarchical feature propagation (HFP) and Gumbel-Sigmoid sampling, converts hierarchical dynamic cues into sparse residual update decisions under differentiable optimization. A multi-level discrete scheme is further adopted to provide fine-grained control over residual updates while preserving intricate dynamic details. Extensive experiments across consumer GPUs, industrial edge IoT devices, and a physical telepresence testbed demonstrate that S$^2$GS consistently reduces per-frame optimization time and storage footprint while maintaining competitive visual quality. Compared with QUEEN, S$^2$GS reduces per-frame optimization time by 59% and storage costs by 85% on an RTX 4090 GPU. On the Jetson AGX Orin, S$^2$GS delivers the highest rendering throughput (60+ FPS) and the lowest energy consumption among the evaluated methods, demonstrating its potential for deployment in resource-constrained systems.

AI.tldr: S^2GS: Structured Sparse Gaussian Streaming for FVV reconstruction that uses a streaming octree and hierarchical gating (HFP + Gumbel-Sigmoid) to update Gaussian residuals sparsely, reducing per-frame optimization time and storage on edge devices while preserving visual fidelity; outperforms QUEEN and enables 60+ FPS on Jetson AGX Orin.
AI.motivation: Address high per-frame optimization time and large storage footprints in streaming FVV on resource-constrained Edge-IoT devices.
AI.method: Spatial: streaming octree to organize Gaussian residuals; Temporal: structured gating with hierarchical feature propagation (HFP) and Gumbel-Sigmoid sampling to decide sparse residual updates; multi-level discrete scheme for fine-grained control; differentiable optimization; structure-aware temporal sparsity.
AI.result: Significant reductions in per-frame optimization time (59% vs QUEEN on RTX 4090) and storage costs (85%); 60+ FPS rendering and lower energy consumption on Jetson AGX Orin; consistent performance across GPUs and edge devices; competitive visual quality.
AI.conclusion: S^2GS enables efficient FVV streaming on edge devices by exploiting spatial-temporal structure, offering practical deployment potential for resource-constrained systems.

title: Beyond Memory Majority: Latent-Source Reasoning for Multi-Agent Memory Arbitration
summary: Long-term multi-agent systems continuously accumulate the memories produced by different agents. Existing memory methods typically treat retrieved memories as independent evidence and combine them through voting or weighting. However, this independence assumption often fails in multi-agent settings: memories written by different agents may inherit the same upstream source or shared bias, causing correlated evidence to be repeatedly counted and creating a false majority. We term this failure mode \textit{Memory Correlation Bias}. To address the issue, we propose the \textbf{C}orrelation-\textbf{A}ware \textbf{M}emory \textbf{A}rbitration (CAMA) framework that jointly decouples retrieved memories and recovers missing independent evidence. We model the retrieved memories as query-conditioned evidence groups and combine neural dependency inference with provenance-based symbolic priors to estimate the effective number of independent evidence sources, thereby preventing correlated memories from forming a false majority. Since critical independent evidence may be absent from the initial retrieval set, \textsc{CAMA} further learns a sequential recovery policy that actively retrieves alternative evidence or traces upstream sources before making the final decision, aiming to recover sufficient independent evidence for reliable arbitration while minimizing retrieval cost. Experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of our method over the state-of-the-art baseline methods, suppressing false majorities induced by correlated memories.

AI.tldr: Introduces Memory Correlation Bias and proposes Correlation-Aware Memory Arbitration (CAMA) to decouple memories, infer independence, and actively retrieve missing evidence to avoid false majorities; shows improved performance on benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Independent evidence assumption fails due to shared upstream sources / biases in long-term multi-agent memory; need to detect and compensate for correlated memories to avoid misarbitration.
AI.method: Model retrieved memories as query-conditioned evidence groups; combine neural dependency inference with provenance-based symbolic priors to estimate effective number of independent sources; sequential recovery policy to fetch alternative evidence or trace sources; arbitration to final decision.
AI.result: Experiments on multiple benchmarks show superiority over state-of-the-art baselines; suppress false majorities induced by correlated memories.
AI.conclusion: CAMA effectively mitigates memory correlation bias, improving reliability of arbitration in long-term multi-agent systems; preserves efficiency by limiting retrieval costs.

title: Complementary, Not Cumulative: Interaction Effects in Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Navier-Stokes Vortex Shedding
summary: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) embed governing partial differential equations directly into the training loss, offering a promising alternative to costly CFD solvers for unsteady flows. Yet the growing list of techniques proposed to improve PINN training is typically validated one at a time, leaving open whether these techniques actually compose. We study this question in depth on the DFG/Schafer-Turek unsteady cylinder wake benchmark. In isolation, nearly every technique performs no better than an untreated baseline. However, combining periodic (SIREN) activations with causal weighting unlocks a previously inaccessible regime, reconstructing velocity and pressure fields to within 4.1% average relative L2 error against an OpenFOAM reference solution. Adding further techniques instead causes catastrophic performance degradation, demonstrating that individually effective PINN interventions can interact nonlinearly and that more elaborate training recipes are not necessarily better.

AI.tldr: PINN technique interactions are nonlinear and not additive; most individual edits do not help, but combining SIREN activations with causal weighting enables accurate recovery in a unsteady cylinder wake benchmark (4.1% error).
AI.motivation: Assess whether commonly proposed PINN training techniques compose well or interfere with each other, addressing reproducibility and practical recipe design.
AI.method: Empirical study on the DFG/Schafer-Turek unsteady cylinder wake benchmark. Systematically evaluate PINN interventions in isolation and in combination; examine periodic (SIREN) activations with causal weighting; compare reconstructed velocity/pressure fields to OpenFOAM references; report relative L2 errors.
AI.result: Most techniques fail to improve over the untreated baseline when used alone. The combination of SIREN activations with causal weighting unlocks a regime achieving 4.1% average relative L2 error against OpenFOAM. Adding further techniques leads to catastrophic degradation due to nonlinear interactions, showing that more elaborate training recipes are not inherently better.
AI.conclusion: Interventions for PINNs interact nonlinearly; effective performance relies on careful, possibly scarce, combinations rather than additive improvements. This underscores the need for systematic evaluation of PINN recipe compatibility and cautions against assuming independent benefits from individual techniques.

title: GOAG: Generative and Object-Agnostic Grasp Planner for Dexterous Robotic Manipulation
summary: Multifingered grasping is a crucial robotic skill, but current deep-learning grasp planners often struggle to generalize to new objects because they are trained on limited, object-specific datasets. We introduce a fundamentally different approach, grounded in the observation that the gripper and the object share identical surface geometry at their mutual contact points. We propose GOAG: Generative and Object-Agnostic Grasp Planner for Dexterous Robotic Manipulation, a novel deep generative model that learns a compact latent representation of a specific gripper's contact surface distribution, enabling the efficient sampling of valid grasp configurations without relying on object-specific training data. We show that by introducing object features only at inference time, our model can effectively retrieve admissible contact areas that are compatible with the gripper's capabilities. We validate our approach through extensive experiments on established grasp protocols in both simulated and real-world scenarios, demonstrating its effectiveness with different grippers from the literature. Our method delivers state-of-the-art results on the objects from the MultiDex dataset, achieving an average success rate of 86.93%. It offers significantly faster processing when generating numerous grasps, while matching the performance of leading approaches specifically trained on this dataset. Unlike these methods, our approach does not rely on object-specific training data, highlighting the advantages of object-agnostic learning. It effectively addresses the generalization challenges faced by traditional data-driven grasp planners. Code and videos are available on our project website https://cea-list.github.io/goagweb/ .

AI.tldr: GOAG is an object-agnostic, generative grasp planner that learns a latent distribution of a gripper's contact surface, enabling rapid sampling of valid grasps without object-specific training and achieving strong performance on MultiDex.
AI.motivation: Traditional deep grasp planners struggle to generalize to unseen objects due to reliance on object-specific training data; a need for object-agnostic grasp generation that leverages contact geometry.
AI.method: A deep generative model learns a compact latent representation of the gripper's contact-surface distribution; at inference time, object features are provided to retrieve admissible contact areas compatible with the gripper; tested across several grippers and datasets.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art on MultiDex with an average 86.93% success; faster across many grasps; matches or exceeds specialized methods without training on object data; demonstrates object-agnostic generalization.
AI.conclusion: Object-agnostic, geometry-based learning can address generalization challenges in dexterous grasping, enabling flexible manipulation across diverse objects and grippers; code and videos are publicly available.

title: When Guidance Goes Off-Scale: Recalibrating Diffusion Transformers under Analog Compute-in-Memory Nonidealities
summary: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) incur high memory traffic and energy costs because sampling repeatedly evaluates large denoisers dominated by linear operations. Analog compute-in-memory (CIM) can alleviate these costs by executing linear operations within weight-storing memory arrays. However, CIM nonidealities perturb effective weights, with errors accumulating along the state-dependent denoising trajectory; their interaction with classifier-free guidance (CFG) remains underexplored. In this paper, we characterize the impact of analog CIM nonidealities on DiT sampling. Although conditional and unconditional predictions can each remain close to their clean counterparts, their difference (the CFG residual) is disproportionately attenuated and rotated. Identifying this residual as a controllable failure channel, we propose a retraining-free, sampler-side recalibration that adjusts only the CFG scale for a given CIM condition. Trajectory-level analysis shows that moderate recalibration strengthens the target-oriented component preserved in the distorted residual, enabling earlier commitment to a prompt-consistent semantic region. In contrast, excessive guidance amplifies the full noisy residual and degrades quality, resulting in a finite, noise-dependent optimum. Extensive experiments on PixArt-Sigma, PixArt-alpha, and DiT-XL/2 show that the optimal guidance scale increases with CIM noise. Using 30,000 samples per condition, guidance recalibration consistently restores generation quality across simulated CIM mappings, closing at least 87% of the CIM-induced FID gap at a CIM noise level of 0.20. It reduces FID from 59.22 to 20.49 on PixArt-Sigma, 72.37 to 21.12 on PixArt-alpha, and 20.89 to 6.62 on DiT-XL/2.

AI.tldr: CIM nonidealities in diffusion transformers perturb the CFG residual during sampling; authors propose a retraining-free, sampler-side recalibration by tuning the CFG scale to counteract CIM effects. Demonstrates substantial restoration of image quality across datasets with noise-aware optimal guidance, reducing FID gaps substantially.
AI.motivation: Understand and mitigate the impact of analog compute-in-memory (CIM) nonidealities on diffusion transformer (DiT) sampling, and address interaction with classifier-free guidance (CFG) to maintain generation quality while leveraging CIM.
AI.method: Characterize how CIM nonidealities affect conditional/unconditional predictions and the CFG residual; identify residual as a controllable failure channel; propose retraining-free recalibration by adjusting CFG scale per CIM condition; perform trajectory-level analysis; extensive experiments on PixArt-Sigma, PixArt-alpha, and DiT-XL/2 across CIM noise levels with 30k samples per condition.
AI.result: The CFG residue is disproportionately attenuated and rotated under CIM errors; calibrated CFG scale strengthens the target-oriented component, enabling earlier commitment to consistent semantic regions. There exists a finite, noise-dependent optimum for guidance. With CIM noise at 0.20, recalibration closes at least 87% of the CIM-induced FID gap; FID reductions: PixArt-Sigma 59.22→20.49, PixArt-alpha 72.37→21.12, DiT-XL/2 20.89→6.62.
AI.conclusion: Sampler-side CFG recalibration is an effective, retraining-free method to mitigate CIM nonidealities in DiT sampling, yielding substantial quality gains and revealing a noise-dependent optimal guidance level for CIM-enabled diffusion models.

title: SafeBranch: Branch-Pair Safety Alignment for Embodied Agents
summary: Vision-language-model-based embodied agents can complete instructed tasks but often violate safety constraints in the process, a problem recently framed as interactive safety. Training such agents to act safely is difficult, since safety and task success are distinct objectives, and safety arises only at a small number of safety-critical steps within a trajectory. Standard supervision is insufficient: imitating safe trajectories teaches behavior without explaining why it is safe, and contrasting arbitrary safe and unsafe trajectories mixes the safety signal with unrelated differences. We propose SafeBranch, a framework that aligns an embodied actor on safety through branch pairs constructed from the actor's own unsafe rollouts via environment rollback. SafeBranch rolls each unsafe rollout back to the safety-critical step that caused the violation, queries the actor for a safe alternative, and pairs the original action with the alternative so that the two branches differ only at that step. The trained actor acts safely at deployment with no critic in the loop. On IS-Bench, SafetyALFRED, and out-of-distribution variants with unseen tasks and objects, it handles safety reliably without sacrificing task success, achieving roughly ten times more safe successes than the untrained baseline on the unseen-object variant.

AI.tldr: SafeBranch aligns an embodied policy with safety by creating branch pairs from the agent's own unsafe rollouts through rollback to the safety-critical step, querying for a safe alternative, and training the agent to prefer the safe branch—achieving safer behavior without a separate critic or sacrificing task success.
AI.motivation: Safety and task success are distinct objectives, and safety often occurs only at a small subset of trajectory steps; imitation-based supervision alone cannot explain safety and can conflate unrelated differences.
AI.method: From unsafe rollouts, rollback to the safety-critical step to form a pair of branches that differ only at that step; prompt the agent for a safe alternative at that point; pair the original action with the safe alternative and train the actor to maximize safety-conditioned signals, without using a critic in the loop.
AI.result: In IS-Bench, SafetyALFRED, and out-of-distribution variants with unseen tasks/objects, SafeBranch produces reliably safer behavior and ~10x more safe successes than the untrained baseline on unseen-object tasks, while maintaining task performance.
AI.conclusion: SafeBranch provides an effective, critic-free safety alignment mechanism for vision-language embodied agents by locally correcting unsafe decisions at safety-critical steps using environment rollback-based branch pairs.

title: Time-Uniform Self-Normalized Concentration for Discounted Least Squares: Limits and Corrections
summary: Self-normalized concentration inequalities are standard tools in bandit and reinforcement-learning analyses. A widely used weighted extension claims an analogous time-uniform guarantee for discounted least-squares estimators in non-stationary problems. A simple scalar Gaussian counterexample with a fixed parameter shows that the claimed bounded radius is crossed with probability one. For fixed discount and regularization parameters, we further show that, when $δ\leq1/2$ and $T/δ$ is sufficiently large, any deterministic anytime boundary valid uniformly over the stated conditionally sub-Gaussian model class must be at least of order $R\sqrt{\log(T/δ)}$ at some time by horizon $T$; for nondecreasing boundaries, this order is required at time $T$. We identify the proof error: different terminal times use different Gaussian mixing distributions, so the fixed-time mixtures do not form one supermartingale, and the stopping-time argument does not repair this failure. Finally, we show that the weighted inequality remains valid at each fixed deterministic time, give valid finite- and infinite-horizon corrections, and discuss consequences for downstream analyses.

AI.tldr: Identifies a critical flaw in a claimed time-uniform self-normalized concentration bound for discounted least-squares in non-stationary settings, demonstrates lower-bound growth for any deterministic boundary, explains the proof error (non-uniform Gaussian mixtures across terminal times), and provides corrected fixed-time results and horizon corrections with implications for downstream analyses.
AI.motivation: Ensure reliability of time-uniform concentration inequalities used in bandit and reinforcement-learning analyses under discounting and non-stationarity; prevent erroneous inferences from flawed bounds.
AI.method: Construct a simple scalar Gaussian counterexample with a fixed parameter to violate the claimed bound; derive lower bounds showing necessity of boundary growth (∼R√log(T/δ)) at horizon T for δ≤1/2 and large T/δ; diagnose the proof error by showing that terminal-time mixtures vary with time, precluding a single supermartingale; establish that the weighted inequality remains valid at fixed times and provide finite- and infinite-horizon corrections.
AI.result: The claimed radius bound is invalid in general; any deterministic anytime boundary uniform over the model class must incur at least Ω(R√log(T/δ)) growth at some time (and at T for nondecreasing boundaries). The identified error stems from using different Gaussian mixtures at different terminal times, violating the supermartingale property; however, the weighted inequality holds at fixed deterministic times, and corrected finite- and infinite-horizon forms are proposed along with implications for downstream work.
AI.conclusion: Time-uniform self-normalized bounds for discounted estimators require careful construction; the paper provides a corrected understanding: (i) the general boundary must grow with log terms, (ii) the previous proof is flawed due to non-stationary mixtures, and (iii) valid fixed-time results and horizon-corrected forms remain usable for downstream analyses.

title: CoToGrasp: Contact-Topology-Conditioned Dexterous Grasp Synthesis via Canonical Workspace Learning
summary: Current dexterous grasp planners primarily optimize for physical stability, focusing on whether an object can be grasped rather than how it should be grasped to support downstream functional tasks.
