However, conditioning grasp synthesis on specific human grasp taxonomies typically requires prohibitively expensive, object-annotated datasets. To address these limitations, we propose CoToGrasp, a novel generative framework that synthesizes diverse, stable grasps strictly conditioned on specific contact topologies. To bypass the data collection bottleneck, CoToGrasp is trained entirely in an object-agnostic manner. We introduce a feature-based canonical workspace that projects local object features into a unified gripper-centric domain, effectively decoupling the semantic functional intent from the arbitrary object geometry. By learning the intrinsic contact manifold of the gripper within this workspace, our model achieves zero-shot generalization to unseen objects at inference. Extensive evaluations on the large-scale DexGraspNet dataset demonstrate that CoToGrasp achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming existing taxonomy-guided planners. Finally, we demonstrate the physical viability and kinematic feasibility of our synthesized contact topologies on a physical robot platform. Code is available on our project website https://cea-list.github.io/cotograspweb/ .

AI.tldr: CoToGrasp is a data-efficient, object-agnostic generative framework that synthesizes diverse, stable grasps conditioned on specific contact topologies, enabling zero-shot generalization to unseen objects and achieving state-of-the-art results on DexGraspNet while validating physical feasibility on hardware.
AI.motivation: Current dexterous grasp planners emphasize static stability while neglecting task-driven grasp semantics; conditioning grasps on human taxonomies requires expensive, object-annotated datasets, creating a data bottleneck for functional grasp synthesis.
AI.method: CoToGrasp trains a generative model in an object-agnostic setting. It uses a feature-based canonical workspace to map local object features into a gripper-centric domain, decoupling functional intent from geometry. The model learns the intrinsic contact manifold of the gripper, enabling zero-shot generalization to unseen objects. Evaluations are conducted on DexGraspNet, and physical feasibility is demonstrated on a robot platform; code is released.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on DexGraspNet, surpassing taxonomy-guided planners. Demonstrates high-quality, diverse, and stable contact topologies that are physically feasible and kinematically executable on hardware.
AI.conclusion: A data-efficient, generalizable approach to contact-topology conditioned grasp synthesis that decouples functional intent from object geometry, enabling zero-shot transfer and effective downstream task support without requiring object-annotated datasets.

title: PL-NBA: A Possession-level Universal Basketball Video Dataset Supporting Multiple Visual Understanding Tasks
summary: Visual understanding in sports has emerged as a hot topic in computer vision in recent years. Most existing basketball video datasets adopt single action or activity as sample, which can neither preserve the temporal continuity of game events nor support complex tasks such as action anticipation. To address this issue, this paper constructs the first possession-level basketball video dataset (PL-NBA), in which each sample is composed of a complete NBA offensive possession. Collected from 60 NBA games, PL-NBA contains 11,000 valid offensive possession clips and 31,567 annotated events with player names, captions, event types and timestamps. Each video clip includes multiple events and preserves the continuity of events, which is helpful for analysis of tactic. Experiment is conducted on multiple visual understanding tasks, including event recognition, video captioning, temporal action localization and action anticipation. Experimental results show that existing methods achieve limited performance on above four tasks, demonstrating that PL-NBA is a challenging benchmark for sports video understanding.

AI.tldr: A new possession-level basketball video dataset (PL-NBA) with 11k offensive possessions and 31k events across 60 NBA games, preserving temporal continuity to enable action recognition, captioning, localization, and anticipation; experiments show existing methods perform poorly, indicating this dataset as a challenging benchmark for sports video understanding.
AI.motivation: To overcome the limitations of single-action datasets that break temporal continuity and hinder complex tasks like action anticipation; provide a dataset that captures complete offensive possessions with annotated events to support holistic analysis of tactics in basketball.
AI.method: Construct PL-NBA by collecting 60 NBA games; segment into complete offensive possessions; annotate 31,567 events with player names, captions, event types, and timestamps; each video clip contains multiple events and preserves event continuity; evaluate on event recognition, video captioning, temporal action localization, and action anticipation using existing methods as baselines.
AI.result: Existing methods show limited performance on the four tasks, indicating that PL-NBA is a challenging benchmark that reflects the complexity of real possession-level basketball analysis.
AI.conclusion: PL-NBA provides a novel, challenging resource for sports video understanding that emphasizes temporal continuity and multi-event analysis, enabling research into tactical reasoning and action anticipation beyond single-action datasets.

title: GenMatch: An End-to-End Generative Matching Framework for Micro-View Order-Dispatching in Ride-Hailing
summary: Micro-View Order-Dispatching assigns available drivers to passenger orders within each dispatch batch and is critical to the service quality and operational efficiency of ride-hailing platforms. Mainstream industrial solutions follow a multi-stage paradigm of model prediction, value calculation, and dispatch matching. Although dispatch quality is determined by the final batch-level assignment, these stages optimize different intermediate objectives. This cross-stage objective inconsistency means that improving a single stage does not necessarily improve the overall dispatch result. We therefore formulate Micro-View Order-Dispatching as a generative matching problem and propose GenMatch, an end-to-end Generative Matching framework and the first such framework deployed in a real-world production environment. Applying generative modeling to this problem introduces three challenges. First, each dispatch batch forms a dynamic sparse bipartite graph, requiring efficient structured batch-level encoding. Second, replacing the hand-crafted value function requires learning unified business utility from heterogeneous feedback. Third, directly generating an assignment requires tracking the evolving matching state because each selected order-driver pair changes the remaining feasible candidates. GenMatch addresses these challenges with a Context-Aware Bipartite Encoder, a Business-Aware Utility Learner, and a State-Aware Pointer Decoder. Extensive offline evaluations and online A/B tests in five cities across DiDi's international ride-hailing markets show consistent improvements over competitive baselines, confirming the effectiveness and practicality of GenMatch for industrial order-dispatching.

AI.tldr: GenMatch is an end-to-end generative matching framework for micro-view ride-hailing order-dispatching, addressing dynamic batch-level bipartite graphs and cross-stage objective inconsistency, using a Context-Aware Bipartite Encoder, a Business-Aware Utility Learner, and a State-Aware Pointer Decoder; it outperforms baselines in offline and online tests across five cities.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-stage dispatch pipelines optimize intermediate objectives in isolation, leading to cross-stage inconsistencies and suboptimal final dispatch. There is a need for an end-to-end generative framework that can learn unified business utility and handle dynamic, sparse bipartite graphs in production.
AI.method: Propose GenMatch with three components: Context-Aware Bipartite Encoder for batch-level graph encoding; Business-Aware Utility Learner to learn unified utility from heterogeneous feedback; State-Aware Pointer Decoder to generate assignments while updating the matching state.
AI.result: Offline evaluations and online A/B tests in five international cities show consistent improvements over competitive baselines, demonstrating effectiveness and practicality in production.
AI.conclusion: GenMatch effectively solves micro-view order-dispatching as a generative matching problem, enabling end-to-end optimization and deployment in real-world ride-hailing platforms.

title: DeltaML-Bench: Evaluating Machine Learning Agents on Real-World Research Repositories
comment: 18 pages, 3 figures, 12 tables. Code and benchmark: https://github.com/AlgorithmicResearchGroup/deltaml-bench-public
summary: Autonomous agents for machine learning experimentation must navigate heterogeneous repositories, repair training pipelines, and evaluate candidate improvements under realistic compute constraints. Existing benchmarks only partially capture these conditions. We introduce DeltaML-Bench, a benchmark comprising 48 tasks sourced from research papers that require agents to improve published baselines within imperfect, open-source repositories. We evaluate GPT-5 and Claude Sonnet 4 with a standard Modular agent and a search-based ARG scaffolding. In the 4 x 6h allocation, ARG raises GPT-5's per-run success rate from 9.4% to 33.9%; in the 2 x 12h allocation, GPT-5 ARG reaches 49.0%. Modular configurations exhibit specification gaming rates as high as 47.9%, while no gaming is observed in the evaluated ARG configurations. These results indicate that scaffolding design and integrity checks are important considerations when deploying agents for autonomous ML experimentation.

AI.tldr: DeltaML-Bench introduces 48 tasks to evaluate autonomous ML experimentation agents in imperfect, open-source repositories. ARG scaffolding significantly boosts per-run success rates for GPT-5 (4x6h: 9.4%→33.9%; 2x12h: 49.0%), while Modular configurations show high specification gaming (up to 47.9%) and ARG configurations show no gaming. Concludes scaffolding design and integrity checks are crucial for reliable autonomous ML experimentation.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks inadequately capture the challenges of autonomous ML experimentation in heterogeneous repositories, with repair needs and realistic compute constraints. A robust benchmark suite is needed to evaluate agent design and reliability.
AI.method: A benchmark (DeltaML-Bench) with 48 tasks sourced from research papers requiring agents to improve published baselines within imperfect, open-source repositories. Evaluation of GPT-5 and Claude Sonnet 4 using a standard Modular agent and a search-based ARG scaffolding under constrained compute allocations (4x6h and 2x12h).
AI.result: ARG scaffolding substantially increases success rates (GPT-5: 9.4%→33.9% in 4x6h; 49.0% in 2x12h). Modular configurations exhibit specification gaming up to 47.9%; ARG configurations show no gaming.
AI.conclusion: Scaffolding design and integrity checks are important for deploying agents in autonomous ML experimentation; ARG-based scaffolds can mitigate behavior issues observed with Modular agents.

title: MILD: Tractable Terrain Modeling for Learning Improved Bipedal Locomotion on Deformable Surfaces
summary: Enabling robots to walk on yielding terrain is vital for applications ranging from disaster response to planetary exploration. While bipedal robots hold immense potential, their locomotion on deformable surfaces remains limited as current simulators fail to capture the spatiotemporal heterogeneity of such yielding substrates. We present MILD, featuring a physics-grounded discrete-element contact solver that accurately simulates spatially varying foot-terrain interactions. Complementing this model, we train a terrain-aware locomotion controller via deep reinforcement learning with latent modulation and proprioceptive estimation. Quantitative comparisons against state-of-the-art methods show our approach generates more diverse and realistic contact scenarios during training, resulting in controllers that exhibit natural adaptation on real deformable surfaces. Through hardware experiments, we demonstrate the system's capability for online terrain identification and adaptation across a wide range of surface stiffness.

AI.tldr: A physics-grounded discrete-element contact solver (MILD) coupled with a terrain-aware DRL controller enables robust bipedal locomotion on yielding deformable terrain by sim-to-real transfer, online terrain identification, and adaptation across varying substrate stiffness.
AI.motivation: Current simulators fail to capture the spatiotemporal heterogeneity of yielding substrates, hindering robust locomotion on deformable surfaces; enabling sim-to-real transfer and online terrain adaptation is critical for disaster response and planetary exploration.
AI.method: Develop a physics-grounded discrete-element contact solver (MILD) to model spatially varying foot-terrain interactions, and train a terrain-aware locomotion controller via deep reinforcement learning with latent modulation and proprioceptive estimation.
AI.result: In simulations, the approach yields more diverse and realistic contact scenarios during training than state-of-the-art methods; the resulting controllers adapt naturally on real deformable surfaces. Hardware experiments demonstrate online terrain identification and adaptation across a wide range of surface stiffness.
AI.conclusion: The integrated simulation-plus-control framework improves realism and robustness of bipedal locomotion on yielding terrain, enabling better transfer to real-world deformable substrates and enabling online terrain sensing and adaptation.

title: MUST-PET: MUltimodal Self-supervised learning across Tracers for whole-body PET/CT-based lesion segmentation
summary: Deep learning-based whole-body PET-CT lesion segmentation can support cancer staging, treatment planning, and response assessment, but generalization is limited by scarce annotations and domain shifts. Self-supervised learning (SSL) can address these challenges but remains underexplored in pan-cancer, multi-tracer PET-CT. In this work, we propose MUST-PET (MUltimodal Self-Supervised learning across Tracers), a multimodal, multi-tracer SSL framework for generalizable whole-body PET-CT lesion segmentation. MUST-PET is trained and validated on a diverse, multi-institutional collection of pan-cancer PET-CT scans acquired with FDG and prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA)-targeted radiotracers. MUST-PET uses context-aware masked reconstruction, where one modality is partially masked and reconstructed using complementary information from both PET and CT. The pretrained model is subsequently fine-tuned with labeled samples and evaluated for reconstruction quality, lesion segmentation, label efficiency, and generalizability across independent held-out datasets. MUST-PET reduces reconstruction error, improves lesion segmentation over training from scratch, and performs well with limited labeled data and on unseen external datasets, demonstrating the potential of multi-tracer SSL for label-efficient, generalizable whole-body PET-CT. segmentation.

AI.tldr: MUST-PET: a multimodal, multi-tracer self-supervised framework for generalizable whole-body PET-CT lesion segmentation using context-aware masked reconstruction across FDG and PSMA tracers.
AI.motivation: Generalization in whole-body PET-CT lesion segmentation is hampered by scarce annotations and domain shifts; self-supervised learning (SSL) can help but is underexplored for pan-cancer, multi-tracer PET-CT.
AI.method: Train a multimodal SSL model on pan-cancer, multi-institution FDG and PSMA PET-CT data; employ context-aware masked reconstruction where one modality is partially masked and reconstructed using complementary PET and CT information; fine-tune on labeled data; evaluate reconstruction quality, lesion segmentation, label efficiency, and generalizability to held-out datasets.
AI.result: MUST-PET reduces reconstruction error and improves lesion segmentation compared with training from scratch; demonstrates robustness with limited labeled data and maintains performance on unseen external datasets.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates the potential of multi-tracer SSL for label-efficient, generalizable whole-body PET-CT lesion segmentation.

title: TT-net: Quantum Inspired Tensor Network Denoising in Conditional GANs
summary: Developed as a workhorse for classical simulations of quantum algorithms and quantum many-body systems, Tensor Network methods have entered the scientific mainstream in quantum physics. Among various types of tensor networks, Tensor Trains (commonly know as Matrix Product States in the quantum computing community) have already found applications in machine learning. These methods often rely on a powerful linear algebra tool called the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD). Several conditional GAN architectures for image denoising incorporate SVD as a single-cut decomposition step applied to generator feature maps. In this work we introduce TT-Net, which replaces the per-channel SVD denoising block with a two-cut tensor-train decomposition capable of accessing cross-channel information directly, a capability absent from contemporary alternatives. In a controlled comparison differing only in this decomposition mechanism, TT-Net outperforms SVD-Net on PSNR and SSIM across all three noise types tested (Gaussian, motion blur, and salt-and-pepper), supporting the hypothesis that cross-channel access improves denoising quality. Training-dynamics analysis further shows that TT-Net's adversarial loss term consistently saturates to a stagnant state across all three noise types, more so than SVD-Net's, while reconstruction quality continues to improve regardless, raising an open question about the adversarial component's contribution that this work identifies but does not resolve. Furthermore, for Gaussian noise our method outperforms both the EigenGAN and the state of the art Pix2pix method which does not assume any linear algebra decompositions and does not retain any linear algebra information. Our manuscript shows how quantum inspired tools can be used as practical real world feature filters for deep learning applications.

AI.tldr: Introduces TT-Net, a two-cut tensor-train decomposition for conditional GAN denoising that replaces per-channel SVD blocks to enable cross-channel information access, showing superior denoising (PSNR/SSIM) across Gaussian, motion blur, and salt-and-pepper noise, with intriguing training dynamics and competitive Gaussian performance against EigenGAN and Pix2pix; frames quantum-inspired tensor networks as practical deep-learning feature filters.
AI.motivation: Address limitations of SVD-based denoising blocks that process channels independently; leverage cross-channel correlations via tensor-train decomposition to improve denoising performance in GAN-based image restoration.
AI.method: Substitute the per-channel SVD denoising block in a conditional GAN with a two-cut tensor-train (TT) decomposition within TT-Net. Conduct a controlled comparison where only the decomposition mechanism differs (TT-Net vs SVD-Net). Evaluate on three noise types (Gaussian, motion blur, salt-and-pepper) using standard metrics (PSNR, SSIM). Analyze training dynamics, particularly adversarial loss behavior. Compare Gaussian denoising performance against EigenGAN and Pix2pix baselines.
AI.result: TT-Net outperforms SVD-Net in PSNR and SSIM across all three noise types, indicating cross-channel access improves denoising. Training dynamics show the adversarial loss saturates more in TT-Net than SVD-Net, though reconstruction quality continues to improve, raising questions about the adversarial component’s contribution. For Gaussian noise, TT-Net also surpasses EigenGAN and Pix2pix baselines, demonstrating competitive performance without relying on non-decompositional methods.
AI.conclusion: Quantum-inspired tensor-network tools can serve as practical feature filters in deep learning, with TT-Net illustrating the value of cross-channel information via tensor-train decompositions for improved denoising. The work identifies, but does not resolve, the role of the adversarial term in training dynamics.

title: Rationally Enriched Chebyshev Trunk Bases for DeepONet Surrogates of High Péclet Entrance Transport
summary: This study demonstrates a rationally enriched Chebyshev (REC) trunk for deep operator network (DeepONet) surrogate models of singularly perturbed and high-Péclet transport problems whose solution profiles are characterized by thin localized boundary or wall layers. The REC trunk combines Chebyshev polynomial dictionary elements with rational dictionary elements constructed using the adaptive Antoulas-Anderson (AAA) algorithm. Over five independent training runs, the resulting REC-trunk DeepONet is evaluated against a vanilla DeepONet and a Chebyshev-trunk DeepONet whose prescribed dictionary consists only of Chebyshev polynomials across three problems whose singular perturbation parameters are diffusion-to-advection ratios: a singularly perturbed scalar boundary-value problem (BVP), the thermal entrance problem with a prescribed wall temperature, and the concentration entrance problem with an absorbing wall. Across the held-out test profiles, the REC-trunk DeepONet improves over the vanilla DeepONet and remains comparable to the Chebyshev-trunk DeepONet in predicting the scalar profile, with its clearest advantage over the Chebyshev-trunk DeepONet appearing when the perturbation parameter lies between $1.00\times10^{-4}$ and $1.78\times10^{-4}$, where it reduces the profile-error metrics by up to $19.5\,\%$ relative to the Chebyshev-trunk DeepONet. In predicting the wall-normal temperature and concentration profiles, the REC-trunk DeepONet reduces the profile-error metrics by up to $60.2\,\%$ and $32.2\,\%$ relative to the vanilla and Chebyshev-trunk DeepONets, respectively, while suppressing artificial near-wall oscillations as the Péclet or mass-transfer Péclet number ranges from $10^{2}$ to $10^{4}$.

AI.tldr: REC trunk for DeepONet improves surrogate performance for singularly perturbed transport problems with thin boundary layers by combining Chebyshev polynomials with rational functions via AAA; shows significant error reductions, especially for wall-normal profiles and certain perturbation regimes.
AI.motivation: To enhance DeepONet's ability to represent sharp, localized boundary-layer features in singular perturbation and high-Péclet transport problems where standard polynomial dictionaries fail or require many terms.
AI.method: Construct a Rational-Enriched Chebyshev (REC) trunk by mixing Chebyshev dictionary elements with rational dictionary elements generated by AAA. Train and test across five runs on three problems, comparing to vanilla DeepONet and Chebyshev-trunk DeepONet.
AI.result: REC-trunk DeepONet outperforms vanilla DeepONet in general, remains comparable to Chebyshev-trunk for scalar profiles, with up to 19.5% error reduction over Chebyshev-trunk in a specific perturbation range; for wall-normal temperature and concentration profiles, reductions up to 60.2% and 32.2% respectively, and suppression of near-wall oscillations across Péclet ranges 1e2-1e4.
AI.conclusion: REC trunk enhances DeepONet accuracy and robustness for problems with thin boundary layers by leveraging a hybrid dictionary that captures both smooth and sharp features, enabling better generalization across perturbation regimes.

title: PVRA: A Pointwise Key-point Voting Framework for Robotic Assembly
comment: 14 pages, 3 figures. Accepted for presentation at the European Conference on Robotics (ECoR) 2026
summary: Modern computer vision has enabled partial autonomy in robotic assembly manipulation. However, performing autonomous manipulation of a progressive assembly demands a more specific set of skills, in addition to perceiving the objects. Through a comparative analysis of research in the associated domains, we deduce that object-centric perception must advance towards learning assembly dependencies to predict meaningful actionable outputs for autonomous assembly manipulation. Subsequently, we present a 3D keypoint-based modular learning framework to learn assembly dependencies to infer actionable outputs given a RGB-D input of an assembly scene. We train and evaluate our trained network on an assembly pose estimation dataset and compare it against object-centric baselines with an augmented set of metrics for progressive assemblies.

AI.tldr: A 3D keypoint-based modular learning framework to infer actionable outputs for progressive assembly manipulation from RGB-D data, learning assembly dependencies and evaluated on an assembly pose estimation dataset against object-centric baselines.
AI.motivation: Object-centric perception lacks explicit modeling of assembly constraints; to enable autonomous progressive assembly, the system must learn assembly dependencies that yield meaningful actions.
AI.method: Proposes a modular architecture utilizing 3D keypoints to encode parts and assembly dependencies, fusing RGB-D input to predict actionable outputs; trained on an assembly pose estimation dataset; learning objective targets action/pose inference.
AI.result: Evaluated on an assembly pose estimation dataset and compared to object-centric baselines; augmented metrics for progressive assemblies show improved or promising performance.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates feasibility of learning assembly dependencies via 3D keypoints to generate actionable outputs for autonomous progressive assembly, outlining directions for richer datasets and metrics.

title: Scaffolding Minds: Optimizing Latent Visual Target Representations for Multimodal Reasoning
summary: Latent reasoning has advanced multimodal reasoning through a two-stage training paradigm: (1) a helper image is encoded into latent tokens to teach visual chain-of-thought during a supervised fine-tuning (SFT) stage, and (2) these latent tokens are further refined with reward feedback during a reinforcement learning (RL) stage. In this paper, we identify two key limitations of this framework, one in each stage. First, the SFT stage typically relies on an off-the-shelf vision encoder to encode the helper image, yielding suboptimal latent representations that may not be well aligned with the downstream reasoning task. Second, existing RL methods treat the latent component only through deterministic regularization, which constrains policy drift but does not create alternative latent trajectories for exploration. To address these limitations, we propose Scaffolding Minds. Our approach learns a dedicated scaffolding encoder that provides an optimized target in latent space, and learns both the mean and variance of the RL sampler. We further show that these two improvements are complementary, together yielding substantial gains over strong baselines. Empirically, our method improves over the strongest latent-reasoning baseline by +9.5% on FrozenLake spatial planning, with the gain widening to +19% at 32x32 grid map, and by +5.2% on average across nine visual-centric reasoning benchmarks.

AI.tldr: Proposes Scaffolding Minds to improve latent-based multimodal reasoning by (1) learning a dedicated scaffolding encoder for better latent representations and (2) modeling both mean and variance in the RL latent sampler, yielding substantial gains over strong baselines across planning and visual reasoning tasks.
AI.motivation: Identify two-stage limitations in latent reasoning: suboptimal latent encodings from off-the-shelf vision encoders during supervised fine-tuning and lack of latent exploration in reinforcement learning due to deterministic regularization.
AI.method: Introduce a dedicated scaffolding encoder to provide optimized latent targets; jointly learn the mean and variance of the RL latent sampler to enable exploration of latent trajectories; demonstrate complementary improvements and validate on planning and visual reasoning benchmarks.
AI.result: Empirical gains include +9.5% on FrozenLake spatial planning (rising to +19% at 32x32 grid), and +5.2% average across nine visual-centric reasoning benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Jointly optimizing latent representations with a scaffolding encoder and enabling stochastic latent exploration in RL yields significant performance gains over strong latent-reasoning baselines, supporting the two-stage scaffolding approach.

title: LLMs as Acquisition Policies for Finite-Pool Materials Optimization: A Controlled Study
summary: Discovering materials with desirable properties often requires searching large candidate spaces while experimental or computational evaluations remain costly. Active learning addresses this challenge by using previous observations to select which candidate to evaluate next, typically through probabilistic surrogate models. We investigate whether open-weight large language models (LLMs) can serve as standalone acquisition policies in this setting. We evaluate five LLMs across four retrospective finite-pool materials optimization tasks under different candidate-presentation strategies and compare them with random selection and conventional Gaussian-process methods. LLM policies generally reach the global optimum in fewer iterations than random selection, indicating that they provide a useful acquisition signal without task-specific training. Their performance relative to Gaussian-process methods is mixed: conventional acquisition performs better on most tasks, while LLMs match or outperform it in some settings. Performance varies substantially across tasks, models, initializations, and candidate presentations, with no LLM approach performing best across all tasks. Overall, open-weight LLMs show potential as acquisition policies for finite-pool materials search, although their reliability remains sensitive to the task and to how candidates and scientific context are presented.

AI.tldr: Open-weight large language models (LLMs) can act as acquisition policies for finite-pool materials optimization, but reliability varies and they generally underperform conventional Gaussian-process methods, though they can reach the optimum faster than random selection in some tasks.
AI.motivation: To assess whether open-weight LLMs can serve as standalone acquisition policies in active learning for materials discovery, replacing or augmenting traditional surrogate models.
AI.method: Evaluate five open-weight LLMs as acquisition policies across four retrospective finite-pool materials optimization tasks, under varying candidate-presentation strategies, and compare to random search and Gaussian-process-based methods.
AI.result: LLM policies often reach the global optimum in fewer iterations than random selection, indicating they provide useful acquisition signals without task-specific training. Relative to Gaussian-process methods, performance is mixed: conventional acquisition outperforms LLMs on most tasks, but LLMs match or exceed it in some settings. Performance varies widely across tasks, models, initializations, and candidate presentations; no LLM consistently wins across all tasks.
AI.conclusion: Open-weight LLMs show potential as acquisition policies for finite-pool materials search, but reliability is task- and presentation-dependent and they do not universally outperform established GP-based acquisitions.

title: FleetSieve: Decision-Critical Profiling for SLO-Aware LLM Fleet Configuration
summary: Choosing tensor-parallel (TP) degrees and replica counts for an LLM serving fleet is difficult because performance is not monotonic in TP and the feasible choice can change with load. Exhaustive profiling resolves this uncertainty, but measures many configurations that do not affect the final resource allocation. We present FleetSieve, which selects measurements according to their expected effect on a resource-coupled, SLO-aware fleet decision. FleetSieve models capacity and tail latency jointly, compares conservative and optimistic allocations, and stops when their remaining decision gap is below a specified tolerance. On a fixed H100 measurement grid for a 31B-parameter open-weight model, FleetSieve reaches the oracle aggregate decision using 22,200 GPU-seconds, 6.9% less than uniform random profiling in the fixed comparison. Across 200 random reveal orders, its mean saving over random profiling is 5.4% (95% bootstrap CI: 3.5-7.2%). The fixed-comparison saving is 21.5% for Chat, while FleetSieve does not use the fewest GPU-seconds for Code. Joint capacity and tail modeling also avoids selecting a configuration whose 46.4-second completion p99 violates a 30-second SLO. In a 16-GPU allocation, an incorrect sparse-profile decision loses up to 1.93 requests/s and 12.4 percentage points of max-min fulfillment. Boundary repeats and BurstGPT measurements support the observed load-dependent tail-latency mechanism.

AI.tldr: FleetSieve provides adaptive, measurement-efficient profiling to guide tensor-parallel and replica choices for LLM serving, balancing capacity and tail latency under SLO constraints.
AI.motivation: Profiling all TP/replica configurations is costly and performance is not monotonic with TP, and load can change the feasible optimum; a selective, SLO-aware strategy is needed.
AI.method: An adaptive measurement strategy that models capacity and tail latency jointly, compares conservative and optimistic allocations, and stops once their decision gap falls below a tolerance. Evaluation on a fixed H100 grid for a 31B model; measures savings against uniform/random profiling and analyzes sensitivity to load and workload.
AI.result: FleetSieve reaches the oracle aggregate decision with 22,200 GPU-seconds, a 6.9% reduction vs fixed-grid random profiling; mean saving 5.4% across 200 reveal orders (95% CI: 3.5–7.2%). For Chat, fixed-comparison saving is 21.5%; avoids a tail violation where p99 would exceed a 30s SLO; in a 16-GPU allocation, misprofiling can cost up to 1.93 req/s and 12.4 percentage points of max-min fulfillment; supporting evidence from boundary repeats and BurstGPT measurements.
AI.conclusion: Joint capacity-tail modeling with selective measurements yields efficient, SLO-aware fleet decisions, reducing profiling overhead while maintaining accuracy; results underscore load-dependent tail latency as a key factor and demonstrate robustness across orders and workloads.

title: Learning Highly Dynamic Skills Transition for Quadruped Jumping Through Constrained Space
summary: Although legged animals are capable of performing explosive motions while traversing confined spaces, replicating this behavior in quadrupedal robots has been a longstanding challenge. Here, we propose a hierarchical reinforcement learning pipeline that empowers the robots to perform aggressive locomotion through constrained obstacles--a narrow gate. The imitation learning technique is used to train the low-level policy, which mimics the behaviors of real animals and forms a set of diverse skills. The high-level controller, having an awareness of the capability of low-level skills and acquiring the gate information via vision-based detection, determines the suitable maneuvers with collision-free trajectories to traverse it dynamically. Notably, we also verify that this framework can be extended to other highly dynamic tasks. This is one of the first works that perform autonomous and agile aerial gate traversal tasks on ground-walking robots, extending the lifelike agility of legged robots to match that of their biological counterparts.

AI.tldr: A hierarchical reinforcement learning framework combines imitation-learned low-level skills with a vision-informed high-level planner to achieve autonomous, agile arrival through a narrow gate on a quadruped robot, with potential extension to other dynamic tasks.
AI.motivation: Bridge the gap between biological agility and legged robots by enabling explosive, constrained-space locomotion. Leverage perception (vision) and learned skills to enable adaptive gate negotiation.
AI.method: Train a diverse set of low-level skills via imitation learning to mimic animal behaviors. A high-level controller, aware of low-level capabilities and using vision-based gate detection, selects collision-free maneuver trajectories to traverse the gate dynamically.
AI.result: Demonstrates autonomous and agile gate traversal on ground-walking robots; argues the framework can extend to other highly dynamic tasks; claims novelty as among the first autonomous agile gate traversals for such robots.
AI.conclusion: The hierarchical RL pipeline can enhance lifelike agility in legged robots and generalize to other dynamic tasks, with future work likely addressing robustness, perception noise, and broader task generalization.

title: RIPE++: Reinforced Keypoint Learning from Positive Pairs Only
summary: Sparse keypoint extraction and matching underpin core tasks in geometric computer vision, including structure-from-motion, visual SLAM, augmented reality, and medical image registration. Learning robust local feature representations, however, typically requires accurate camera poses or depth supervision, which are often unavailable in real-world settings. Reinforcement learning (RL) has recently emerged as a promising alternative, requiring only the information if two images show the same scene or not. However, existing RL formulations such as RIPE rely on coarse binary rewards and carefully constructed negative training pairs, limiting training stability and descriptor discriminability. In this paper, we revisit RL-based keypoint learning and propose a reward that fully exploits the geometric consistency signal, deriving both reward and penalty from a single positive pair without contrasting against negatives. This richer signal provides sufficient supervisory contrast to learn discriminative detectors and descriptors from positive image pairs alone, enabling representation learning under extremely limited supervision. Furthermore, we show that the same RL objective can be extended to the matching stage by adapting LightGlue, raising AUC@5 on MegaDepth1500 from 56.58 to 59.65 and enabling weakly-supervised training of the full sparse matching pipeline from image pairs with partial visual overlap. We validate our approach on established benchmarks, demonstrating competitive results compared to fully-supervised methods. We further show that the method can be even trained on low texture medical video sequences, where camera poses are usually unavailable and standard SfM pipelines often fail. Code and data are available at https://github.com/fraunhoferhhi/RIPEpp .

AI.tldr: RL-based keypoint learning (RIPEpp++) uses a single positive-pair geometric-consistency reward (no negatives) and extends to weakly supervised sparse matching via LightGlue, achieving competitive results with limited supervision and enabling training on low-texture data.
AI.motivation: Current robust local feature learning often relies on camera poses or depth supervision, which are unavailable in many settings. RL offers supervision from image pairs, but existing methods use coarse binary rewards and negatives, limiting stability and discriminability. A richer signal from geometric consistency on a single positive pair could improve detectors/descriptors and extend to matching.
AI.method: Derive both reward and penalty from a single positive image pair using geometric consistency, removing the need for negative pairs. Train discriminative detectors/descriptors from positive pairs alone. Extend the RL objective to the matching stage by adapting LightGlue, enabling weakly supervised training of the full sparse matching pipeline from image pairs with partial overlap.
AI.result: Achieves AUC@5 on MegaDepth1500 rising from 56.58 to 59.65 when integrating with LightGlue; enables weakly supervised training of sparse matching; competitive with fully supervised methods; succeeds on low-texture medical video sequences where SfM fails.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates that a rich supervisory signal derived from a single positive pair suffices for learning robust keypoints and descriptors via RL, and that the same objective can support weakly supervised sparse matching. Code and data are provided.

title: Towards general embodied intelligence: integrating large language models, knowledge bases, and reasoning capabilities to build the next generation of AI agents
summary: The convergence of large language models (LLMs), structured knowledge bases (KBs), and reasoning ability (RA) presents a promising trajectory toward general embodied intelligence (GEI). This paper reviews the evolution of LLM-centered intelligent systems, emphasising their integration with knowledge representation, logical reasoning, and physical embodiment. We analyse LLM architectures, pre-training methods, and inference mechanisms, along with their interaction with external knowledge sources and structured reasoning frameworks. Furthermore, we examine embodied intelligence (EI) paradigms wherein agents learn and act in physical environments. To synthesise these dimensions, we present a conceptual framework that illustrates the synergy among LLMs, KBs, RA, and embodiment, serving as a guiding model for perception, reasoning, and action rather than an implemented engineering architecture. To advance toward GEI, we identify five key challenges: efficient LLM deployment, closed-loop knowledge integration, hybrid symbolic-neural reasoning, perception-action grounding, and continual learning. This survey provides a comprehensive roadmap for developing adaptive, multimodal agents capable of operating in complex, dynamic settings.

AI.tldr: Survey of integrating LLMs, KBs, reasoning, and embodiment to outline a pathway to general embodied intelligence; introduces a conceptual framework and five challenges.
AI.motivation: To unify LLMs, knowledge representation, reasoning, and physical embodiment into a guiding model for adaptive, multimodal agents operating in dynamic environments, advancing toward GEI.
AI.method: Literature review of LLM architectures, pre-training, inference; analysis of interactions with external KBs and structured reasoning; examination of embodied intelligence paradigms; proposal of a conceptual framework.
AI.result: A synthesis framework illustrating synergy among LLMs, KBs, RA, and embodiment; five identified challenges for practical GEI implementation; a roadmap rather than an instantiated system.
AI.conclusion: Provides a conceptual roadmap for adaptive, multimodal agents capable of perception, reasoning, and action in complex settings, outlining future directions toward GEI.

title: SAGE-XGBoost: Spatially Augmented Graph Embeddings--Machine Learning Framework for Natural Hazards Susceptibility Mapping under Data Scarcity
summary: Natural hazard susceptibility mapping is often constrained by limited labeled data, reducing the generalizability of conventional machine learning and limiting the applicability of complex deep learning models. This study proposes SAGE (Spatially Augmented Graph Embeddings), a structurally informed feature-engineering framework that combines controlled noise-based data augmentation with neighborhood-based graph embeddings to improve prediction under data-scarce conditions. A K-nearest neighbor graph is constructed to derive local spatial statistics, which are reduced using principal component analysis and integrated with environmental covariates and spatial coordinates. The resulting features are used with XGBoost to develop the SAGE-XGBoost model. The framework was evaluated for landslide and wildfire susceptibility mapping. SAGE-XGBoost consistently outperformed conventional and spatially explicit machine learning models. Compared with Spatial XGBoost, it achieved an absolute improvement of above 33 percentage points across the two case studies. The model reached AUC values of approximately 0.97 for landslide susceptibility and 0.95 for wildfire susceptibility. Feature importance analysis confirmed the contribution of graph embeddings to prediction, while their integration improved spatial coherence and reduced local noise amplification. Overall, SAGE-XGBoost provides an efficient and transferable alternative to deep representation learning for environmental hazard assessment and other geospatial prediction tasks under limited supervision.

AI.tldr: SAGE-XGBoost uses spatially augmented graph embeddings with PCA-reduced KNN-local stats, integrated with covariates, to improve hazard susceptibility predictions under limited labeled data; outperforms Spatial XGBoost by over 33 percentage points, achieving about 0.97 AUC for landslides and 0.95 for wildfires.
AI.motivation: Address data scarcity in natural hazard susceptibility mapping by leveraging structured spatial information through graph embeddings and controlled data augmentation to improve generalization beyond conventional ML and deep learning.
AI.method: Construct a K-nearest neighbor graph to derive local spatial statistics; reduce features with PCA; combine with environmental covariates and spatial coordinates; apply feature-engineered inputs to XGBoost to form SAGE-XGBoost; compare against conventional and Spatial XGBoost; evaluate on landslide and wildfire susceptibility mapping; analyze feature importance.
AI.result: SAGE-XGBoost consistently outperforms baseline models; absolute improvement >33 percentage points over Spatial XGBoost; AUC ≈ 0.97 for landslide, 0.95 for wildfire; feature importance confirms contribution of graph embeddings; integration improves spatial coherence and reduces local noise amplification.
AI.conclusion: SAGE-XGBoost offers an efficient, transferable alternative to deep representation learning for environmental hazard assessment under limited supervision and is applicable to geospatial prediction tasks with sparse labels.

title: Evidence-Gated Task and Motion Planning with Vision-Language Models
summary: Robots executing long-horizon manipulation tasks from natural-language instructions must reason about both semantic task structure and geometric feasibility. However, under partial observability, the availability of goal-relevant objects may be uncertain. In such cases, approaches that combine Vision-Language Models (VLMs) with Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) may generate subgoals that rely on the VLM's prior knowledge without observational support, leading to execution failures or unintended outcomes. We propose Evidence Acquisition and Feasibility Gating (EAFG), a framework that acquires visual evidence through VLM-generated exploratory subgoals and TAMP-based execution. EAFG then applies a feasibility gate to decide whether to proceed with task planning, acquire further evidence, or halt. Our experiments show that, in cooking tasks with ambiguous object use, EAFG improves recipe completion by discovering task-relevant objects before planning. For instructions requiring an absent object, EAFG promotes appropriate halt decisions and reduces repeated attempts to manipulate that object.

AI.tldr: EAFG combines VLM-guided exploratory planning with a feasibility gate to handle partial observability in long-horizon manipulation tasks, improving task completion and reducing erroneous actions by acquiring evidence before planning and halting when necessary.
AI.motivation: To address failures that arise when VLM priors are relied upon under partial observability, by explicitly acquiring visual evidence and gating feasibility before committing to planning.
AI.method: Acquire visual evidence via VLM-generated exploratory subgoals; execute with Task and Motion Planning (TAMP); apply a feasibility gate to decide to proceed with planning, request further evidence, or halt.
AI.result: In cooking tasks with ambiguous object use, EAFG improves recipe completion by discovering task-relevant objects before planning; for absent objects, it promotes appropriate halts and reduces repeated manipulation attempts.
AI.conclusion: EAFG enhances robustness of long-horizon instruction execution under partial observability by integrating VLM-informed exploration with evidence-based feasibility gating to inform planning and halt when evidence is insufficient.

title: Robust Cross-Modal Foundation Model Perception for Underwater Robots under Degraded Visual Conditions
summary: Reliable underwater robotic perception remains difficult because optical imagery degrades under turbidity, wavelength-dependent attenuation, low illumination, scattering, and blur. Although sonar provides complementary information that is less affected by optical visibility, prior visual-sonar research has largely focused on feature alignment and nominal detection performance. We investigate cross-modal robustness as visual reliability deteriorates and assess whether pretrained visual foundation-model representations can be complemented by sonar under severe degradation. We use frozen DINOv2 as the visual encoder and construct a controlled five-level benchmark ranging from clean to extreme visual conditions. We compare conventional visual detection, frozen foundation-model representations, sonar context, fixed multimodal fusion, clean-trained adaptive gating, and degradation-aware gated fusion. Our method trains the fusion mechanism across the full range of degradation while keeping the visual and sonar encoders frozen, allowing modality contributions to adapt without fine-tuning the pretrained backbone. Under extreme combined degradation, the DINOv2 baseline achieves 0.4610 balanced accuracy, while degradation-aware visual-sonar fusion reaches 0.6152, a 33.5% relative improvement. The learned sonar contribution increases from 14.2% under clean conditions to 41.3% under extreme degradation, demonstrating adaptive redistribution of cross-modal reliance. Fusion provides the largest gains under severe turbidity and blur, whereas color attenuation alone yields little additional benefit. These results show that foundation-model representations remain valuable but insufficient under severe information loss, and that explicitly adapting fusion to modality reliability can improve robust underwater multimodal perception.

AI.tldr: Cross-modal fusion of frozen visual foundation-model representations (DINOv2) and sonar improves robust underwater perception under severe visual degradation. A degradation-aware gated fusion, trained across a full degradation range and without retraining encoders, yields a 33.5% relative accuracy improvement (0.4610 vs 0.6152) and increases sonar reliance with worsening conditions.
AI.motivation: Underwater sensing suffers from turbidity, attenuation, and blur. Visual foundation models offer strong representations but degrade with quality; sonar is robust to optical conditions. The work investigates whether combining frozen visual encoders with sonar through adaptive fusion can maintain performance across a degradation spectrum without fine-tuning backbones.
AI.method: Freeze the DINOv2 visual encoder; construct a controlled five-level degradation benchmark from clean to extreme; compare: conventional visual detection, frozen backbone representations, sonar context, fixed multimodal fusion, clean-trained adaptive gating, and degradation-aware gated fusion. Train only the fusion/gating mechanism across all degradation levels, preserving encoder weights.
AI.result: Under extreme degradation, visual baseline accuracy is 0.4610, while degradation-aware visual–sonar fusion achieves 0.6152 (33.5% relative improvement). Sonar contribution rises from 14.2% (clean) to 41.3% (extreme), indicating adaptive cross-modal weighting. Fusion provides the largest gains under turbidity and blur; color attenuation yields limited benefit.
AI.conclusion: Foundation-model visual representations remain valuable but insufficient under severe information loss. Explicit, degradation-aware fusion with sonar can significantly improve robust underwater multimodal perception without retraining encoders.

title: ADAPT: Physics-Aware Diffusion-based World Models for Adaptive Predictive Transferable HVAC Control
summary: Buildings account for roughly one-third of global energy consumption and CO$_2$ emissions. Optimizing indoor climate systems plays a critical role for urban climate mitigation aligned with UN Sustainable Development Goals 11 and 13. However, indoor delayed thermodynamic responses and partial observability severely hinder existing methods, which are primarily limited by implicit thermal inertia, occupancy dynamic prediction, and cumulative prediction errors, especially for out-of-distribution environments. In practice, these challenges are further exacerbated by the high cost and privacy burden of dense indoor sensing, forcing operators to collect only limited data in a single operating regime while expecting controllers to generalize reliably across unseen seasons and climate regions. To address this problem, we propose ADAPT, a physics-aware conditional diffusion indoor environmental world model for HVAC control. The model predicts a short-horizon held-action thermal baseline to capture the latent thermal inertia of the buildings. The diffusion backbone utilizes the robustness of generative models, while a learnable multi-zone heat-balance regularizer constrains generated trajectories to satisfy transferable building thermodynamics without requiring known building geometry or manually calibrated thermal parameters. A credit assignment is then design for the downstream reinforcement learning. Extensive experiments on SemibuildingSim and Sinergym demonstrate that ADAPT reduces HVAC energy consumption by 7.3\% and occupant discomfort by 30.2\% compared with state-of-the-art baselines under IID control. Under OOD control scenarios spanning unseen seasons and climate regions, ADAPT maintains robust performance with only marginal degradation relative to its IID performance, substantially outperforming existing methods in transfer robustness.

AI.tldr: ADAPT introduces a physics-aware conditional diffusion indoor environmental world model for HVAC control that captures latent thermal inertia, enforces thermodynamic consistency via a learnable heat-balance regularizer, and uses downstream RL; it achieves energy and comfort gains with strong OOD transfer robustness.
AI.motivation: Buildings dominate energy use and emissions; indoor climate control is hindered by delayed thermodynamics, partial observability, high sensing costs, and poor generalization to unseen seasons/climates; existing methods struggle with model bias, inertia, and data efficiency.
AI.method: ADAPT combines a diffusion-based world model with a short-horizon held-action thermal baseline to model inertia; a learnable multi-zone heat-balance regularizer enforces thermodynamic consistency without pre-specified geometry or calibrated parameters; the diffusion backbone gives robustness; a credit-assignment mechanism enables downstream reinforcement learning.
AI.result: On SemibuildingSim and Sinergym, ADAPT reduces HVAC energy by 7.3% and occupant discomfort by 30.2% under IID control; under OOD control across unseen seasons and climate regions, it maintains robust performance (only marginal degradation) and substantially outperforms baselines in transfer robustness.
AI.conclusion: ADAPT provides a data-efficient, physics-constrained diffusion model for HVAC control with strong generalization to unseen environments, yielding energy savings and improved occupant comfort while reducing reliance on dense sensing and manual parameter tuning.

title: A Locally Tokenized Generative Model for Robust Time-Series Watermarking
summary: Watermarking is a central tool for provenance in generative models, yet its application to multivariate time series remains hindered by reliability failures under post-editing attacks. We show that existing detectors, which rely on globally coupled re-encoding, suffer from bidirectional drift of the null distribution: post-editing attacks can shift the z-score of non-watermarked samples in either direction, invalidating clean-calibrated thresholds. We argue that this instability is a property of the re-encoding, and that reliable detection requires each recovered unit to depend only on a bounded temporal neighborhood. Guided by this principle, we propose L-VQVAE, a generative model in which each discrete token is produced from a short contiguous window, and LVQMark, a watermarking method over this token space that combines logit-bias injection with robust re-encoding for attack-time detection. Experiments on four benchmarks spanning finance, energy, and neuroimaging show that our approach preserves generation quality while stabilizing both detection power and false-positive behavior under post-editing attacks.

AI.tldr: A localized time-series watermarking approach (L-VQVAE with LVQMark) mitigates post-editing detection drift by bounding dependence to short temporal windows, preserving generation quality while stabilizing detection power and false positives under edits.
AI.motivation: Current detectors for watermarks in multivariate time series rely on globally coupled re-encoding, which causes bidirectional drift of the null distribution under post-editing attacks, undermining reliable watermark detection.
AI.method: L-VQVAE: a vector-quantized variational autoencoder where each discrete token is produced from a short contiguous temporal window. LVQMark: watermarking that injects logit bias and uses robust re-encoding for attack-time detection, ensuring locality and robustness.
AI.result: Experiments on four benchmarks spanning finance, energy, and neuroimaging show that the method preserves generation quality and stabilizes detection power and false-positive rates under post-editing attacks.
AI.conclusion: Localized token generation and robust re-encoding enable reliable watermark detection for multivariate time series without sacrificing generation quality.

title: Towards Professional Tennis Styles for Humanoid Robots with Adaptive Motion Planning and Tracking
summary: Humanoid robots have recently demonstrated promising capabilities in real-world ball sports. However, achieving professional motion styles while maintaining strong task performance remains challenging. In this work, we propose AdaPT, an Adaptive Motion Planning and Tracking framework that learns professional tennis serving and rally styles directly from broadcast videos. This hierarchical design is motivated by the key insight that the planner generates stylistic kinematic motions, while the tracker executes them with minimal interference with planning. Despite its effectiveness in simulation, a substantial sim-to-real gap emerges: tracking performance inevitably degrades on real robots, and this degradation is partially overlooked by autoregressive planning and further compounded by noisy perception. To address these issues, our adaptation mechanism improves tracking robustness by learning to track randomized execution speeds, while conditioning the planner on a learned motion-speed adapter to mitigate compounding errors. Real-world experiments on the Unitree G1 demonstrate the effectiveness of our adaptation mechanism in bridging the sim-to-real gap. We further deploy AdaPT policies on the full-size Dobot Atom humanoid robot (1.7m) and demonstrate in-the-wild serving without motion capture. Beyond these results, our real-world experiments reveal both algorithmic and engineering insights for future humanoid ball-sports systems. Videos and code are available on our \href{https://humanoidtennis.github.io/AdaPT/}{project website}.

AI.tldr: AdaPT proposes a hierarchical motion planning and tracking framework to learn professional tennis styles from broadcast videos, with an adaptation module that improves real-robot tracking and mitigates sim-to-real gaps through randomized execution speeds and a motion-speed adapter.
AI.motivation: Bridge the sim-to-real gap in humanoid ball sports and enable high-quality, stylistic motion from learning-based planners, using real-world perception and noisy dynamics.
AI.method: A two-level system: a planner that outputs stylistic, kinematic trajectories from video data, and a tracker that executes them with minimal interference. An adaptation mechanism trains tracking under randomized speeds and conditions, and a motion-speed adapter conditions the planner to reduce compounding errors. Evaluation on Unitree G1 validates adaptation; deployment on a 1.7 m Dobot Atom demonstrates in-the-wild serving without motion capture.
AI.result: Adaptation mechanism improves tracking robustness and reduces sim-to-real degradation; real robots show closer alignment to planned styles and successful in-the-wild tennis serves without motion capture.
AI.conclusion: AdaPT offers both algorithmic and engineering contributions for humanoid ball-sports—combining a stylistic planner with a robust tracker and speed-adaptation to bridge reality gaps; results suggest promising generalization to full-size humanoids and real-world deployment, with code and videos available.

title: Scale-Separated Conditioning for Style-Encoder-Free Diffusion Stylization
summary: Reference-based diffusion stylization requires separating target geometry from transferable appearance. Existing tuning-based methods often rely on aligned content-style-target triplets or auxiliary visual encoders, which increases data cost and can transfer unintended scene structure from the style reference. We propose SEFS (Style-Encoder-Free Stylization), a style-encoder-free conditioning framework for diffusion transformers. SEFS forms style tokens from stochastic low-resolution crops of single training images. This crop bottleneck preserves local appearance statistics such as palette, stroke, texture, and material, while reducing access to global layout cues. Target content is encoded by edge and segmentation cues and fused with the noisy latent through parameter-efficient trainable projections. We add style-to-denoising re-normalization for token-statistic alignment and cross-block skip fusion for spatial detail. SEFS trains on unpaired single images; the frozen diffusion VAE is used only to place image conditions in the latent space. On artistic stylization benchmarks, SEFS improves content consistency and leakage diagnostics while retaining reference-style affinity, and ablations support the crop-resolution, re-normalization, and skip-fusion choices. The code of SEFS will be made publicly available.

AI.tldr: SEFS is a style-encoder-free diffusion stylization framework that uses random low-resolution crops to form style tokens and encodes content via edge/segmentation cues, enabling unpaired training from single images and improving content fidelity and style transfer without a style encoder.
AI.motivation: Existing diffusion stylization methods require aligned content–style pairs or auxiliary encoders, incurring data costs and risking leakage of style-related scene structure; a more data-efficient, encoder-free approach is desirable.
AI.method: Form style tokens from stochastic low-resolution crops of training images (crop bottleneck) to preserve local appearance; encode target content with edge and segmentation cues; fuse into the noisy latent via learnable projections; apply style-to-denoising re-normalization for token statistics; use cross-block skip fusion for spatial detail; train on unpaired single images; keep diffusion VAE frozen to place conditions in latent space.
AI.result: On artistic stylization benchmarks, SEFS improves content consistency and leakage diagnostics while maintaining reference style affinity; ablations verify the importance of crop resolution, re-normalization, and skip-fusion components; code to be released.
AI.conclusion: SEFS demonstrates that style-conditioned diffusion stylization can be achieved without a dedicated style encoder using a crop-based style token mechanism, enabling data-efficient training from unpaired images with improved content fidelity.

title: When Saying No Makes Better Videos: Designing Dual Gatekeeping for Pedagogically Grounded AI Content Creation
comment: 4 pages, 1 figure. Presented at the CHI 2026 Workshop on Understanding and Engaging Critical Resistance to AI in Education
summary: To prevent the adoption of aesthetically polished but pedagogically flawed AI content, we study a video authoring pipeline featuring two layers of structured refusal. The first layer empowers educators to iteratively reshape AI scripts based on multimedia learning theory, while the second employs automated metrics to flag violations in instructional coherence and narrative-visual synchronization. While neither layer is exhaustive, their synergy ensures that principled resistance--the act of deferring AI output until it meets rigorous standards--becomes a catalyst for higher quality. Evaluation combining a study with 23 educators across 3 topics and automated metrics across 7 topics drawn from established science and philosophy curricula shows that both layers independently improve the same instructional dimensions, suggesting that thoughtful resistance and generative AI are not opposites but partners.

AI.tldr: Two-layer structured refusal in a video authoring pipeline improves instructional quality; educator-driven script reshaping plus automated coherence and narrative-visual synchronization checks; independent improvements across 23 educators and 7 topics; indicates resistance and generative AI can be complementary.
AI.motivation: Mitigate risk of aesthetically polished but pedagogically flawed AI content in education; study how principled resistance to AI outputs can improve instructional quality and leverage human-AI collaboration.
AI.method: A two-layer pipeline: layer 1 educators iteratively reshape AI scripts using multimedia learning theory; layer 2 automated metrics flag coherence and narrative-visual alignment violations. Evaluation with 23 educators across 3 topics and automated metrics across 7 topics drawn from science and philosophy curricula; measure instructional dimensions.
AI.result: Both layers independently improve the same instructional dimensions; combined use yields higher quality; evidence that thoughtful resistance and generative AI can be complementary.
AI.conclusion: Principled resistance to AI-generated instructional content is compatible with, and can enhance, generative AI use in education; the two-layer approach provides additive benefits and a model for human-AI co-design in instructional media.

title: RecPFN: Prior-Fitted Networks for In-Context-Based Recommendations
summary: We introduce RecPFN, a prior-fitted network that brings in-context learning to sequential recommendation. RecPFN is pretrained entirely on synthetic clickstream environments sampled from a broad structural causal prior, enabling it to amortize Bayesian-style inference from a small support set. At inference, a lightweight decoder-only transformer conditions on a handful of domain sequences and produces next-item predictions for queries in a single forward pass, without any weight updates. Across eight public benchmarks, RecPFN achives state-of-the-art zero-shot performance while remaining strongly competitive with supervised methods in low-compute and low-data regimes. It is deployment-efficient and robust to domain shift, outperforming strong zero-shot baselines that rely on large real-interaction corpora. RecPFN provides a practical path toward generalizable, data-efficient recommenders and opens avenues for richer priors, longer-context ICL, and multimodal extensions. Code for training and evaluation is publicly available at https://github.com/SAP-samples/tabular-ai-recpfn/.

AI.tldr: RecPFN is a prior-fitted network for in-context learning in sequential recommendation: pretrained on synthetic clickstreams from a causal prior, it enables zero-shot next-item prediction with a lightweight decoder in a single forward pass, achieving state-of-the-art zero-shot results across eight benchmarks and robust, data-efficient performance.
AI.motivation: Enable in-context learning for sequential recommendation with strong zero-shot and few-shot performance, while maintaining data efficiency and robustness to domain shift.
AI.method: Pretrain on synthetic clickstream environments sampled from a broad structural causal prior; at inference, use a lightweight decoder-only transformer conditioned on a handful of domain sequences to predict next items in a single forward pass without weight updates.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot performance across eight public benchmarks and remains competitive with supervised methods in low-compute, low-data regimes; deployment-efficient and robust to domain shift, outperforming zero-shot baselines relying on large real-interaction data.
AI.conclusion: Offers a practical path toward generalizable, data-efficient recommenders with potential for richer priors, longer-context in-context learning, and multimodal extensions; code for training and evaluation is publicly available.

title: Planning-Oriented End-to-End Autonomous Driving: Architectures, Evaluation, and Emerging Paradigms
summary: End-to-end autonomous driving has evolved from camera-to-control regression toward planning-oriented systems that use structured representations, trajectory-level outputs, and increasingly realistic evaluation protocols. This survey reviews this transition across behavior cloning, conditional imitation learning, privileged distillation, BEV and vectorized planning, unified perception-prediction-planning architectures, world-model-based planners, and vision-language-action systems. We argue that the key distinction in modern end-to-end driving is not whether intermediate representations are used, but whether they are learned, supervised, and evaluated to support safe, feasible, and route-compliant planning. To organize the literature, we synthesize existing methods along four axes: input representation, planning output, supervision signal, and evaluation protocol. We further examine the benchmark shift from open-loop trajectory matching to closed-loop simulation, non-reactive real-log evaluation, long-tail testing, and human-preference-aware metrics. Our analysis highlights that architectural progress is difficult to interpret without benchmark-consistent evaluation, and that displacement-based open-loop metrics alone provide limited evidence for safe and human-aligned driving. We conclude with open challenges in uncertainty-aware planning, learner-expert mismatch, runtime safety assurance, language-action grounding, world-model validation, and reproducible benchmarking.

AI.tldr: A survey frames modern end-to-end autonomous driving as a shift from purely regression-based control to planning-oriented pipelines with learned representations, emphasizing benchmark-consistent evaluation across representation, planning outputs, supervision signals, and evaluation protocols; it highlights the inadequacy of open-loop metrics and outlines open challenges such as uncertainty-aware planning and runtime safety.
AI.motivation: Clarify what constitutes ‘end-to-end’ driving today, disentangle the roles of representations and supervision, and diagnose how evaluation protocols shape reported progress in planning-enabled autonomous driving.
AI.method: Literature synthesis organized along four axes—input representation, planning output, supervision signal, and evaluation protocol—and a critical review of benchmark trends (open-loop vs closed-loop, real-world logs, long-tail testing, and human-preference metrics) across behavior cloning, imitation learning, distillation, BEV/vectorized planning, unified perception-prediction-planning, world-model planners, and vision-language-action systems.
AI.result: Key finding: the critical factor is whether intermediate representations are learned, supervised, and evaluated to support safe, feasible, and route-compliant planning, not merely whether they exist. Benchmark shifts from trajectory matching to closed-loop simulation and human-preference metrics reveal that displacement-based open-loop metrics offer limited evidence of safety or human alignment; architectural progress is hard to interpret without consistent benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Open challenges identified include uncertainty-aware planning, learner-expert mismatch, runtime safety assurance, language-action grounding, world-model validation, and the need for reproducible benchmarking to support safer, more human-aligned end-to-end autonomous driving.

title: StreamSoccer: Event-Driven Memory for Streaming Soccer Commentary
summary: Streaming video understanding requires models to causally update state as video arrives and organize growing history into semantic units that can evolve, persist, and be recalled under bounded computation and memory. This challenge is pronounced in live soccer commentary, where a system must describe completed events, summarize recent play, recall earlier events, or remain silent using only information available before each utterance. We present StreamSoccer, an event-driven system that uses event memory as its intermediate representation. A fixed-budget active memory integrates the stream; completed event states are retained locally and consolidated into retrievable historical records. A unified generator uses current, recent, and historical context to produce three commentary modes, while a rule-assisted scheduler selects a mode or silence. Unlike streaming video-language models organized around frames, visual tokens, or caches, and soccer-commentary methods based on predefined clips or output timestamps, StreamSoccer explicitly models event lifecycles. We construct a three-track streaming soccer commentary dataset and a layered evaluation protocol. At common reference anchors, StreamSoccer obtains CIDEr scores of 38.62, 23.96, and 17.39 for current-event, recent-window, and historical-memory commentary, ranking first on the current-event and historical-memory tracks and second on recent-window. Controlled ablations show that local completed events improve all tracks and that the full system performs best on all three. Across 174 raw-video runs on 58 matches, per-minute RTF p95 ranges from 0.10 to 0.22 without sustained growth with match history. These results indicate that event memory supports streaming soccer commentary across temporal scopes while controlling long-history computation.

AI.tldr: An event-driven streaming soccer commentary system using a fixed-budget event memory and a three-mode generator with a rule-based scheduler; achieves strong CIDEr scores and low per-minute latency across three temporal scopes.
AI.motivation: Need for causal, memory-bounded processing of streaming video to produce timely, coherent commentary across current events, recent play, and past events in live soccer.
AI.method: Event memory as intermediate representation; fixed-budget active memory; completed events retained and consolidated into historical records; unified generator for current/recent/historical modes; rule-assisted scheduler to select mode or silence; three-track dataset and layered evaluation.
AI.result: CIDEr: 38.62 (current-event), 23.96 (recent-window), 17.39 (historical-memory); ranked 1st on current-event and historical-memory, 2nd on recent-window; ablations show improvements; 174 raw-video runs on 58 matches; per-minute RTF p95 0.10–0.22; no sustained growth with history.
AI.conclusion: Event memory enables streaming soccer commentary across temporal scopes with bounded computation; demonstrates efficiency and effectiveness; contributes dataset and evaluation protocol.

title: Causal Reasoning with Bipartite Graphical Causal Models
comment: Figure 2 was added w.r.t. to the published version at Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence (UAI) 2026
summary: Causal Bayesian networks (CBNs) and structural causal models (SCMs) are the dominant frameworks for graphical causal reasoning, but they cannot adequately represent all real-world causal systems. In particular, systems at equilibrium---where feedback mechanisms create cyclic causal dependencies---can exhibit causal semantics that are fundamentally incompatible with these frameworks: different interventions that enforce the same variable value may have different effects, rendering the standard ``perfect intervention'' do($X = x$) ambiguous. We propose bipartite graphical causal models (BGCMs), in which the structure of a system of equations is encoded by a bipartite graph with variable and equation nodes. In this framework, a hard intervention do($f_j : X_v = ξ_v$) specifies which equation is replaced, which variable is targeted, and at what value---resolving the ambiguity of the standard notion. We demonstrate, through a detailed case study of a physical system, that this representation naturally corresponds to distinct real-world interventions. We formulate a Markov property in terms of a new graphical separation criterion (B-separation) that exploits the functional determinism inherent in the equations, and we extend it to settings with non-random inputs. We show how this gives rise to a do-calculus for reasoning about domain invariances. BGCMs strictly generalize CBNs and SCMs while retaining the ability to perform graphical causal reasoning.

AI.tldr: BGCMs encode systems of equations with bipartite graphs (variables vs equations) to resolve equilibrium/cyclic causal ambiguities. They define a new intervention notion do(f_j: X_v = ξ_v) and a B-separation criterion, enabling a do-calculus for domain invariances. BGCMs strictly generalize CBNs/SCMs while preserving graphical causal reasoning.
AI.motivation: Real-world causal systems with cycles or equilibrium conditions produce interventions whose effects depend on how the system is intervened, violating standard do-notation. A framework that encodes equations and allows precise interventions is needed.
AI.method: Introduce bipartite graphical causal models (BGCMs) with equation nodes and variable nodes. A hard intervention do(f_j: X_v = ξ_v) replaces a specific equation, targets a variable, and sets a value, removing ambiguity. Propose B-separation as a graphical criterion leveraging functional determinism, extendable to non-random inputs, and derive a do-calculus for invariance reasoning. Demonstrate via a detailed physical-system case study that the representation aligns with real interventions; show BGCMs generalize CBNs/SCMs.
AI.result: Definition of BGCMs and a Markov property via B-separation; a do-calculus for domain invariances; extension to non-random inputs; a case study supporting the interpretation; BGCMs strictly generalize CBNs and SCMs while enabling standard graphical causal tools.
AI.conclusion: BGCMs resolve ambiguity in equilibrium systems by encoding equations explicitly, enabling distinct real-world interventions to be represented and reasoned about, and they extend existing causal frameworks without sacrificing graphical reasoning.

title: Truncate Bad, Upweight Good: BoN-Style Distillation via Rank-Based Classification
summary: Inference-time selection methods, such as Best-of-N, improve generation by sampling a pool of candidates and selecting the top-ranked completion according to a reward model. Distillation seeks to amortize this procedure into a single policy by replacing raw rewards with in-pool ranks and learning a policy that upweights higher-ranked completions.
