However, existing rank-based policies typically use smooth full-support reweighting, so low-ranked completions receive less mass but remain in the target support. Although a sharper reweighting reduces lower-tail mass, it also increases reliance on brittle ranking at the top made by a single reward model. We propose TUP: a Truncate-bad, Upweight-good Policy that removes low-ranked completions from the support and reweights only the retained upper tail with a tunable sharpness. TUP admits a closed-form, prompt-independent normalization and can be trained fully offline via binary cross-entropy, using shifted-truncated win-rates as soft labels and distilled-to-reference log-likelihood ratios as logits. Theoretically, under certain assumptions, we show that for any unknown oracle reward, the best monotone rank-reweighting can be matched by a lower-tail truncation rule, providing formal support for removing the lower tail rather than merely downweighting it. Empirically, we show that TUP is competitive with strong offline alignment baselines.

AI.tldr: Proposes TUP: a truncate-bad, upweight-good policy to distill Best-of-N rewards into a single policy by removing the low-ranked tail and reweighting the upper tail; provides a closed-form prompt-independent normalization; trains offline with binary cross-entropy using shifted-truncated win-rates as soft labels and distilled-to-reference LLRs as logits; theory shows lower-tail truncation can match any monotone rank-reweighting; empirically competitive with strong offline alignment baselines.
AI.motivation: address brittleness and bias of full-support rank reweighting in distillation of in-pool rankings from a reward model; enable robust, offline-friendly policy that preserves high-ranked information while discarding noisy lower tail.
AI.method: Define TUP by truncating the lower tail of in-pool ranks, upweight only the retained upper tail with tunable sharpness; derive a closed-form, prompt-independent normalization; train offline via binary cross-entropy using shifted-truncated win-rates as soft labels and distilled-to-reference log-likelihood ratios as logits.
AI.result: Empirically competitive with strong offline alignment baselines on standard benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Lower-tail truncation is formally supported as a viable alternative to full reweighting; TUP provides a robust, offline-friendly distillation method with controllable sharpness and a simple normalization, reducing reliance on brittle top-ranked signals while maintaining alignment quality.

title: Video2DoorTraversal: Push Door Traversal via Simulated Door Twins
summary: Door opening and traversal is a long-horizon loco-manipulation task that requires precise handle interaction and coordinated base-arm control. We present Video2DoorTraversal, a single-video real-to-sim-to-real framework for wheel-legged mobile manipulators. Given one RGB video of a real door, DoorTwin reconstructs an instance-aligned, articulated, and simulation-ready door twin with realistic geometry and appearance. A simulation-in-the-loop agent converts the recovered articulation into a parameterized skill program and iteratively refines failed rollouts to generate physically executable demonstrations. These demonstrations are used to train ArticuACT, a dual-depth policy that predicts coordinated base, arm, and gripper commands using robot-centric camera conditioning and interaction-aware supervision. With all perception and policy inference running onboard, the system achieves a 96.57% average success rate across five real doors and an 80.95% zero-shot success rate on structurally similar unseen doors, while completing the full approach, opening, and traversal sequence in approximately 13s on average. Project Page: https://video2doortraversal.github.io/.

AI.tldr: A single-video real-to-sim-to-real framework that reconstructs a door from one video, uses simulation-in-the-loop to generate executable demonstrations, and trains a dual-depth policy for fast, onboard wheel-legged manipulation to open and traverse doors with high success.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon loco-manipulation tasks like door opening require precise interaction and robust perception-to-action planning; bridging real-world perception to executable policies remains challenging due to sim-to-real gaps. The approach aims to enable rapid, onboard, perception-to-action learning from a single real video.
AI.method: 1) DoorTwin reconstructs an instance-aligned articulated, simulation-ready door from a single RGB video. 2) A simulation-in-the-loop agent converts the recovered articulation into a parameterized skill program and iteratively refines failed rollouts to produce executable demonstrations. 3) These demonstrations train ArticuACT, a dual-depth policy that fuses robot-centric camera conditioning and interaction-aware supervision to predict base, arm, and gripper commands. 4) All perception and policy inference run onboard.
AI.result: Achieves 96.57% average success over five real doors; 80.95% zero-shot success on structurally similar unseen doors; full approach/open/traversal completes in ~13 seconds on average.
AI.conclusion: The end-to-end real-to-sim-to-real framework enables effective, fast, onboard manipulation for wheel-legged mobile manipulators with high success and quick execution; the use of a door twin and demonstration-generated policies reduces sim-to-real gaps and improves onboard autonomy.

title: TempJail: Temporal Jailbreak Attack against Large Vision-Language Models via Subtitle Scheduling
summary: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) have achieved remarkable progress in video understanding and reasoning. Despite extensive studies on text- and image-based jailbreaks, video jailbreaks against LVLMs remain largely unexplored. Existing video jailbreak methods mainly manipulate textual content embedded in videos, while overlooking how such information is organized over time. Our analysis reveals that jailbreak effectiveness depends not only on the semantics of textual information but also on its temporal presentation, including duration and timing-slot allocation. Motivated by this finding, we use subtitles, which are common in real-world videos and allow semantic content to be presented under precise temporal control without appearing visually intrusive, as a natural attack medium. Based on this insight, we propose TempJail, a black-box video-based jailbreak framework that constructs query-aligned dialogue-style subtitle sequences and optimizes their temporal scheduling to exploit temporal vulnerabilities in LVLMs and elicit responses that satisfy the harmful intent of the source query. Extensive experiments on four representative LVLMs and two datasets demonstrate that TempJail achieves the highest attack success rate across all evaluated model--dataset settings, outperforming the strongest baseline by 53 and 18 percentage points in dataset-averaged ASR on GPT-5 and Gemini 3.5-Flash, respectively.

AI.tldr: TempJail is a black-box video-based jailbreak framework that uses query-aligned dialogue-style subtitles and optimized temporal scheduling to exploit LVLM temporal vulnerabilities, achieving the highest attack success rate across models and datasets.
AI.motivation: Video jailbreaks for LVLMs are underexplored. Existing methods manipulate textual content but ignore how information is temporally organized; subtitles offer precise temporal control with minimal visual intrusion. This enables more effective malicious prompts.
AI.method: Constructs query-aligned dialogue-style subtitle sequences and optimizes their temporal scheduling in a black-box setting to elicit harmful responses from LVLMs.
AI.result: TempJail achieves the highest attack success rate across model-dataset settings, outperforming the strongest baseline by 53 and 18 percentage points in dataset-averaged ASR on GPT-5 and Gemini 3.5-Flash respectively.
AI.conclusion: Temporal presentation of textual content is a critical factor in video jailbreak effectiveness; subtitles are a potent medium for exploiting LVLMs, indicating a need for defenses that address temporal dynamics.

title: Specification-delta-driven data governance: an empirical study of the «spec-delta» as the unit of change in lakehouse data platforms
summary: Spec Driven Development SDD has consolidated the idea that the specification rather than the code should be the primary artefact governing AI assisted work. Tools such as GitHub Spec Kit, and proposals such as Constitutional SDD, have formalised this principle in the software domain, while the executable data-contracts literature has extended it to schema and quality enforcement at run time. Nevertheless, the treatment of the specification delta OpenSpec's core idea that every change should produce a reviewable increment of requirements as the unit of change in data platforms remains empirically unexplored, even though many data-platform changes are contractual (new datasets, service-level agreements, metric semantics, access policies) rather than purely code changes. This work formalises the spec-delta concept, proposes a taxonomy of data platform changes according to their suitability for incremental specification, and defines a controlled experiment comparing a spec-delta-driven workflow against a conventional code pull-request workflow without a delta. The response variables are discovery to deployment time, the density of defects reaching the Silver and Gold lakehouse layers, cross-tool metric divergence, and reviewer cognitive load measured with NASA TLX. The paper explicitly reserves a demonstration-and-laboratory section for instantiation on a real lakehouse environment. The contribution is not a tool but reproducible evidence and an applicability guide that helps to avoid the up front over specification antipattern.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes spec-delta for data platforms and proposes an empirical evaluation comparing a spec-delta workflow to a conventional PR workflow, with metrics on deployment speed, defect density, metric divergence, and reviewer cognitive load; aims to provide reproducible evidence and guidelines for incremental specification.
AI.motivation: Builds on spec-driven development (SDD) trends in software and the executable data-contracts literature, arguing that many data-platform changes are contractual rather than pure code changes. Seeks empirical validation and practical guidance for using spec-delta in data platforms.
AI.method: Formalize the spec-delta concept, develop a taxonomy of data platform changes suitable for incremental specification, and design a controlled experiment comparing a spec-delta-driven workflow against a traditional code PR workflow. Outcome measures include discovery-to-deployment time, defect density reaching Silver/Gold lakehouse layers, cross-tool metric divergence, and reviewer cognitive load via NASA TLX. Includes a plan for real-lakehouse demonstration.
AI.result: The abstract outlines a research plan; no empirical results are presented. The contribution is framed as reproducible evidence and an applicability guide rather than a software tool.
AI.conclusion: The work aims to provide evidence-based guidance to avoid up-front over-specification antipatterns and to promote the use of spec-delta in data-platform development, with an instantiation on a real lakehouse environment forthcoming.

title: Credit Without Ground Truth: Auditing Step-Level Credit Assignment in LLM Agents Against Executed Replay
comment: 49 pages, 7 figures. Pre-registered; frozen analysis plans and prompts included in the appendices. Under review
summary: Audited against causal ground truth from executed replay in a single-agent tool environment (ALFWorld), none of the step-level credit signals used to train LLM agents -- LLM-judge scores, outcome-conditioned logprob ratios, or the policy's own confidence -- identifies which steps causally matter better than chance. Existing evaluations grade these signals against annotated step *correctness*; we audit them against step *contribution* -- what re-sampling the policy's own alternatives at each decision point and rolling forward actually changes about the outcome -- and the two come apart. The ground truth itself is structured: causal contribution is sparse (30.5% of decision points where ground truth is defined carry measurable effect), and measurability is model-dependent -- the fraction of points with no policy-supported counterfactual differs by a factor of two (13.1% vs. 26.8%) between two similar-scale policies. The failure mode is identifiable: implicit credit echoes the policy's fluency (median rank correlation +0.75, replicating at +0.70 in a second family under a corrected instrument), while conditioning on the outcome adds no causal information (partial correlation -0.004, Qwen). A confidence-only router recovers pivotal steps at chance level, but cuts judge cost by 13.1% per turn (14.0% per trajectory). In a seven-arm pre-registered training experiment, no arm reliably outperforms the untrained policy, and the checkpoints' apparent instrument signature is fully explained by training dose -- sparser credit retains fewer examples, an order-of-magnitude spread in optimizer steps -- not credit content. Comparisons of credit rules must therefore match effective sample size, or they measure dose, not credit.

AI.tldr: Audited step-level credit signals fail to identify causally pivotal steps in ALFWorld; signals reflect fluency or training dose rather than true causal contribution; effective sample size matters.
AI.motivation: To assess whether LLM-level credit signals (judge scores, logprob ratios, confidence) align with actual causal contribution of decisions, not just correctness or fluency.
AI.method: Construct causal ground truth via executed replay in ALFWorld; at each decision point, re-sample policy alternatives and roll forward; compare signal scores against this causal contribution; examine model-dependence of measurability; test a confidence-only router; run seven-arm pre-registered training with varying dose; analyze whether instrument signatures reflect credit content vs dose.
AI.result: No signal reliably identifies causally important steps beyond chance; contribution is sparse; measurability differs by policy; implicit signals track fluency; conditioning on outcome provides no causal info; confidence router reduces decision-cost but not improve causal detection; training dose explains instrument-like signals; effective sample size matters for comparing credit rules.
AI.conclusion: Current step-level credit signals do not measure true causal contribution; comparisons must match effective sample size; otherwise results reflect dose and data scarcity; need better evaluation frameworks linking counterfactual contribution to signals.

title: DART-S: Reachability-Audited Active-Suspension Preconditioning for Off-Road Vehicle Jumps
summary: Airborne torque reaction cannot recover takeoff errors beyond the wheel angular-momentum budget. DART-S applies ramp-face suspension preconditioning to change pitch, pitch rate, and wheel spin before liftoff, thereby shifting the queried state and altering the remaining authority budget. To predict how each suspension action reshapes this state-budget pair, DART-S employs a local calibration map. A support-aware selector combines the predicted shift with local outcome evidence and an interval-reachability screen; an exact-pair audit reports residual authority. Across 600 new runs in 72 independent BeamNG sessions, every positive, negative, and boundary query follows its prespecified branch. At the confirmed 40°/13 m/s boundary, DART-S attains 24/24 post-touchdown attitude-criterion successes versus 0/24 for DART (session-level Holm-adjusted p=0.0234). At 11.5 m/s, a 0.35 s timing action attains 23/24 versus 0/24 for the static preset (p=0.0156). The 200 rad/s command guard keeps drivetrain hard-limit exceedance at zero across all 600 runs. The source code will be available at https://github.com/MeridianCAS/DART-S

title: Learning to Beat: Phenotype-Guided Latent Flow with Regional Motion Priors for Biventricular Motion Synthesis
summary: Full-cycle biventricular geometry is essential for characterizing cardiac function. However, dense and temporally consistent 3D+t biventricular meshes are not routinely available, whereas end-diastolic (ED) anatomy can often be obtained reliably. We therefore investigate full-cycle biventricular motion synthesis from a single ED mesh. This task is challenging because cardiac deformation is spatially heterogeneous and phenotype dependent, while conventional global generative models often obscure localized motion patterns. In this study, we propose a region-specific and phenotype-adaptive framework that integrates motion-informed functional parcellation with conditional latent flow. A functional partition learned from reconstructed motion organizes the ventricular surface into regions with coherent dynamics and enables topology-aware regional feature exchange. A phenotype-conditioned rectified-flow model subsequently maps the ED anatomy to full-cycle motion latents through fine-grained conditioning and prototype-routed motion adapters. An optional control branch further incorporates available motion descriptors for controllable synthesis. Experiments on ACDC, M\&Ms, and M\&Ms-2 demonstrate consistent improvements in geometric accuracy and functional fidelity. Under ED-only synthesis, our method achieves biventricular ASSD, HD95, and vRMSE of \(1.49\pm0.34\)~mm, \(3.77\pm1.06\)~mm, and \(3.31\pm1.03\)~mm, respectively, outperforming all competing methods. Complementary functional and robustness evaluations further demonstrate that the synthesized sequences preserve physiologically plausible ventricular dynamics and generalize across cohorts and disease phenotypes. The code will be released publicly upon acceptance of the manuscript for publication.

AI.tldr: Region-specific, phenotype-adaptive framework to synthesize full-cycle biventricular motion from a single ED mesh, using functional parcellation and conditional latent flow; achieves improved geometric accuracy and functional fidelity on ACDC, M&Ms datasets.
AI.motivation: Dense and temporally consistent 3D+t biventricular meshes are not routinely available; end-diastolic (ED) anatomy is more readily obtainable. There is a need to reconstruct full-cycle biventricular dynamics from ED data, accounting for spatially heterogeneous deformation and phenotype dependence that global models often fail to capture.
AI.method: Learn a functional partitioning of the ventricular surface to identify regions with coherent dynamics; enable topology-aware regional feature exchange. Use a phenotype-conditioned rectified-flow (conditional latent flow) model to map ED anatomy to full-cycle motion latents with fine-grained conditioning and prototype-routed motion adapters. An optional control branch incorporates available motion descriptors to allow controllable synthesis.
AI.result: On ACDC, M&Ms, and M&Ms-2 datasets, the method shows consistent improvements in geometric accuracy and functional fidelity. ED-only synthesis achieves ASSD 1.49±0.34 mm, HD95 3.77±1.06 mm, and vRMSE 3.31±1.03 mm, outperforming competing methods. Functional and robustness evaluations indicate synthesized sequences preserve physiologically plausible ventricular dynamics and generalize across cohorts and disease phenotypes.
AI.conclusion: The proposed region-specific, phenotype-adaptive framework effectively enables accurate, physiologically plausible full-cycle biventricular motion synthesis from a single ED mesh. The combination of motion-informed functional partitioning and conditioned latent flow yields superior generalization across phenotypes and cohorts, with public code to be released upon acceptance.

title: SAPO: Single-Rollout Autoregressive Policy Optimization for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
summary: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) has become a critical stage in the post-training of large language models. Existing critic-free, group-relative methods estimate policy advantages from multiple rollouts, avoiding the substantial memory overhead of conventional proximal policy optimization (PPO) and achieving strong performance on long-horizon interactive tasks. Despite their success, recent studies revealed three limitations: (1) Lack explicit value generalization and effective temporal credit assignment; (2) Suffer from potential advantage collapse in long-horizon complex tasks; (3) Require a costly trade-off between sampling budget and policy performance. In this work, we propose Single-rollout Autoregressive Policy Optimization (SAPO), a low-memory and compute-efficient framework in which the policy and value functions share a single autoregressive backbone. SAPO exploits the autoregressive structure of LLMs to produce policy and value predictions at distinct causal boundaries with shared parameters, while independently optimizing the PPO objectives and auxiliary on-policy SARSA objectives. To robustly estimate the contribution of each turn, we further introduce a trajectory-level generalized advantage estimator that combines lambda-returns with batch normalization. Experiments across ALFWorld and WebShop with Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B show that SAPO trains stably and outperforms PPO and GRPO by mean +15.1 and +12.1 percentage points, respectively, while eliminating the memory cost of a separate critic model and reducing per-iteration runtime by 33.2% over PPO.

AI.tldr: SAPO introduces a memory-efficient, critic-free RL framework for LLMs by sharing a single autoregressive backbone for policy and value. It uses independent PPO objectives and on-policy SARSA objectives, plus a trajectory-level generalized advantage estimator. Empirically, it outperforms PPO and GRPO on ALFWorld/WebShop with reduced memory and roughly one-third lower per-iteration runtime.
AI.motivation: Critic-free, group-relative RL methods for LLMs face three limitations: (i) insufficient value generalized credit assignment, (ii) potential advantage collapse in long-horizon tasks, and (iii) a trade-off between sampling budget and policy performance.
AI.method: Single-rollout Autoregressive Policy Optimization (SAPO) shares an autoregressive backbone for policy and value with distinct causal boundaries. It optimizes PPO objectives and auxiliary on-policy SARSA objectives independently, and introduces a trajectory-level generalized advantage estimator that combines lambda-returns with batch normalization to robustly estimate each turn's contribution.
AI.result: On ALFWorld and WebShop using Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B, SAPO trains stably and outperforms PPO and GRPO by mean +15.1 and +12.1 percentage points, respectively. It eliminates the memory cost of a separate critic and reduces per-iteration runtime by 33.2% over PPO.
AI.conclusion: SAPO provides a low-memory, computation-efficient alternative to critic-based methods for long-horizon RL with LLMs, achieving improved stability, better value generalization and credit assignment, and substantial efficiency gains across tested tasks and model scales.

title: Finite-Horizon Input-Output Dynamics of Minibatch Perturbations in AdamW
summary: A minibatch can influence training beyond the update at which it is observed because AdamW stores past gradient information in its optimizer states. We study this delayed effect through paired trajectories that differ only in one gradient update and share the same subsequent training sequence. We formulate AdamW as a finite-horizon input--state--output (ISO) system whose state contains the model parameters and first- and second-moment estimates. Linearizing the joint dynamics yields a signed response operator that maps a localized gradient perturbation to its future loss effects, revealing how optimizer memory shapes their magnitude, timing, and sign. We further derive an exact multistep error decomposition and establish first-order finite-horizon accuracy under local smoothness and controlled activation switching. Experiments validate the response mechanism and optimizer-state effects, while repeated-future analyses reveal substantial prospective structure in delayed influence that can be partially recovered from ISO approximations. Code is available at https://github.com/Kanyooo/Loss_ISO.

AI.tldr: AdamW's optimizer memory induces delayed effects of a single gradient update; modeling AdamW as a finite-horizon ISO system reveals a signed response operator linking localized gradients to future losses, with first-order accuracy and substantial recoverable delayed structure.
AI.motivation: Quantify and predict how past gradient information stored in AdamW's states influences future training outcomes beyond the observed update.
AI.method: Treat AdamW as a finite-horizon input-state-output (ISO) system; state includes parameters and first/second-moment estimates; linearize joint dynamics to derive a signed response operator mapping gradient perturbations to future losses; derive a multistep error decomposition; prove first-order finite-horizon accuracy under local smoothness and controlled activation switching; validate via experiments; analyze delayed influence through repeated-future analyses; release code.
AI.result: The response operator characterizes how optimizer memory affects the magnitude, timing, and sign of delayed effects; provides an exact multistep error decomposition; establishes first-order finite-horizon accuracy; experiments validate the mechanism and reveal substantial prospective structure recoverable from ISO approximations.
AI.conclusion: Offers a principled framework for understanding how optimizer-state memory shapes training dynamics, with implications for minibatch design and hyperparameter tuning; code available at the provided repository.

title: Question-Guided Evidence Acquisition for Multimodal Visual Question Answering
summary: Multimodal LLMs can see a document, but they often can't read it reliably. Small text, tables, visual cues, and topological elements still trip them up under direct visual inference, even when the page is already sitting in the model's context. Most document-VQA systems treat perception as fixed: they encode the page once, ask the question, and answer from whatever the model happened to extract in that single fast pass. We think document VQA needs slower, more deliberate perception: rather than answering from one fixed encoding, the model should spend a bit of extra compute at inference time working out what to look at next, and only then answer. We build this into \textbf{Q-Guide}, a small agent that reads a question, works out what evidence it is still missing, and calls targeted tool(s) to recover it---reading text where text is needed, zooming in where detail is needed, or grounding a region where position matters. On DocVQA2026 and Manga109, Q-Guide outperforms both direct prompting and recent multi-agent document systems ($65.0\%$ vs.\ $40.0\%$ on DocVQA2026, $32.4\%$ vs.\ $24.4\%$ on Manga109), and the improvement holds across three Claude backbones (Opus 4.6, Sonnet 4.6, and Opus 4.5). We find that accuracy scales with the perception budget---most of the gain appears within two to three deliberate rounds---and that the gain comes from directing perception to the right place, not from complex control logic: adding planners, routers, or multiple collaborating agents does not help.

AI.tldr: Q-Guide enables deliberative, evidence-directed perception for document-VQA via an iterative agent that selectively reads, zooms, and grounds; achieves large accuracy gains over single-pass encodings and recent multi-agent baselines on DocVQA2026 and Manga109.
AI.motivation: Multimodal LLMs struggle to read small text, tables, and complex page structures when relying on a fixed single-pass encoding. A slower, targeted perception loop could selectively retrieve missing evidence and improve reliability.
AI.method: Introduce Q-Guide, a small agent that reads the question, identifies missing evidence, and calls targeted tools (text reading, zooming, grounding) to recover it. Perception is budgeted and iterated over 2–3 rounds. Evaluated on DocVQA2026 and Manga109 across Claude backbones (Opus 4.6, Sonnet 4.6, Opus 4.5).
AI.result: Q-Guide outperforms direct prompting and recent multi-agent document systems (DocVQA2026: 65.0% vs 40.0%; Manga109: 32.4% vs 24.4%), with gains consistent across backbones.
AI.conclusion: Accuracy scales with the perception budget; most gains occur within two to three deliberate rounds. Gains arise from directing perception to the right locations rather than relying on complex control logic; additional planners/routers/collaborating agents do not help.

title: PolicyGuide: From Guarding One Action to Guiding the Whole Workflow for Policy-Compliant LLM Agents
summary: Customer-service LLM agents must follow organizational policy when acting on a user's behalf. Compliance failures arise from either forbidden actions, such as granting an ineligible change, or omitted procedural requirements, such as identification or confirmation. Runtime safeguards can intervene on risky actions, but action-local checks do not guide an agent through a multi-step procedure. Workflow-following systems support prescribed process execution, but primarily target workflow completion rather than safeguarding agent behavior. PolicyGuide instead compiles each domain policy into a workflow graph and invokes a proactive verifier at user-turn boundaries. From persisted graph state, the verifier reconciles open requests and returns step-specific remediation along a policy-compliant path. Across the $τ^2$-bench airline, retail, and telecom domains with a GPT-5.4 agent and verifier, PolicyGuide raises mean $\mathrm{Pass}^4$ from $0.42$ to $0.62$, with the largest gain on telecom ($0.19$ to $0.61$), the most workflow-structured domain. The same workflows transfer to Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Gemini 2.5 Pro agents. Complementary evaluations find the lowest observed attack-success rate under adversarial users and the strongest procedural compliance in an author-designed workflow-level validation.

AI.tldr: PolicyGuide converts domain policies into a proactive workflow-graph and uses a user-turn verifier to guide multi-step actions, improving policy compliance and robustness across multiple LLM agents and domains.
AI.motivation: Prevent policy violations and incomplete procedural steps in customer-service LLMs by addressing gaps left by action-local safeguards and typical workflow systems that don’t guide behavior end-to-end.
AI.method: Translate domain policies into a persisted workflow graph. At each user turn, a proactive verifier reconciles open requests against the graph state and returns step-specific remediation along a policy-compliant path. Evaluate across τ^2-bench domains (airline, retail, telecom) with a GPT-5.4 agent and verifier, then transfer workflows to Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Gemini 2.5 Pro; perform complementary adversarial and workflow-level validation.
AI.result: Mean Pass^4 rises from 0.42 to 0.62; telecom domain shows the largest gain (0.19 to 0.61). Workflows transfer to other agents (Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 2.5 Pro). Complementary tests show reduced attack success under adversarial users and stronger procedural compliance in author-designed workflow-level validation.
AI.conclusion: PolicyGuide provides end-to-end, policy-aligned decision guidance by coupling domain-policy graphs with a proactive verifier, yielding improved compliance, robustness to adversaries, and cross-model portability.

title: Unsupervised Anomaly Detection Using Flow Matching on Tabular Data
summary: Financial anomaly detection often relies on large unlabeled transaction logs, where anomalous samples may already be present during training. Such training-set contamination violates the clean-normal data assumption underlying many anomaly detection methods. Although flow matching has demonstrated strong performance in generative modeling, its robustness in unsupervised tabular anomaly detection remains underexplored. In this work, we study flow-matching-based anomaly detection under contaminated training data by comparing Time-Conditioned Contraction Matching (TCCM) with Forest-Flow and evaluating multiple anomaly scoring functions. Our results show that the choice of anomaly score is critical. The original single-step Decision score used by TCCM is sensitive to contamination, whereas trajectory-based Deviation and Reconstruction scores provide more stable anomaly signals. With these scores, Forest-Flow becomes competitive with, and in some cases outperforms, TCCM. These findings highlight the importance of anomaly scoring for flow-matching methods in financial anomaly detection under severe class imbalance.

AI.tldr: Flow-matching-based anomaly detection under contaminated training data; comparing Time-Conditioned Contraction Matching (TCCM) with Forest-Flow and evaluating anomaly scoring functions. Finding: anomaly score choice is critical; trajectory-based Deviation and Reconstruction scores are more robust to contamination; Forest-Flow can match or surpass TCCM under contamination; highlights importance of anomaly scoring in financial anomaly detection with severe class imbalance.
AI.motivation: Assess robustness of flow-matching-based unsupervised anomaly detection in the presence of training-set contamination, a common scenario in financial data, and identify how anomaly scoring impacts performance.
AI.method: Empirical comparison between TCCM and Forest-Flow on contaminated data, evaluating multiple anomaly scoring functions including a single-step Decision score and trajectory-based Deviation and Reconstruction scores.
AI.result: Score choice significantly affects robustness to contamination. Deviation and Reconstruction scores provide more stable anomaly signals than the original Decision score, enabling Forest-Flow to be competitive with or superior to TCCM in contaminated settings.
AI.conclusion: Anomaly scoring is a crucial design choice for flow-matching anomaly detectors in finance under contamination and severe class imbalance; improving or selecting robust scores can shift competitiveness between methods.

title: Gallileo-4D: Frozen Backbone Ensemble for Dynamic 4D Reconstruction
comment: Technical report for the PhysAI Dynamic 4D Reconstruction Challenge at the ECCV 2026 Workshop on Physical AI. Third of 27 teams. 14 pages, 10 figures. Code: https://github.com/odaxai/Gallileo-4D Weights: https://huggingface.co/OdaxAI/gallileo-4d-weights
summary: We describe our entry to the PhysAI Dynamic 4D Reconstruction Challenge, which placed third of 27 teams at 0.58356 APD on the final leaderboard, without a single gradient update. This was not the plan: of thirteen fine-tuning configurations of a pre-trained 4D backbone, twelve degraded the challenge score, and eleven of those twelve improved local validation at the same time. We trace this inversion to the structure of the benchmark: only 25% of the evaluation set belongs to the data variant released for training, so updates that fit the available data damage the pre-trained features the remaining 75% relies on. Our system therefore freezes the backbone and spends its budget at inference time, fusing three decoding configurations -- temporal stride-3, horizontal-flip test-time augmentation, and dense stride-1 -- under a convex weighting. The ensemble recovers +0.041 APD over the frozen baseline, more than any training run achieved, at zero training cost.

AI.tldr: A third-place entry shows freezing a pre-trained 4D backbone and relying on inference-time fusion of three decoding configurations yields a performance gain over all training-based fine-tuning, due to data-variant mismatch in the benchmark that makes gradient updates harmful.
AI.motivation: Investigate why gradient-based fine-tuning degrades performance on this benchmark and whether zero-training-cost inference-time ensembling can outperform traditional training.
AI.method: Freeze the backbone; ensemble three decoding configurations (temporal stride-3, horizontal-flip test-time augmentation, dense stride-1) using convex weighting; compare against thirteen fine-tuning configurations on a 4D reconstruction backbone.
AI.result: The ensemble achieves +0.041 APD over the frozen baseline, surpassing all training runs, with zero training cost.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark’s data_variant distribution (only 25% overlap with training data) causes updates to harm generalization; inference-time ensemble can outperform training-time fine-tuning under such distribution shifts, highlighting the risk of relying on training data when benchmark structure is misaligned.

title: EnvHarness: Awakening Static Worlds for Agent Learning
summary: LLM agents learn by interacting with environments, yet these environments are hand-built and static: blind to an agent's weaknesses, and quickly left behind as it improves. While recent environment generation methods attempt to address this, they require domain-specific pipelines, rely on expensive or unreliable verifiers, and still produce static environments. To alleviate the engineering burden of rebuilding environments from scratch, we propose Environment Harness (EnvHarness), a programmable layer of plug-in components that wraps a static environment to reshape its behavior without modifying the underlying logic. Operating through standard interfaces, EnvHarness applies across diverse domains while ensuring every reshaped environment retains its original verifier. To automate this process, we introduce EnvRigger, which treats the target policy as a black box, observing its execution trajectories to synthesize EnvHarness components targeting diagnosed flaws, and validating them via fresh rollouts. Across five benchmarks in four domains, EnvHarness outperforms both original environments and domain-specific environment generation pipelines, achieving up to a 9.0-point improvement on held-out instances with 9.8% fewer execution steps. Furthermore, EnvHarness provides a superior optimization signal for reinforcement learning, enabling continuous, targeted co-evolution of the policy and its environment.

AI.tldr: EnvHarness is a programmable wrapper around static environments that reshapes agent-environment interactions via plug-in components, and EnvRigger automatically synthesizes these components by observing policy trajectories, enabling targeted, verifiable environment co-evolution across domains.
AI.motivation: Static, hand-built environments fail to reveal and adapt to an agent's weaknesses; existing environment generation pipelines are domain-specific, expensive, or unreliable, creating a need for a general, pluggable, verifiable shaping layer that reduces engineering effort.
AI.method: EnvHarness provides a layer of plug-in components with standard interfaces that wrap a static environment without changing its core logic, preserving its verifier. EnvRigger treats the policy as a black box, analyzes execution trajectories to diagnose flaws, and synthesizes EnvHarness components to address those flaws, validated through fresh rollouts.
AI.result: On five benchmarks across four domains, EnvHarness outperforms the original environments and domain-specific pipelines, achieving up to a 9.0-point improvement on held-out instances and 9.8% fewer execution steps. It also offers a stronger optimization signal for RL, enabling continuous co-evolution of policy and environment.
AI.conclusion: A general, transferable environment-shaping framework (EnvHarness) plus automated component synthesis (EnvRigger) can reduce engineering burden, preserve verifiers, and improve learning efficiency and robustness across diverse tasks.

title: MileGPO: Milestone Inference with Local Evidence for Graph-Based Policy Optimization of Long-Horizon LLM Agents
summary: Credit assignment is challenging in long-horizon agentic reinforcement learning, where supervision often comes only from final rewards. Existing methods refine trajectory-level signals into step-level credits through step grouping or graph-based advantage estimation, but can overlook meaningful intermediate milestones. We propose MileGPO (Milestone Inference with Local Evidence for Graph-Based Policy Optimization), which derives process-level credit from grouped on-policy rollouts through three designs. Milestone Discovery identifies candidate milestones on successful rollouts and recurring traps on failed ones. Reliability-Calibrated Shaping (RCS) weights these candidates by outcome-based confidence, strengthening reliable milestones and traps while down-weighting uncertain ones. Progress-Contrastive Calibration (PCC) further tests whether a candidate reflects local progress and whether its incoming ansition outperforms observed alternatives from the same state.MileGPO requires neither auxiliary models nor additional environment interaction. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop show state-of-the-art performance and a small in-distribution to out-of-distribution gap on ALFWorld. Ablations and credit diagnostics indicate that reliability weighting, local progress, and same-state branch evidence complement milestone discovery and resolve ambiguous intermediate credit.

AI.tldr: MileGPO derives process-level credit from milestones inferred from on-policy rollouts, using reliability weighting and progress-contrastive checks to improve long-horizon policy optimization without extra interactions; achieves state-of-the-art results on ALFWorld and WebShop, with ablations validating the components.
AI.motivation: Credit assignment in long-horizon RL is difficult when supervision comes only from final rewards. Existing step-division or graph-based methods may miss meaningful milestones; MileGPO aims to extract milestone-based signals to provide richer supervision.
AI.method: Three design components: (1) Milestone Discovery to identify milestones on successful rollouts and traps on failures; (2) Reliability-Calibrated Shaping (RCS) to weight milestones by outcome-based confidence; (3) Progress-Contrastive Calibration (PCC) to verify that a candidate reflects local progress and that its incoming transition outperforms same-state alternatives. MileGPO operates on grouped on-policy rollouts and requires no auxiliary models or extra environment interactions.
AI.result: Empirical results on ALFWorld and WebShop show state-of-the-art performance and a small gap for ID→OOD generalization on ALFWorld. Ablations and credit diagnostics indicate that reliability weighting, local progress, and same-state branch evidence complement milestone discovery and resolve ambiguous intermediate credit.
AI.conclusion: Process-level milestone inference with local evidence enables effective credit assignment in long-horizon RL without additional data or models, yielding strong performance and robust diagnostic insights.

title: Far from the Crowd: Scalable Self-Supervised Learning via Geographic Isolation
summary: Self-supervised pretraining on remote sensing imagery typically treats all samples as equally informative, despite large variability in geographic and visual structure. We propose a curriculum learning strategy for self-supervised Earth observation that ranks samples by geographic isolation, a label-free proxy derived entirely from geolocation metadata already present in geospatial datasets, requiring no image decoding, no model feedback, and no manual annotation. Unlike visual complexity proxies, it scales as O(D log D) with dataset size D and is well-defined for both contrastive and reconstructive objectives. We integrate the proposed measure into MoCoV2 and MAE pretraining and evaluate across three downstream tasks from CopernicusBench (BigEarthNet, DFC-2020, LCZ). Our curriculum reaches baseline final-epoch performance using as few as 20% of the training budget (MAE) and at most 40% (MoCo) of the training budget, and improves final downstream performance by up to +5 mAP on BigEarthNet, with gains of 1-5 points across benchmarks, matching visual-complexity curricula while reducing pre-computation cost by more than 140x (4 s vs. 568 s on SSL4EO). A CKA and effective-rank analysis further reveals that curriculum-trained encoders develop higher-dimensional, more uniformly utilized embedding spaces throughout training.

AI.tldr: A curriculum learning strategy for self-supervised Earth observation uses a label-free measure of geographic isolation to rank samples, improving training efficiency and downstream performance across SSL methods.
AI.motivation: To address heterogeneity and unequal informativeness in remote-sensing data during self-supervised pretraining by using an automatic, scalable proxy derived from geolocation metadata, reducing reliance on image complexity or manual labels.
AI.method: Introduce geographic-isolation-based curriculum, computed from geolocation alone (no decoding, no feedback, no labels). Integrate into MoCoV2 (contrastive) and MAE (reconstructive) pretraining. Scales as O(D log D) with dataset size D. Evaluate on three CopernicusBench tasks (BigEarthNet, DFC-2020, LCZ).
AI.result: Curriculum achieves baseline final-epoch performance with only 20% (MAE) to 40% (MoCo) of the training budget; improves downstream performance by up to +5 mAP on BigEarthNet and 1–5 point gains across benchmarks; matches visual-complexity curricula while reducing precomputation by >140x (4 s vs. 568 s on SSL4EO). CKA and effective-rank analyses show curriculum-trained encoders have higher-dimensional, more uniformly utilized embedding spaces.
AI.conclusion: Geographic-isolation-based curriculum is an effective, scalable strategy for self-supervised Earth observation pretraining, compatible with multiple SSL objectives, delivering substantial efficiency gains and improved representations.

title: TESTNAV: Pareto-Guided Search for Compositional Robustness Testing
summary:
Deep learning models remain vulnerable to real-world input perturbations, especially when multiple corruptions co-occur in the same input (e.g., brightness shifts and motion blur). Compositional testing reveals these interaction effects but introduces two challenges: combinatorial growth of the perturbation space as dimensions and severity levels increase, and uneven diagnostic value-many combinations yield unrealistically degraded inputs with limited practical relevance.
  We present TESTNAV, 1 a Pareto-guided robustness testing framework for efficiently exploring discrete, compositional perturbation spaces when only a limited number of perturbation configurations can be evaluated. TESTNAV prioritises severe yet realistic failures by formulating robustness testing as bi-objective optimisation: maximise performance degradation while preserving input fidelity measured by modality-specific metrics (e.g., SSIM and KID for vision; chrF and BERT-F1 for language and code). It uses NSGA-II to approximate the bi-objective Pareto front. Across four benchmarks spanning vision, natural language, and code generation, TESTNAV recovers Pareto fronts up to 2.15x faster than search-based baselines, using 35.8%-89.3% of the discrete perturbation space defined by four perturbation dimensions with six levels each.

AI.tldr: A Pareto-guided robustness testing framework (TESTNAV) that efficiently explores discrete compositional perturbations using NSGA-II to maximize degradation while preserving input fidelity; achieves up to 2.15x faster Pareto-front discovery across vision, NLP, and code benchmarks, evaluating only a fraction of the perturbation space.
AI.motivation: Deep models are vulnerable to real-world input perturbations, especially when multiple perturbations co-occur. Compositional testing reveals interaction effects but suffers combinatorial explosion and yields unrealistic failures with limited relevance; there is a need for efficient, realistic robustness exploration.
AI.method: Formulate robustness testing as a bi-objective optimization: maximize performance degradation and preserve input fidelity using domain-specific metrics (SSIM and KID for vision; chrF and BERT-F1 for language/code). Employ NSGA-II to approximate the Pareto front over a discrete perturbation space with four perturbation dimensions and six levels each, enabling efficient prioritization of severe yet realistic failures.
AI.result: TESTNAV recovers Pareto fronts up to 2.15x faster than search-based baselines, using 35.8%-89.3% of the discrete perturbation space across four benchmarks spanning vision, natural language, and code generation.
AI.conclusion: TESTNAV provides an efficient, principled approach to robustness testing for compositional perturbations, delivering faster Pareto-front discovery while focusing on realistic failure modes; the framework generalizes across modalities and perturbation spaces and can inform more robust model deployment.

title: Answer-Level Trust Selection for Physical Vision-Language Reasoning
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) can estimate physical quantities such as duration, speed, and acceleration from visual observations, but existing benchmarks primarily assess overall model performance against annotated ground truth. In deployment, a key question is whether an individual prediction can be trusted when its ground truth is unavailable. Self-consistency alone may fail to capture important failure modes: a VLM may produce stable-but-wrong estimates or rely on textual priors rather than visual evidence. We formulate answer-level selective prediction for quantitative physical reasoning and propose Answer-Level Trust Selection (ATS), a post-hoc, model-agnostic framework for accepting or rejecting individual VLM predictions. ATS requires no fine-tuning, auxiliary verifier, or access to the model's internal logits. Instead, it aggregates eight interpretable behavioral diagnostic scores derived from repeated queries and controlled interventions into a unified trust score. We evaluate ATS in depth on Qwen2.5-VL-7B and across 20 VLM backbones, examining selective performance, diagnostic behavior, and targeted failure modes. Our results show that intervention-based diagnostics help identify stable-but-wrong and prior-tracking predictions that repeated agreement alone may miss. However, improved failure-case rejection can come at the cost of lower retention of correct predictions. ATS therefore complements model-level capability evaluation with answer-level reliability assessment for quantitative VLM predictions. Code will be released upon publication.

AI.tldr: Post-hoc, model-agnostic Answer-Level Trust Selection (ATS) for selective prediction in quantitative visual reasoning. It aggregates eight intervention-based diagnostic scores into a unified trust score to accept/reject individual VLM outputs without fine-tuning or access to logits.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks judge overall accuracy; in deployment, trusted per-answer predictions are needed when ground truth is unavailable. Self-consistency alone can miss failure modes such as stable-but-wrong predictions or priors.
AI.method: ATS uses repeated queries and controlled interventions to derive eight interpretable diagnostic scores, which are fused into a single trust score. It is post-hoc, model-agnostic, requires no fine-tuning, auxiliary verifier, or internal logits access.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on Qwen2.5-VL-7B across 20 VLM backbones shows ATS can detect stable-but-wrong and priors that simple agreement miss; however, increased rejection can reduce retention of correct predictions, highlighting a trade-off.
AI.conclusion: ATS complements model-level capability checks by enabling answer-level reliability assessment for quantitative VLM predictions, offering a practical, ready-to-deploy trust mechanism; code will be released.

title: Coupled Optimal Transport with Landmark Constraints
summary: Existing optimal transport (OT) models primarily seek an OT map or plan between distributions by minimizing a prescribed transport cost or distortion. However, minimizing transport cost or distortion alone may fail to identify a geometrically meaningful transformation between the two distributions. To address this limitation, this paper proposes a novel coupled OT framework that leverages a small number of annotated landmarks to guide the recovery of an underlying deformation governing the distribution transformation. The coupled OT framework integrates the optimization of the transport plan and the deformation field into a unified model, where the landmark-guided deformation field and the cost-driven transport plan are coupled through a mutual-consistency constraint. As a result, the deformation is jointly determined by the annotated landmarks and cost-driven distribution matching. The proposed framework provides a principled connection between landmark-based registration and transport-based distribution matching, enabling the recovery of transport maps from sparse geometric supervision. We establish the well-definedness of the proposed model in a general variational setting and develop a finite-element-based numerical algorithm for computation whose convergence properties are systematically analyzed. The practical effectiveness of the proposed approach is verified in shape matching.

AI.tldr: A landmark-guided, coupled optimal transport framework jointly learning transport plans and a deformation field from sparse geometric supervision (landmarks), with a variational formulation and finite-element solver; proven well-posedness and convergent numerics; validated on shape matching.
AI.motivation: OT models often focus on minimizing transport cost or distortion, which can miss geometrically meaningful transformations. Incorporating sparse landmark supervision can guide the deformation to reflect true geometry, bridging registration and distribution matching.
AI.method: Introduce a coupled OT model where the transport plan and an underlying deformation field are optimized jointly under a mutual-consistency constraint with landmark guidance. Formulate as a variational problem with regularization on deformation and transport costs; discretize with finite elements and develop a solver; provide convergence analysis for the algorithm.
AI.result: The approach yields a well-defined model in a general variational setting, with a finite-element-based numerical algorithm whose convergence properties are analyzed. Empirically effective for shape matching, demonstrating the ability to recover transport maps using sparse supervision.
AI.conclusion: The framework links landmark-based registration and transport-based distribution matching, enabling recovery of transport maps from limited geometric supervision and providing a principled route to geometry-aware OT.

title: Write Once, Run Everywhere: The Axon DSL for Shape-Safe and Framework-Agnostic LLM Architectures
summary: The entire ecosystem of open-source language models effectively relies on a single platform. What if this platform was forced to shut down tomorrow? Implementing and maintaining efficient model definitions and translating them between different training and inference regimes is a resource-heavy task that severely limits model efficiency and portability, hindering both scaling and deployment. Here, we present Axon, a strongly typed domain-specific language with Haskell-like syntax, that enables a write-once, run everywhere paradigm for LLM architectures. By basing collaboration on a language specification rather than a specific framework's vision, Axon fosters open cooperation and empowers researchers to implement highly specialized architectures without giving up optimization infrastructure or accepting deployment lock-in. Axon allows for concise, auditable specifications that can be automatically compiled to standalone implementations for leading frameworks: PyTorch, PyTorch with Triton, JAX, MLX and vLLM. In 467 inference benchmarking experiments on models ranging from 135M to 32B parameters, we demonstrate median speedups of 7% on PyTorch, 12% on PyTorch with Triton, 91% on JAX, and 107% on MLX, compared to the reference implementations from Transformers. When deployed as native vLLM architectures with PagedAttention and KV-cache, Axon models achieve a 58% median speedup over Transformers implementations.

AI.tldr: Axon: a strongly typed DSL (Haskell-like syntax) enabling a write-once, run-everywhere paradigm for LLM architectures, compiling to PyTorch, PyTorch+Triton, JAX, MLX, and vLLM. In 467 inference benchmarks across 135M–32B models, median speedups vs Transformers: 7% (PyTorch), 12% (PyTorch+Triton), 91% (JAX), 107% (MLX); with native vLLM architectures (PagedAttention & KV-cache) 58% faster.
AI.motivation: Single-platform dependence for LLMs creates bottlenecks, hindering efficiency, portability, and deployment; translating definitions across regimes is resource-intensive; a specification-driven approach can unlock openness and optimization parity without lock-in.
AI.method: Introduce Axon, a strongly typed DSL with Haskell-like syntax that specifies LLM architectures. It enables a write-once, run-everywhere workflow by compiling specifications to standalone implementations for multiple backends: PyTorch, PyTorch+Triton, JAX, MLX, and vLLM. Evaluation conducted via 467 inference benchmarks across model sizes 135M–32B, comparing against Transformers reference implementations; includes deployment with PagedAttention and KV-cache.
AI.result: Median speedups across backends: PyTorch 7%, PyTorch+Triton 12%, JAX 91%, MLX 107%; native vLLM architectures with PagedAttention & KV-cache yield 58% median speedup over Transformers.
AI.conclusion: A write-once, run-everywhere DSL enables framework-agnostic LLM deployment, fostering open collaboration and reducing deployment lock-in while delivering meaningful efficiency gains across multiple backends.

title: FAR-DPO: Feasibility-Aware and Robust Direct Preference Optimization for Cyclic Peptide Design
comment: 16 pages, 6 figures, and 7 tables. Includes supplementary materials
summary: Cyclic peptides are emerging as promising molecular scaffolds in drug discovery due to their high binding affinity and structural stability. However, extending generative models from linear to cyclic peptide design remains challenging, as cyclization sharply restricts the feasible design space through coupled geometric and biophysical constraints. Moreover, limited training data has led existing approaches to rely largely on zero-shot generation or post hoc filtering, resulting in low yields of feasible designs and limited control over multi-objective trade-offs. To address these limitations, we propose FAR-DPO (Feasibility-Aware and Robust Direct Preference Optimization), an architecture-agnostic framework that steers generative models toward structurally and biophysically feasible cyclic peptide designs, particularly for challenging targets. FAR-DPO integrates feasibility-aware preference construction with difficulty-aware group-robust optimization. Specifically, it constructs within-target preference pairs through feasibility-gated multi-objective dominance and adaptively reweights predefined difficulty groups according to their current preference losses. On the CPSea LNR benchmark, under a fixed generation budget, FAR-DPO increases overall success rate from 46.89% to 57.79% on PepGLAD and from 47.96% to 49.57% on PepFlow. These gains also extend to the hardest target quartile and are accompanied by more favorable best-per-target binding scores. Together, these results demonstrate FAR-DPO's effectiveness in improving feasibility and target-wise robustness.

AI.tldr: FAR-DPO is a feasibility-aware, architecture-agnostic framework that guides cyclic peptide generative models toward structurally and biophysically feasible designs using feasibility-gated dominance and difficulty-aware reweighting, improving feasibility and target-wise robustness on CPSea LNR benchmarks (PepGLAD and PepFlow).
AI.motivation: Cyclic peptide design faces a restricted design space due to cyclization constraints and limited training data, leading to low feasible yields and poor control over multi-objective trade-offs.
AI.method: FAR-DPO integrates feasibility-aware preference construction with difficulty-aware group-robust optimization: it builds within-target preference pairs via feasibility-gated multi-objective dominance and adaptively reweights predefined difficulty groups based on current preference losses; architecture-agnostic.
AI.result: With a fixed generation budget on CPSea LNR, FAR-DPO increases overall success rate from 46.89% to 57.79% for PepGLAD and from 47.96% to 49.57% for PepFlow; gains extend to the hardest target quartile and are accompanied by more favorable best-per-target binding scores.
AI.conclusion: FAR-DPO effectively improves feasibility and target-wise robustness in cyclic peptide design and shows strong performance on challenging targets.

title: Core-KAN: Continuous Vision Kernels with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks
summary: Conventional convolutional kernels are typically defined on fixed discrete grids, limiting their ability to accommodate heterogeneous local structures. Existing adaptive operators improve flexibility but often couple geometric scale variation with content-dependent filtering, while incurring high computational cost from per-location kernel generation. To decouple geometric scale adaptation from content-dependent filtering while avoiding expensive per-location kernel generation, we propose Continuous Relative-scale KAN (Core-KAN), a relative-scale-conditioned continuous convolution operator. Core-KAN maps input features into a compact latent basis space and uses a lightweight scale controller to predict local scales relative to an exponential moving average reference. A KAN-based generator represents depth-wise kernel bases as continuous coordinate functions, allowing the operator to synthesize spatial filters at arbitrary resolutions rather than being confined to a fixed lattice. Instead of synthesizing independent kernels at every location, it constructs a compact bank of scale-conditioned kernel responses and interpolates them according to the predicted local scale map. An independent mixing controller further combines the interpolated basis responses based on local content, explicitly decoupling geometric scale adaptation from content-dependent filtering. Together with lightweight pointwise projections, this design forms a low-rank dynamic convolution that scales efficiently with kernel size and integrates readily into hierarchical vision backbones. Experiments across three representative vision tasks show Core-KAN consistently outperforms strong convolutional and dynamic-kernel baselines with only marginal parameter and computational overhead, offering an efficient, general framework for continuous, scale-adaptive convolution.

AI.tldr: Core-KAN introduces a continuous, scale-aware depthwise convolution that decouples geometry from content filtering by using a KAN-based continuous kernel generator and a scale mixer, enabling arbitrary-resolution filters with low overhead and improving performance across three vision tasks.
AI.motivation: Fixed-grid convolutions limit adaptability to heterogeneous local structures; existing adaptive operators either couple scale with content or incur high per-location kernel costs. A decoupled, efficient scale-adaptive convolution is desired that can operate at multiple resolutions without per-location kernel synthesis.
AI.method: Map inputs into a compact latent basis space; use a lightweight scale controller to predict local scales relative to an EMA reference; represent depthwise kernel bases as continuous coordinate functions via a KAN-based generator; synthesize spatial filters at arbitrary resolutions; build a compact bank of scale-conditioned kernel responses and interpolate according to the predicted local scale; employ an independent mixing controller to combine interpolated basis responses based on local content; apply lightweight pointwise projections to form a low-rank dynamic convolution and integrate into hierarchical vision backbones.
AI.result: Empirical results on three representative vision tasks show Core-KAN consistently outperforms strong convolutional and dynamic-kernel baselines with only marginal increases in parameters and computation.
AI.conclusion: Core-KAN provides an efficient, general framework for continuous, scale-adaptive convolution that decouples geometric scale adaptation from content-dependent filtering and integrates readily into standard vision backbones while achieving superior performance.

title: EXIMO: VLM Guided Exploration of VLA Policies
summary: How to efficiently finetune robot policies to learn new tasks on the fly? State of the art robotic manipulation policies are based on behaviour cloning of large vision-language-action (VLA) models with billions of parameters on huge teleoperation datasets. While this simple approach has enabled significant advances for robotic manipulation, finetuning of VLA policies for learning new tasks still remains an open problem. In particular, collecting teleoperation datasets requires hundreds of hours of expensive human labour and the alternative, reinforcement learning (RL), can be notoriously sample-inefficient especially for long-horizon tasks. In addition, RL with VLAs imposes several challenges due to the model's size and architectural design. In this work, we propose EXIMO, an efficient algorithm for finetuning of VLA policies. EXIMO operates in three stages: explore, imitate, and optimize. During the explore phase, EXIMO equips the VLA with a vision language model (VLM) that acts as a planner. The VLM thinks and breaks down challenging long-horizon problems into shorter ones for the VLA. The VLM, together with the VLA, is used to collect an orchestrated dataset on new tasks. During the imitate phase, the VLA is finetuned with the orchestrated data. Finally, during the optimize stage, we use residual off-policy RL to further finetune the policy. In our experiments, we ablate all three stages of EXIMO and show that it outperforms existing approaches significantly in terms of sample-efficiency and final performance.

AI.tldr: EXIMO is a three-stage fine-tuning framework for VLA policies in robotic manipulation: Explore (VLM-based planning and data collection), Imitate (finetuning on orchestrated data), and Optimize (residual off-policy RL). It achieves improved sample efficiency and final performance over baselines.
AI.motivation: Current state-of-the-art uses large vision-language-action models trained on teleoperation data, but collecting such data is expensive and RL is sample-inefficient for long-horizon tasks. RL with VLAs is also challenging due to model size. EXIMO aims to reduce data and compute requirements while maintaining performance.
AI.method: Three-stage pipeline: Explore – equip the VLA with a vision-language model as a planner to break long-horizon tasks into shorter subtasks and collect an orchestrated dataset with the VLM+VLA; Imitate – finetune the VLA on the orchestrated data; Optimize – apply residual off-policy RL to further refine the policy.
AI.result: Ablation studies show exam stages contribute; overall EXIMO outperforms existing approaches in both sample-efficiency and final performance on the targeted tasks.
AI.conclusion: EXIMO offers a practical, data-efficient framework for adapting VLA policies to new tasks by combining planning, imitation, and RL refinement, reducing data requirements while achieving strong performance.

title: Adaptive Probabilistic Shielding by Learning MDPs for Safe Reinforcement Learning
comment: 19 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. To be published in the proceedings of RV 2026
summary: Probabilistic shielding is a technique for safe reinforcement learning (RL). Typically, a static observer -- called the shield -- constrains the learning agent's actions to those for which acting safely remains feasible. Traditionally, the shield is computed from the transition probabilities of the underlying Markov decision process (MDP). Thus, this technique is not applicable when the MDP model is not given a priori, which, unfortunately, is the case in typical RL applications. In this paper, we study the problem of computing a shield in the setting where the transition graph of the MDP is known, but the transition probabilities are unknown. Our approach integrates probabilistic shielding with online model learning: as the RL agent explores the environment, we estimate the transition probabilities. From this estimate, we compute a shield. While the shield may be conservative initially, it adapts as the model estimate becomes more precise. Thus, the shield improves in tandem with the RL agent. This paradigm of adaptive probabilistic shielding raises a number of challenges, such as when to recompute the shield and how to balance between exploration and safety during learning. We empirically evaluate multiple variants of this paradigm across several environments.

AI.tldr: Adaptive probabilistic shielding for safe RL with unknown transition probabilities but known transition graph; online learning estimates probabilities and recomputes the shield to align safety with learning progress.
AI.motivation: Traditional shields rely on full knowledge of the MDP probabilities; in many RL settings the model is unknown. An adaptive shield that learns as the agent explores can enable safe exploration despite uncertainty.
AI.method: Interactively estimate transition probabilities from experience, compute a shield from the current estimate, and adaptively decide when to recompute the shield and how to balance exploration versus safety.
AI.result: Preliminary empirical evaluation across multiple environments suggesting the adaptive shield is feasible and can become less conservative as the model estimate improves; performance depends on recomputation strategy.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive shielding that co-evolves with the RL agent is viable and beneficial for safety; key future work includes formalizing safety guarantees, optimizing shield update schedules, and assessing scalability.

title: DECOWAM: Decoupled Whole-Body World-Action Model for Legged Mobile Manipulation
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures. Introduces DECOWAM, a decoupled whole-body world-action model for legged mobile manipulation, and the ARMDOG real-robot dataset
summary: Mobile manipulation requires a robot to predict how locomotion and arm motion jointly alter future observations and control. Existing world-action models, developed largely for fixed-base platforms, do not explicitly distinguish camera ego-motion from base and arm actions. Here we introduce DECOWAM, a whole-body world-action model that separates these factors through dedicated conditional interfaces. DECOWAM freezes an adapted FastWAM backbone and trains residual adapters, an action-equivalent future bottleneck distilled from privileged observations, adversarially separated base and arm latents, and base-velocity conditioning for video prediction. We further introduce ARMDOG, a real-robot dataset that synchronizes video, whole-body state and action, and language. On a fixed replay protocol, DECOWAM improved both future-video and action prediction over FastWAM, reducing action MSE by 21.7% with 25.95M trainable adaptation parameters. Across 79 closed-loop trials per method, it achieved the highest observed whole-body coordination and base-displacement robustness among the compared systems, while task completion remained comparable to the strongest baseline. These results show that embodiment-aware factorization can support parameter-efficient joint visual prediction and whole-body control under moving viewpoints.

AI.tldr: DECOWAM introduces embodiment-aware factorization in a world-action model by separating ego-camera motion from base and arm actions; it uses residual adapters on a frozen FastWAM backbone and an action-equivalent bottleneck, achieving improved future-video and action prediction with 25.95M trainable parameters, and ARMDOG validates real-robot performance with robust whole-body coordination.
AI.motivation: Existing world-action models are designed for fixed-base platforms and do not disentangle ego-motion (camera) from base/arm actions, leading to degraded predictions under moving viewpoints.
AI.method: Freeze an adapted FastWAM backbone and train residual adapters; learn an action-equivalent future bottleneck distilled from privileged observations; adversarially separate base and arm latent representations; condition video prediction on base velocity; use the ARMDOG real-robot dataset to synchronize video, full-body state and actions, plus language.
AI.result: Under a fixed replay protocol, DECOWAM improved future-video and action prediction relative to FastWAM, decreasing action MSE by 21.7%. Across 79 closed-loop trials per method, it showed the strongest whole-body coordination and base-displacement robustness among the compared systems, with task completion remaining comparable to the best baseline.
AI.conclusion: Embodiment-aware factorization enables parameter-efficient joint visual prediction and whole-body control under moving viewpoints.

title: Towards Clinically Faithful Medical Image Captioning via Enhanced Vision-Language Alignment
comment: 10 pages, 2 figures, 7 tables. Preprint submitted to IEEE for possible publication
summary: Medical image captioning is a technique that accelerates early-stage diagnostic workflows and enhances the interpretability of medical diagnostic AI systems. However, unlike general image captioning, clinically reliable captioning remains challenging due to grayscale-based modalities, subtle anatomical cues, specialized medical phrasing, and variations in data quality. Despite recent advances in large vision-language models, fluent outputs do not necessarily guarantee sufficient alignment with clinical concept spaces or evaluation criteria. To address this issue, we propose a framework that strengthens clinical alignment by separating and enhancing training-time alignment and inference-time alignment. We build a medical image captioning pipeline that integrates single/dual vision encoders based on BioMedCLIP and SigLIP2, a Q-Former, and a LLaMA-based decoder, and examine the contribution of auxiliary learning for UMLS concept/type prediction. At inference, we apply single-embedding-based reranking to select the best caption among candidates, while at training we introduce MedPAIR-SCST, which combines clinically relevant rewards to shift the generative distribution toward improved clinical alignment. Our experiments show that complementary visual representations with a multi-encoder design and concept-level auxiliary learning help preserve clinically meaningful information. Furthermore, inference-time reranking provides a practical way to improve semantic and clinical alignment without additional training, whereas MedPAIR-SCST goes beyond selection by directly improving the model's distribution to generate more consistent and clinically grounded captions. These findings suggest that jointly leveraging selection-based alignment and reinforcement-learning-based alignment can promote more trustworthy medical image captioning even in data-constrained settings.

AI.tldr: Proposes MedPAIR-SCST framework for medical image captioning with a multi-encoder architecture and inference-time reranking, separating training-time and inference-time alignment to improve clinical alignment under data constraints.
AI.motivation: Clinical image captioning remains challenging due to grayscale modalities, subtle anatomical cues, specialized phrasing, and variable data quality; fluent outputs from large models do not guarantee alignment with clinical concepts or evaluation criteria.
AI.method: A medical image captioning pipeline with single/dual vision encoders (BioMedCLIP, SigLIP2), a Q-Former, and a LLaMA-based decoder. Introduces MedPAIR-SCST for training-time alignment via clinically relevant rewards and auxiliary UMLS concept/type prediction; uses inference-time single-embedding-based reranking to select best captions.
AI.result: Demonstrates that complementary visual representations with multi-encoder design and concept-level auxiliary learning preserve clinically meaningful information; inference-time reranking improves semantic/clinical alignment without extra training; MedPAIR-SCST shifts the model distribution to generate more clinically grounded captions; jointly leveraging selection- and reinforcement-learning-based alignment improves trustworthy captioning in data-constrained settings.
AI.conclusion: Separating and combining training-time alignment with inference-time alignment yields more clinically aligned captions; data-constrained medical image captioning benefits from using both reranking and reinforcement-learning-based distribution shaping.

title: Bringing analytic rigor to agentic AI for science: The Brain Researcher platform for neuroimaging data analysis
summary: AI agents can execute scientific analyses, but an analytic output becomes a defensible claim only after alternatives are weighed and the claim is limited to what the evidence supports. Agents may reproduce failures including selective analysis, premature declarations of success and optimization of imperfect criteria. We present Brain Researcher, an agentic research harness operating in a neuroimaging researcher's computational environment under rules for admissible analyses, required checks and claim scope. In benchmarks, Brain Researcher increased first-choice tool-selection accuracy across seven models by 70.2 percentage points (23.3% without it versus 93.6% with it) and verifiable grounding from 4.6% to 22.0%. In collaborator-led and self-evolving studies, multiverse analyses exposed analytic-choice sensitivity, and scientific review classified claims as accepted, qualified, revised, blocked, rejected or deferred. By linking decisions to evidence and provenance, Brain Researcher embeds methodological judgment within the workflow, not after it.

AI.tldr: Agentic neuroimaging research harness that embeds admissible analyses and evidentiary provenance, improving tool-choice accuracy and grounding, and enabling multiverse analyses for transparent claims.
AI.motivation: To curb analytic bias and ensure defensible claims by enforcing checks, provenance, and scope within the research workflow.
AI.method: Develop Brain Researcher, an agent operating in a neuroimaging workflow with rules for admissible analyses, required checks, and claim scope; employ multiverse analyses; support collaborator-led and self-evolving studies; evaluate via first-choice tool-selection accuracy and verifiable grounding; classify claims through scientific review.
AI.result: Quantitative gains: first-choice tool-selection accuracy increased by 70.2 percentage points (23.3% without it vs 93.6% with it); verifiable grounding rose from 4.6% to 22.0%. Multiverse analyses reveal analytic-choice sensitivity; scientific reviews classify claims as accepted, qualified, revised, blocked, rejected, or deferred.
AI.conclusion: Integrating methodological judgment into the research workflow enhances reproducibility and defensible conclusions in neuroimaging analyses.

title: Inadvertent Context Leakage in Language Models
summary:
For AI agents to be useful beyond simple chat, they must hold sensitive user context such as calendars, credentials, health records, and financial data.
